     THE MODEL THEORY OF

CERTAIN INFINITE SOLUBLE GROUPS




          ELIZABETH WHARTON

            ST HUGH’S COLLEGE




     A dissertation submitted for the degree of

               Doctor of Philosophy


               University of Oxford

                   Hilary 2006
      The model theory of certain infinite soluble groups

                                      Elizabeth Wharton

                            St Hugh’s College, University of Oxford

                        A dissertation submitted for the degree of

                                     Doctor of Philosophy

                                         Hilary 2006


This thesis is concerned with aspects of the model theory of inﬁnite soluble groups. The

results proved lie on the border between group theory and model theory: the questions

asked are of a model-theoretic nature but the techniques used are mainly group-theoretic

in character.

   We present a characterization of those groups contained in the universal closure of a

restricted wreath product U wr G, where U is an abelian group of zero or ﬁnite square-free

exponent and G is a torsion-free soluble group with a bound on the class of its nilpotent

subgroups. For certain choices of G we are able to use this characterization to prove

further results about these groups; in particular, results related to the decidability of

their universal theories.

   The latter part of this work consists of a number of independent but related topics.

   We show that if G is a ﬁnitely generated abelian-by-metanilpotent group and H

is elementarily equivalent to G then the subgroups γn (G) and γn (H) are elementarily

equivalent, as are the quotient groups G/γn (G) and G/γn (H).

   We go on to consider those groups universally equivalent to F2 (VNc ), where the

free groups of the variety V are residually ﬁnite p-groups for inﬁnitely many primes p,

distinguishing between the cases when c = 1 and when c ⩾ 2.

   Finally, we address some important questions concerning the theories of free groups

in product varieties Vk · · · V1 , where Vi is a nilpotent variety whose free groups are

torsion-free; in particular we address questions about the decidability of the elementary

and universal theories of such groups. Results mentioned in both of the previous two

paragraphs have applications here.

    Part I

INTRODUCTION
    AND
BACKGROUND
                                       Chapter 1


                                INTRODUCTION



This thesis is concerned with aspects of the model theory of inﬁnite soluble groups. We

will give a characterization of those groups contained in the universal closure of a restricted

wreath product U wr G, where U is an abelian group of zero or ﬁnite square-free exponent

and G is a torsion-free soluble group satisfying certain conditions. For certain choices of

G we are able to use this characterization to prove further results about these groups.

We will also address some important questions concerning the theories of free groups in

product varieties Vk · · · V1 , where each Vi is a nilpotent variety whose free groups are

torsion-free; in particular, we consider questions about the decidability of the elementary

and universal theories of such groups. These results have close links with a number of

major model-theoretic problems.

   We begin with a discussion of these model-theoretic questions, which include some

of the most signiﬁcant mathematical problems of the twentieth century; in particular

Hilbert’s Tenth Problem, which took seventy years to be answered and the extensions of

which are taxing mathematicians to this day: there is still no consensus on whether the

version of Hilbert’s Tenth Problem for the rational numbers has a positive or a negative

answer. Another major set of problems which we discuss are those posed by Tarski in the

1940s which gave rise to the brand new subject of algebraic geometry over groups.

   The results proved in this work lie on the border between group theory and model

theory. The techniques used are mainly group-theoretic in character but the questions

asked are of a model-theoretic nature and there is much model-theoretic notation and

terminology. In order to make this thesis more accessible to group theorists with little




                                            –2–
knowledge of model theory and to model theorists with little knowledge of group theory,

we include a brief introduction to each of these subjects, with particular reference to those

areas of relevance to the content of the thesis. A list of notation used in this thesis can

be found in the front matter together with a page reference guiding the reader to where

this notation is explained in more detail. For coverage of the group-theoretic topics in

greater depth see Robinson’s book [53] and for coverage of the model-theoretic topics in

greater depth see the book by Chang and Keisler [10].

   We ﬁnish the introduction with an overview of our main results and an outline of the

content of each chapter.



1.1     Background

Motivation for our work is provided by two very natural and long-standing problems

relating to the elementary theory of groups, which were posed by Tarski in the 1940s and

which were open until recently.

   • Do free groups of distinct ranks have distinct elementary theories?

   • Is the elementary theory of a free group decidable?

   It is clear that the free group of rank 0 can be distinguished from those of higher rank

by the sentence

                                        ∀x (x = 1),

and that the free group of rank 1 can be distinguished by the sentence


                                      ∀xy ([x, y] = 1).


However there is no obvious sentence which allows us to diﬀerentiate between the free

group of rank 2 and the free group of rank 3.

   Eﬀorts to solve these questions have led to a wide variety of interesting results. In

particular, the whole theory of equations over groups grew out of the following question,

posed by Vaught to test the elementary equivalence of free groups: does the sentence

                                                              
                              ∀xyz x2 y 2 z 2 = 1 → xy = yx


                                           –3–
hold in all free groups? This question was answered in the aﬃrmative by Lyndon [29]

using a combinatorial argument to show that the only solutions of the equation x2 y 2 z 2 = 1

in a free group occur when x, y and z are powers of a common element. It was later shown

by Lyndon and Schützenberger [30], again using combinatorial methods, that if elements

x, y and z of a free group satisfy the equation xm y n z p = 1 with m, n, p ⩾ 2 then hx, y, zi

is cyclic. Since the inception of this subject, sets of solutions of equations over groups

have been studied extensively.

   Signiﬁcant progress towards an answer to Tarski’s questions was made by Makanin

who showed that the universal and positive theories of a free group are decidable [36]. He

also constructed an algorithm which determines whether a system of equations over a free

group has a solution [35]. The development by Baumslag, Myasnikov and Remeslennikov

of algebraic geometry over groups [7] made possible further progress and, using techniques

from this blossoming subject, Kharlampovich and Myasnikov [23] and Sela [58] have

addressed these questions.

   It is natural to consider the corresponding questions for relatively free groups. It was

shown by Szmielew [63] that free abelian groups of distinct ﬁnite ranks are not elementarily

equivalent: consider, for example, the sentence


                    ∃xy∀z∃u (u2 = z ∨ u2 = zx ∨ u2 = zy ∨ u2 = zxy).


Tarski observed that this sentence singles out the free abelian group of rank 2 from

the free abelian groups of higher rank. It is also the case that free nilpotent groups of

diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks have diﬀerent elementary theories: this was proved by Oger [45]

using an argument involving ultrapowers. In [54], Rogers, Smith and Solitar show that

free nilpotent groups of diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks have diﬀerent ∀∃∀-positive theories. To this

end they construct positive universal sentences s(n, c) such that if F is a free nilpotent
                                                             c
                                                             X
group of class c and rank r then F |= s(n, c) if and only if   w(r, i) < n, where w(r, i) is
                                                               i=1
the number of basic commutators of weight i. They show also that free soluble groups of

diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks have diﬀerent ∀∃∀-positive theories: using the fact that the last non-

trivial term of the derived series of a free soluble group is self-centralizing, they construct a

positive universal formula deﬁning this subgroup. In [13], Chapuis uses Szmeliew’s result



                                             –4–
about free abelian groups to show that free soluble groups of diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks have

diﬀerent ∀∃-theories by constructing existential formulae deﬁning terms of the derived

series. He comments that it is possible to strengthen this result for free soluble groups

of derived length at most 3. In this case, groups of diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks have diﬀerent

∀∃-positive theories. Lawrence [26] shows that free groups of diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks in

a soluble variety have diﬀerent ∀∃∀-positive theories: he constructs a normal subgroup

which contains the derived subgroup and which is deﬁnable by a positive universal formula.

Work in Chapter 10 will extend the results of Chapuis to free groups in product varieties

Vk · · · V1 , where each Vi is a nilpotent variety whose free groups are torsion-free. We

note also that it follows from a result of Timoshenko [66, Theorem 1] that all non-cyclic

free soluble groups have the same universal theory as do all free nilpotent groups of class

c and rank at least c.

   The question of the decidability of the theories of relatively free groups has close

links to one of the big mathematical questions of the twentieth century. Hilbert’s Tenth

Problem:


     Determination of the solvability of a diophantine equation.

           Given a diophantine equation with any number of unknown quantities and

     with rational integral numerical coeﬃcients: To devise a process according

     to which it can be determined by a finite number of operations whether the

     equation is solvable in rational integers.


   This problem was posed by Hilbert at the Second International Congress of Mathe-

maticians in 1900 (his speech is translated into English in [20]) and it was not until 1970

that Matijasevich [39] showed that no such process exists. The analogous problem over

the ﬁeld Q of rational numbers is a major open problem. Many of the results in this area

seem to point to the answer being a negative one, as over the ring of integers. However a

number of mathematicians (mainly number theorists) conjecture a positive answer. For

a more general and recent discussion of Hilbert’s Tenth Problem see [48].

   The elementary theory of a free abelian group is decidable [63]. However, as soon

as we move away from abelian groups, things become more diﬃcult. For example, the



                                           –5–
elementary theory of a ﬁnitely generated non-abelian free nilpotent group is undecidable

[38]: this is proved by obtaining an interpretation of the ring of integers in a non-cyclic

free nilpotent group of class 2, and the result then follows from the undecidability of

the elementary theory of the ring of integers [64]. It is not known whether the universal

theory of a non-cyclic free nilpotent group is decidable. In [55], Roman′ kov showed that

the decidability of the universal theory of the free nilpotent group of class and rank 2 would

imply the decidability of the universal theory of the ﬁeld of rationals. The problem of the

decidability of the universal theory of Q is equivalent to Hilbert’s Tenth Problem over Q.

Roman′ kov’s proof uses the fact that a free nilpotent group is universally equivalent to

its Q-completion: he associates to each universal sentence φ in the language of ﬁelds a

universal sentence φ′ in the language of groups such that φ holds in Q if and only if φ′

holds in the Q-completion of the free nilpotent group of class and rank 2.

   In [37], Mal′ cev proves that the elementary theory of a non-abelian free soluble group

is undecidable. He uses the deﬁnability of the terms of the derived series to interpret

the ring of integers in a non-abelian ﬁnitely generated free soluble group. His proof

involves formulae with two constant symbols representing free generators. Chapuis [13]

strengthens this result to give good bounds on the number of quantiﬁers: he shows that a

non-abelian free soluble group F has undecidable ∀∃-theory with no constants. Chapuis

gives an algorithm which associates to each polynomial P (X) in several variables with

coeﬃcients in Z, a ∀∃-sentence ψ such that P (X) has a zero in Z if and only if F |= ψ.

The negative answer to Hilbert’s Tenth Problem over the integers [39] then gives the

required result. Chapuis showed in [11] that the universal theory of a free metabelian

group is decidable. As for nilpotent groups, it is unknown whether the universal theory

of a non-cyclic free soluble group of derived length at least 3 is decidable. Using similar

techniques to those above, Chapuis showed in [13] that the decidability of the universal

theory of a non-cyclic free soluble group of derived length at least 3 would imply that there

exists an algorithm to determine whether a homogeneous polynomial in several variables

with coeﬃcients in Z has a non-trivial zero in Z. It is well known that such an algorithm

exists if and only if the universal theory of the ﬁeld of rationals is decidable [48, §9]. In

Chapter 10, we extend these results about the decidability of elementary and universal



                                            –6–
theories to free groups in product varieties Vk · · · V1 , where each Vi is a nilpotent variety

whose free groups are torsion-free.

    During a problem day held at the First All-Union Symposium on Group Theory at

Kourovka the following two problems were posed by Kargapolov [41, Problems 1.26 and

1.27]:

   • Describe the universal theory of free groups.

   • Describe the universal theory of free nilpotent groups of class n.

The ﬁrst problem is still open. Makanin’s work towards the second Tarski problem shows

that the universal theory of a free group is decidable. Steps towards deriving an explicit

description of the universal theory have been taken by Remeslennikov who gave a cha-

racterization of those groups with the same universal theory as a non-cyclic free group

[49], [50]. The links between the decidability of the universal theory of a non-abelian free

nilpotent group and Hilbert’s Tenth Problem over the rationals, as discussed above, indi-

cate that the second problem is very diﬃcult. However there are varieties where progress

can be made on questions of this type.

    A group G is in the universal closure of a free abelian group F if and only if it is

torsion-free and abelian. It is easy to write down a collection of universal sentences U

such that G is in the universal closure of F if and only if G satisﬁes the sentences U. We

can, for example, take the collection of sentences


                 U = {∀xy ([x, y] = 1)} ∪ {∀x (xn = 1 → x = 1) | n ∈ N} .


    In [12] Chapuis gives an explicit description of the universal theory of a non-cyclic

free metabelian group and of those groups in its universal closure. These are precisely

those groups such that a ﬁnitely generated subgroup can be embedded in a restricted

wreath product Z(r) wr Z(s) for some non-negative integers r and s. Work in Part II

provides similar descriptions in the case of restricted wreath products U wr G, where U

is an abelian group of zero or ﬁnite square-free exponent and G is a torsion-free soluble

group satisfying certain conditions.




                                            –7–
1.2    A brief introduction to group theory

Throughout this section let G be a group. The order of an element g ∈ G, denoted by

o(g), is the order of the cyclic subgroup generated by g. The group G is periodic if every

element g ∈ G has ﬁnite order. For a prime p, the group G is p-group if every element

of G has order some power of p. The exponent of G is the least positive integer n such

that gn = 1 for all g ∈ G, if such an integer exists. If every non-trivial element of G has

inﬁnite order then G is torsion-free. We say that a torsion-free group has exponent zero.

We denote by Cn the cyclic group of exponent n for any non-negative integer n.

   The group G is an extension of a group A by a group H if G has a normal subgroup

N such that N ∼
              = A and G/N ∼
                          = H. Let P and Q be properties of groups. The group
G is a P-by-Q group if G is an extension of a group with property P by a group with

property Q.

   For g, h ∈ G, the conjugate of g by h is the element gh := h−1 gh. Let G and H

be groups such that G acts on H by conjugation. The semi-direct product of H by G,

denoted by H ⋊ G, is the set of ordered pairs G × H with multiplication deﬁned by


                               (g1 , h1 )(g2 , h2 ) = (g1 g2 , hg11 h2 ).


   For g, h ∈ G, the commutator of g and h is the element [g, h] := g−1 h−1 gh and we use

the left-normed convention for commutators. We deﬁne a simple commutator of weight n

recursively by the rule

                              [g1 , . . . , gn ] := [[g1 , . . . , gn−1 ], gn ],

where g1 , . . . , gn are elements of G. If X and Y are subsets of G then we deﬁne the

commutator subgroup of X and Y , denoted by [X, Y ], to be the subgroup of G generated

by all commutators [x, y] with x ∈ X, y ∈ Y . The derived subgroup of G is the subgroup

G′ := [G, G]. The group G is abelian if and only if G′ is trivial. The centre of G, denoted

by Z(G), is the normal subgroup of G deﬁned by


                          Z(G) := {g ∈ G | [g, h] = 1 for all h ∈ G}.




                                                   –8–
Soluble, nilpotent and polynilpotent groups

The group G is soluble if it has a subnormal series with abelian factors:

                              {1} = G0 ⊳ G1 ⊳ · · · ⊳ Gd = G

such that Gn /Gn−1 is abelian for n = 1, . . . , d. The length d of the shortest such series

in G is the derived length of G. We deﬁne the terms of the derived series of G, denoted

by G(n) for n ⩾ 0, as follows:

                             G(0) := G,

                             G(1) := G′ = [G, G],

                           G(n+1) := [G(n) , G(n) ]    for n ⩾ 1.

If G is soluble then this series reaches the trivial subgroup after ﬁnitely many steps. The

derived length of a soluble group G is equal to the length of the derived series of G. The

group G is metabelian if it is soluble of derived length 2.

   The group G is nilpotent if it has a normal series with central factors:

                              {1} = G0 ⩽ G1 ⩽ · · · ⩽ Gc = G

such that Gn ⊳ G and Gn /Gn−1 is in the centre of G/Gn−1 for n = 1, . . . , c. The length

c of the shortest such series is the nilpotent class of G. We deﬁne the terms of the lower

central series of G, denoted by γn (G) for n ⩾ 1, as follows:

                             γ1 (G) := G,

                           γn+1 (G) := [γn (G), G]     for n ⩾ 2.

We note that [γm (G), γn (G)] ⩽ γm+n (G) and that γm (γn (G)) ⩽ γmn (G) for all positive

integers m and n [53, 5.1.11]. We deﬁne the terms of the upper central series of G, denoted

by ζn (G) for n ⩾ 0, as follows:

                                   ζ0 (G) := {1},

                      ζn+1 (G)/ζn (G) := Z(G/ζn (G))          for n ⩾ 1.

If G is nilpotent then the lower central series reaches the trivial subgroup after ﬁnitely

many steps and the upper central series reaches the group G after ﬁnitely many steps;


                                              –9–
in this case the lower central series and the upper central series have the same length

and this length is equal to the nilpotent class of G. If G is nilpotent of class c then

γn (G) ⩽ ζc+1−n (G) for n = 1, . . . , c.

    The Fitting subgroup of G, denoted by Fitt(G), is the subgroup of G generated by

all the nilpotent normal subgroups of G. This subgroup may not be nilpotent but every

ﬁnitely generated subgroup of Fitt(G) is nilpotent.

    The group G is polynilpotent if it has a subnormal series with nilpotent factors:


                                 {1} = G0 ⊳ G1 ⊳ · · · ⊳ Gk = G


such that Gn /Gn−1 is nilpotent for n = 1, . . . , k. If Gn /Gn−1 is nilpotent of class at most

cn for n = 1, . . . , k then we say that G has class sequence at most c = (c1 , . . . , ck ). The

group G is metanilpotent if it is polynilpotent with class sequence (c1 , c2 ) for some c1 , c2 .


Free groups

A group F is free on a subset X if, for each function α : X → G, where G is any group,

there is a unique homomorphism β : F → G such that xβ = xα for all x ∈ X. A

group which is free on some set is an (absolutely) free group. If F is free on a set X of

cardinality n then F is free of rank n. The countably inﬁnite free group F∞ is free on the

set X∞ = {x1 , x2 , . . .}.

    A word w is an element of F∞ . A word w can be written uniquely as a string
                                −1 where X −1 = {x−1 , x−1 , . . .} with no occurrences of
w = y1 · · · yr with yi ∈ X∞ ∪ X∞         ∞       1     2

x−1          −1                                                 −1
 i xi or xi xi . A generator xj occurs in w if yi = xj or yi = xj for some i. If only the

generators x1 , . . . , xn occur in w then we say that w is a word in the variables x1 , . . . , xn

or a word in n-variables.



1.3      A brief introduction to first-order logic

First-order formulae in the language of groups Lgp := {· ,−1 , 1} are certain ﬁnite strings

consisting of the following symbols:

    • variables representing group elements;



                                              – 10 –
   • the symbols · ,−1 and 1 representing group multiplication, inverse and the identity

      element;

   • the equality symbol =;

   • the logical symbols → (“implies”), ∧ (“and”), ∨ (“or”), ¬ (“not”) and quantiﬁers

      ∀ (“for all”) and ∃ (“there exists”) ranging over all elements of G .

A ﬁrst-order formula is constructed in a speciﬁc way: an atomic formula in Lgp is of the

form w(x) = u(x) where w(x) and u(x) are words in variables x1 , . . . , xn and a formula

in Lgp is deﬁned recursively as follows:

   • an atomic formula is a formula;

   • if φ is a formula then ¬φ is a formula;

   • if φ and ψ are formulae then φ ∧ ψ, φ ∨ ψ and φ → ψ are formulae;

   • if φ is a formula then ∀xφ and ∃xφ are formulae for any variable x.

Abbreviations are permitted where the meaning is clear. We commonly use the following

abbreviations:

   • xy for x · y;

   • xn for |x · x{z· · · x} ;
                     n

   • xy for y −1 xy;

   • [x, y] for x−1 y −1 xy;

   • x 6= y for ¬(x = y).

   A formula is quantifier-free if it contains no occurrences of ∀ or ∃. A variable occurs

freely in a formula if it is not bound by a quantiﬁer. A sentence is a formula with no free

variables. For example,

   • the formula [x, y] = 1 ∧ z 7 = 1 is quantiﬁer-free;




                                           – 11 –
    • in the formula ∀y ([x, y] = 1), the variable y is bound by the quantiﬁer ∀ and the

       variable x occurs freely;

    • the formula ∃x∀y ([x, y] = 1) is a sentence.

If φ(x1 , . . . , xn ) is a formula in n free variables and g1 , . . . , gn are elements of a group G

then we write G |= φ(g1 , . . . , gn ) if φ(g1 , . . . , gn ) is true in G . If φ(x) is a formula in one

free variable then φ(x) deﬁnes the subset φ(G) of G where


                                   φ(G) := {g ∈ G | G |= φ(g)}.


For example, for any group G, the formula ∀x ([x, y] = 1) deﬁnes the centre of G.

    Sentences φ and ψ are logically equivalent if φ is true in a group G if and only if ψ

is true in G. A quantiﬁer-free formula in Lgp is in disjunctive normal form if it is of the

form
                                  s ^
                                  _ t
                                           (uij (x) = 1 ∧ vij (x) 6= 1),
                                 i=1 j=1

where uij (x) and vij (x) are words in the variables x1 , . . . , xr . Every quantiﬁer-free for-

mula is logically equivalent to one in disjunctive normal form. A formula in Lgp is in

prenex normal form if it consists of a string of quantiﬁers (possibly empty) followed by a

quantiﬁer-free formula in disjunctive normal form. Every ﬁrst-order formula is logically

equivalent to one in prenex normal form and every sentence in Lgp is logically equivalent

to one of the form
                                            s ^
                                           _ t                                
                       Q1 x1 . . . Qr xr           (uij (x) = 1 ∧ vij (x) 6= 1) ,
                                            i=1 j=1

where Qk is a quantiﬁer and uij (x) and vij (x) are words in the variables x1 , . . . , xr .

    The elementary theory of a group G, which we denote by Th(G), is the collection of

sentences which hold in G. Two groups G and H are elementarily equivalent if they have

the same elementary theory.


Universal and existential theory

A formula φ is universal (respectively existential) if the only quantiﬁer which occurs

when φ is written in prenex normal form is the universal quantiﬁer ∀ (respectively the


                                                  – 12 –
existential quantiﬁer ∃). A universal sentence in Lgp is logically equivalent to one of the

form
                                        s ^
                                       _ t                               
                        ∀x1 . . . xr          (uij (x) = 1 ∧ wij (x) 6= 1) ,
                                        i=1 j=1
and an existential sentence in Lgp is logically equivalent to one of the form
                                    s ^
                                   _  t                             
                      ∃x1 . . . xr       (uij (x) = 1 ∧ wij (x) 6= 1) ,
                                        i=1 j=1

where uij (x) and wij (x) are words in the variables x1 , . . . , xr .

    The universal (respectively existential) theory of a group G, denoted by Th∀ (G) (res-

pectively Th∃ (G)), is the collection of universal (respectively existential) sentences which

hold in G. A group G satisﬁes the universal theory of a group H if and only if H sa-

tisﬁes the existential theory of G. Two groups G and H are universally equivalent if

Th∀ (G) = Th∀ (H). The universal closure of a group G, denoted by ucl(G), is the class

of all groups which satisfy the universal theory of G:

                         ucl(G) := {H | H |= ψ for all ψ ∈ Th∀ (G)}.

Two groups G and H are existentially equivalent if Th∃ (G) = Th∃ (H). A group G is

existentially equivalent to a group H if and only if G is universally equivalent to H. If

H satisﬁes the universal theory and the existential theory of G then H is universally

equivalent to G.

    Other subsets of the elementary theory of a group are also of interest; in particular,

those subsets determined by the number of alternations of quantiﬁers allowed in the

sentences when in prenex normal form and those which contain no occurrences of the

negation symbol when in prenex normal form.

    A formula is a ∀∃-formula if, when written in prenex normal form, it consists of a

string of universal quantiﬁers, followed by a string of existential quantiﬁers, followed by

a quantiﬁer-free formula. A ∀∃-sentence in Lgp is logically equivalent to one of the form
                                                s ^
                                               _ t                             
               ∀x1 . . . xr1 ∃xr1 +1 . . . xr2      (uij (x) = 1 ∧ wij (x) 6= 1) ,
                                                  i=1 j=1

where uij (x) and wij (x) are group words in the variables x1 , . . . , xr2 . The ∀∃-theory of a

group G, denoted by Th∀∃ (G), is the collection of ∀∃-sentences which hold in G. We may

extend these deﬁnitions to arbitrarily many alternations of quantiﬁers.


                                                   – 13 –
   A formula is positive if it contains no occurrences of the negation symbol when written

in prenex normal form. A positive sentence in Lgp is logically equivalent to one of the

form
                                                 s ^
                                                _ t                  
                            Q1 x1 . . . Qr xr              uij (x) = 1 ,
                                                 i=1 j=1

where Qk is a quantiﬁer and uij (x) is a word in the variables x1 , . . . , xr . The positive

theory of a group G, denoted by Th+ (G), is the collection of positive sentences which

hold in G. We may combine the two concepts and consider the ∀∃-positive theory of a

group.

   Finally in this section we deﬁne a universal sentence which we will require in each of

the four subsequent chapters. We deﬁne φgp to be

                                                              
                       ∀xyz x(yz) = (xy)z ∧ 1x = x ∧ x−1 x = 1 .


This sentence ensures that the assignment of the constant and function symbols from the

language Lgp is consistent with the deﬁnition of a group.



1.4      Overview of thesis

In Chapter 2 we give a brief introduction to varieties of groups and recall some useful

results. These results include the link between residual properties and discrimination,

the Kaloujnine–Krasner, Magnus and Shmel′ kin embeddings, conditions for a subgroup

of a free group in a variety V to itself be free in V and information about the nilpotent

subgroups of a free group in a product variety satisfying certain conditions. We also

recall some known results about the universal theories of L-structures for a language L.

Although these results apply more generally, we formulate them speciﬁcally in the case

of groups as this is the situation in which we shall be applying them. Ultraproducts are

a useful tool in dealing with elementary classes of groups and we take this opportunity

to recall the deﬁnitions of ultraﬁlters, ultraproducts and ultrapowers and to state some

standard results.

   In Part II (Chapters 3 to 7) we consider the universal theory of restricted wreath

products of abelian groups by certain soluble groups.



                                                – 14 –
   In Chapter 3 we prove some preliminary results which we need in the subsequent

four chapters. These results split into two types: group-theoretic results about restricted

wreath products and results related to the universal theory of restricted wreath products.

Of the former type, Lemmas 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 will prove crucial in what follows.

Lemma 3.3.1. Let A and B be torsion-free groups and suppose that A is abelian. Let G

be a finitely generated group with a normal subgroup N such that N ∼
                                                                   = A and G/N ∼
                                                                               = B.
If Z[G/N ] is an Ore domain and N is torsion-free as a Z[G/N ]-module then G embeds

in U wr B, for some torsion-free abelian group U .

Lemma 3.3.2. Let A be an abelian group of finite square-free exponent n and let B be

a torsion-free group. Let G be a finitely generated group with a normal subgroup N such

that N ∼
       = A and G/N ∼
                   = B. For each prime divisor p of n, suppose that Fp [G/N ] is
an Ore domain and that the submodule of N of elements of order p is torsion-free as an

Fp [G/N ]-module. Then G embeds in U wr B, for some abelian group U of exponent n.

We begin the chapter by recalling the deﬁnitions of an integral domain and an Ore do-

main and some suﬃcient conditions for a group ring, over the integers or over a ﬁeld,

to be an Ore domain. The focus of the latter type of result is on showing that certain

restricted wreath products are universally equivalent. We note that an easy adaptation

of Timoshenko’s proof that the restricted wreath product preserves universal equivalence

yields the following result.

Lemma 3.4.1. Let A1 , A2 , B1 and B2 be groups. If A1 |= Th∀ (A2 ) and B1 |= Th∀ (B2 )

then A1 wr B1 |= Th∀ (A2 wr B2 ).

If A is a non-trivial torsion-free abelian group then A is universally equivalent to Z

by [16, Lemma 1]. Thus, if B1 and B2 are groups such that B1 |= Th∀ (B2 ), then

A wr B1 |= Th∀ (Z wr B2 ). If the group A has ﬁnite exponent then the corresponding

result requires more work.

Lemma 3.4.2. If B is a torsion-free group and A is an abelian group of exponent n for

some n ∈ N then A wr B |= Th∀ (Cn wr B).

   In Chapter 4 we give a complete description of the universal theory of a non-cyclic

free group in the variety An A, where n is a square-free positive integer, and of the ﬁnitely

generated groups in its universal closure.

                                             – 15 –
Theorem 4.1.1. If G is a group then the following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G satisfies the universal theory of a non-cyclic group free in An A;

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Un ;

 (3) G is a σn -group or G is torsion-free abelian;

                                                                        (r)     (s)
 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in Cn wr Z                for some

     r, s ∈ N.

The collection Un of universal sentences is deﬁned in Section 4.2 (on pages 57 to 59)

and the property of being a σn -group is deﬁned on page 55. We use this description to

prove that a free group in this variety has decidable universal theory. We also use the

description to prove some further results about those groups universally equivalent to a

non-cyclic free group in the variety An A.

   In Chapter 5 we consider left-iterated wreath products of torsion-free abelian groups.

Chapuis proved in [11] that such groups have decidable universal theory; however, no

description of this theory exists in the literature. We give such a description and use it

to give a characterization of those ﬁnitely generated groups contained in the universal

closure of one of these groups.

Theorem 5.1.2. Let S be a left-iterated wreath product of d non-trivial torsion-free abe-

lian groups. If G is a finitely generated group then the following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(S);

 (2) G can be embedded in wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N;

 (3) G is a ρd -group.

The property of being a ρd -group is deﬁned on page 74.

   In Chapter 6 we consider the universal theory of groups of the form U wr H, where

H is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free nilpotent group and U is a non-trivial abelian group

of exponent n, where n is a square-free positive integer or zero. We give an explicit

description of the universal theory of the group U wr H modulo the universal theory of

H and of the ﬁnitely generated groups in the universal closure of U wr H.


                                             – 16 –
Theorem 6.1.1. Let H be a finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent group of class c and

let U be a non-trivial abelian group of exponent n. If G is a group then the following

conditions are equivalent:
                   
 (1) G ∈ ucl U wr H ;

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Wn,H ;

 (3) G is a ρn,H -group or G |= Th∀ (H);

                                                                   (r)

     and some K such that K |= Th∀ (H).

The collection Wn,H of universal sentences is deﬁned in Section 6.2 (on pages 85 to 91)

and the property of being a ρn,H -group is deﬁned on page 84. This description provides

a method of proof of the decidability of U wr H, provided that there exists a recursive

collection of sentences describing the universal and existential theory of H. We ﬁnish the

chapter by considering some examples of groups H for which we can write down explicitly

a collection of sentences VH such that if K ∈ ucl(H) then K is universally equivalent to

H if and only if K |= VH .

Proposition 6.7.1. If G is in ucl(F2 (Nc )) then G is universally equivalent to F2 (Nc ) if

and only if G contains a 2-generator subgroup which is not in Nc−1 .

   In Chapter 7 we generalize the results of Chapters 4, 5 and 6 to groups of the form

U wr P , where P is a torsion-free soluble group satisfying certain conditions and U is a

non-trivial abelian group of exponent n, where n is a square-free positive integer or zero.

We require that there exist a bound on the class of the nilpotent subgroups of P . We give

an explicit description of the universal theory of the group U wr P modulo the universal

theory of P and use this to give a characterization of those ﬁnitely generated groups in

the universal closure of this group.

Theorem 7.1.2. Let P be a finitely generated torsion-free group in Pc ∩ Bk and let U

be a non-trivial abelian group of exponent n. If G is a finitely generated group then the

following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(U wr P );


                                           – 17 –
                               (r)
 (2) G can be embedded in Cn wr Q for some r ∈ N and some Q such that Q |= Th∀ (P );

 (3) Either G is a ρn,Q -group for some subgroup Q of P or G |= Th∀ (P ).

The property of being a ρn,P -group is deﬁned on page 110. If F = F/N ′ where F is

an absolutely free group and F/N ∼
                                 = G satisﬁes the conditions above then ucl(F ) ⊆
ucl(Cn wr G); this yields necessary conditions for a group to be in ucl(F ). We show that

in many cases this inclusion is strict.

   In Part III (Chapters 8 to 10) we establish a collection of results concerning various

aspects of the elementary and universal theory of certain inﬁnite soluble groups.

   We say that a group G is a Cn -group if there exists an integer t such that each

element of γn (G) can be written as a product of t commutators [h1 , g1 ] · · · [ht , gt ] with

gi ∈ G and hi ∈ γn−1 (G) for i = 1, . . . , t. In Chapter 8 we extend a number results about

commutator lengths in derived subgroups. It is known that ﬁnitely generated abelian-

by-metanilpotent groups are C2 -groups, as are extensions of abelian groups by groups

satisfying the maximal condition on normal subgroups (see [2], [19] and [52]). We extend

these results to provide examples of groups which are Cn -groups for all n ⩾ 2 and in

many cases give an explicit bound on the value of t. We show that G is a Cn -group for

all n ⩾ 2 if G is in one of the following classes:

   • ﬁnitely generated ﬁnite-by-abelian-by-metanilpotent groups;

   • ﬁnite-by-soluble groups satisfying the maximal condition on normal subgroups.

We go on to consider the elementary theory of groups which are Cn -groups for all n ⩾ 2.

We obtain one-variable ﬁrst-order formulae deﬁning the terms of the lower central series

in such a group and use these formulae to prove the following result.

Theorem 8.2.1. Fix a positive integer n and let H be a Cr -group for 2 ⩽ r ⩽ n. If the

group G is elementarily equivalent to H then γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to γn (H)

and G/γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to H/γn (H).

   In [66], Timoshenko determines those 2-generator groups ﬁnitely presented in the va-

riety of soluble groups of derived length d which are universally equivalent to a non-cyclic

free soluble group of derived length d: there are precisely two such groups, namely the free


                                            – 18 –
soluble group of derived length d and rank 2, and the verbal wreath product Z wrSd−1 Z.

His proof that these two groups are indeed universally equivalent appears to contain a

small error. In Chapter 9 we correct this error and prove the following more general

result.

Proposition 9.1.1. Let V be a variety containing A such that the free groups of V are

residually finite p-groups for infinitely many primes p. Suppose further that V is gene-

rated by its k-generator groups for some positive integer k. The free group of finite or

infinite rank r ⩾ 2 in VA is universally equivalent to Z wrV Z.

Thus there are at least two isomorphism classes of 2-generator groups universally equiva-

lent to F2 (VA). However, in a product variety VNc , with c ⩾ 2, the situation is diﬀerent,

as can be seen by the following proposition.

Proposition 9.2.1. Let V be a variety whose free groups are residually finite p-groups

for infinitely many primes p and let c ⩾ 2. Let G be a 2-generator group finitely presented

in VNc . Then G is universally equivalent to F2 (VNc ) if and only if G is isomorphic to

F2 (VNc ).

We also give the following necessary and suﬃcient condition for a group in the universal

closure of a free group F in ANc to be universally equivalent to F .

Proposition 9.2.2. Let G be in ucl(F2 (ANc )) for c ⩾ 2. Then G is universally equiva-

lent to F2 (ANc ) if and only if G contains a 2-generator subgroup which is not in ANc−1 .

   In Chapter 10 we prove some results about the theories of free groups in certain so-

luble varieties. Let V1 , . . . , Vk be non-trivial nilpotent varieties whose free groups are

torsion-free and suppose that k ⩾ 2. We begin by obtaining one-variable formulae deﬁ-

ning a number of verbal subgroups of a free group F in Vk · · · V1 . We use the deﬁnability

of the derived subgroup to extend the result of Romanovskii and Timoshenko [57] that if

F is a free soluble group of rank n and G is an n-generator group elementarily equivalent

to F then G is isomorphic to F .

Theorem 10.2.1. Let F be the free group of rank n in Vk · · · V1 . An n-generator group

G is elementarily equivalent to F if and only if G is isomorphic to F .

We also use our deﬁnability results to extend a number of results of Chapuis [13] about




                                           – 19 –
the elementary and universal theories of free soluble groups.

Proposition 10.3.1. The free groups in Vk · · · V1 of different finite ranks have different

∀∃-theories.

Theorem 10.4.1. A free group F of finite rank r ⩾ 2 in Vk · · · V1 has undecidable

∀∃-theory.

Theorem 10.5.1. The decidability of the universal theory of the free group of finite rank

r ⩾ 2 in Vk · · · V1 with c1 ⩾ 2 implies the decidability of the universal theory of the field

of rationals.

Theorem 10.5.2. The decidability of the universal theory of a non-cyclic free group in

Vk · · · V2 V1 with k ⩾ 3, V1 = A and V2 = Nc2 implies the decidability of the universal

theory of the field of rationals.

These results contrast with the positive answers to Tarski’s questions about the elemen-

tary theory of absolutely free groups which have been announced by Kharlampovich and

Myasnikov [23] and Sela [58].

   Finally, in Chapter 11, we summarize the results proved in this thesis, highlighting

those which we believe to be of particular interest. We also suggest areas where further

work could be done.




                                           – 20 –
                                         Chapter 2


       PRELIMINARY RESULTS ON VARIETIES AND

                UNIVERSAL THEORIES OF GROUPS



In this chapter we give a brief introduction to varieties of groups and recall some useful

results. For a more general discussion of these topics see the book by Hanna Neumann

[44]. We also recall some useful results about the universal theories of structures in a

langauge; we formulate these results in the case of groups.



2.1     The basic facts

A word is an element of the free group F∞ on the set X∞ = {x1 , x2 , . . .}. The image

of w under a homomorphism from F∞ to a group G is a value of w in G. If only the

generators x1 , . . . , xn occur in w then, for any n-tuple g1 , . . . , gn in G, the map xi 7→ gi

for i = 1, . . . , n and xi 7→ 1 for i > n extends to a homomorphism F∞ → G. We write

w(g1 , . . . , gn ) for the image of g under this map.

   The word w is a law in the group G if the only value of w in G is 1. The verbal

subgroup V (G) of G corresponding to a set of words V is the subgroup generated by all

values in G of words from V :

                          V (G) := hwα | w ∈ V, α ∈ Hom(F∞ , G)i.

Thus w is a law in G for all w ∈ V if and only if V (G) = {1}. If V consists of a single

word w, we write w(G) for V (G).

   The variety deﬁned by a set of words V is the class of all groups G such that each

word in V is a law in G. We list some examples of varieties which will be important in

what follows.

                                              – 21 –
Examples of varieties

   • The variety O of all groups, deﬁned by the empty set of words.

   • The variety E, which contains only the trivial group, deﬁned by the word x.

   • The variety A of abelian groups, deﬁned by the word [x, y].

   • The variety An of abelian groups of exponent n, deﬁned by the words {xn , [x, y]}.

   • The variety Nc of nilpotent groups of class at most c, deﬁned by the word

     [x1 , . . . , xc+1 ].

   • The variety Sd of soluble groups of derived length at most d, deﬁned by the word

     sd (x) where:


                                               s1 (x, y) = [x, y],

                                               si+1 (x) = [si (y), si (z)].


     Here x = (y, z), where y and z are each 2i−1 -tuples of elements of X∞ .

   • The variety Pc of polynilpotent groups with class sequence at most c = (c1 , . . . , ck ),

     deﬁned by the word sc (G), where sc (x) = sck (x) and:


                             sc1 (x1 , . . . , xc1 +1 ) = [x1 , . . . , xc1 +1 ],

                                              sci (x) = [sci−1 (x1 ), . . . , sci−1 (xci +1 )].


     Here x = (x1 , . . . , xci +1 ), where x1 , . . . , xci +1 are each (c1 + 1) · · · (ci−1 + 1)-tuples

     of elements of X∞ , and the sequence ci is the subsequence (c1 , . . . , ci ) of c.


   A group G is relatively free if G ∼
                                     = F/V (F ) for some absolutely free group F and
some set of words V . Let V be a variety deﬁned by a set of words V . The free group of

rank n in V, denoted by Fn (V), is the relatively free group Fn /V (Fn ), where Fn is the

absolutely free group of rank n. We denote by F∞ (V) the free group of countably inﬁnite

rank in V. A group G belongs to a variety V if and only if it is isomorphic to a quotient

group of a free group of suitable rank in V.




                                                       – 22 –
Examples of relatively free groups

Let Fn be the absolutely free group of rank n.


   • The free group of rank n in O is Fn .

   • The free abelian group of rank n is Fn /Fn′ .

   • The free nilpotent group of class c and rank n is Fn /γc+1 (Fn ).

                                                                         (d)
   • The free soluble group of derived length d and rank n is Fn /Fn .

   • The free polynilpotent group of rank n with class sequence c is

      Fn /γck +1 (· · · γc1 +1 (Fn )).



2.2     Discrimination and residual properties

A set X of groups is discriminating (as deﬁned in [8]) if, for every ﬁnite set W of words

in at most n variables with the property that, for each word w ∈ W , there is a homo-

morphism fw : Fn → G with G ∈ X such that fw (w) 6= 1, there is a group G ∈ X and

a homomorphism f : Fn → G such that f (w) 6= 1 for all w ∈ W . A set X of groups

discriminates the variety V if X ⊆ V and, for every ﬁnite set W of words in at most

n variables which are not laws in V, there exists a group G ∈ X and a homomorphism

f : Fn → G such that f (w) 6= 1 for all w ∈ W . A set X is discriminating if and only if it

discriminates the variety which it generates. The set of all free groups of ﬁnite rank in a

variety V discriminates V.

Example 2.2.1. The infinite cyclic group Z is discriminating and, therefore, Z discri-

minates the variety of abelian groups A.

Proof. This follows immediately from the fact that a ﬁnite set of linear equations can be

simultaneously falsiﬁed.

   Let P be a property of groups. A group G is residually P if, for every non-trivial

element g ∈ G, there is a normal subgroup Ng of G such that g 6∈ Ng and G/Ng has the

property P. The following conditions are equivalent:


                                           – 23 –
  1. G is residually P;

        T
  2.          N = {1} where X = {N ⊳ G | G/N has property P};
       N ∈X

  3. G is a subcartesian product of groups with property P.

The following result illuminates the link between residual properties and discrimination.

Theorem 2.2.1 ([44, 17.81]). If P is a property inherited by subgroups and by finite

direct products then the free groups of a variety V are residually P if and only if the

finitely generated groups with the property P in V discriminate V.

   The property of being residually a ﬁnite p-group is of particular interest to us. This

property is inherited by subgroups and by ﬁnite direct products. Thus, since the free

groups of ﬁnite rank discriminate a variety, in order to show that the free groups in V

are residually P, it is enough to show that the free groups of ﬁnite rank are residually P.

Lemma 2.2.1. If V ⊆ Nc is a variety whose free groups are torsion-free then the free

groups of V are residually finite p-groups for every prime p.

Proof. This result follows from a theorem of Gruenberg [18] which says that a ﬁnitely

generated torsion-free nilpotent group is residually a ﬁnite p-group for every prime p.



   The Nielsen–Schreier Theorem states that a subgroup of a free group is free. In

general the same will not be true for relatively free groups: Shmel′ kin [59] proves that

a subgroup G of a free polynilpotent group F is itself a free polynilpotent group with

the same class sequence as F if and only if G has a generating set whose elements are

linearly independent modulo the derived subgroup F ′ . This result has been extended by

Baumslag [4, Theorem 1] to a larger class of relatively free groups.

Theorem 2.2.2 (Baumslag, 1963). Let F be a free group in the variety V such that F

is residually a finite p-group for infinitely many primes p. A subgroup G of F is free in

V if and only if G has a generating set whose elements are linearly independent modulo

F ′ ; moreover, such a generating set freely generates G.




                                          – 24 –
    This next result of Baumslag, Neumann, Neumann and Neumann [8, Lemma 2.16]

provides us with examples of ﬁnitely generated discriminating groups.

Theorem 2.2.3 (Baumslag, Neumann, Neumann and Neumann, 1964). If G is

residually a finite p-group for infinitely many primes p then G is discriminating.

Proof. Let W = {wi | i = 1, . . . , m} be a set of words in at most n variables which are not

laws in G. For each word wi ∈ W we may choose a prime pi and a normal subgroup Ni ⊳G

such that wi g1 , . . . , gn     is non-trivial and deﬁne elements α1 , . . . , αn of the direct

2.3     Wreath products

The unrestricted wreath product
                                                                          Q
The Cartesian product of a family of groups {Gλ | λ ∈ Λ}, denoted by C      λ∈Λ Gλ , is
                                  S
the group of all functions f : Λ → λ∈Λ Gλ with f (λ) ∈ Gλ , multiplied componentwise.

The Cartesian power of G by Λ, denoted by GΛ , is the Cartesian product of groups

{Gλ | λ ∈ Λ}, where Gλ ∼
                       = G for each λ ∈ Λ. In GΛ we single out a special subgroup:
for each g ∈ G we deﬁne the constant function g◦ ∈ GΛ by g◦ (λ) = g for all λ ∈ Λ; the

diagonal subgroup G◦ is the set of all constant functions. The unrestricted wreath product

of G by H, denoted by G Wr H, is the semi-direct product of GH by H, where the action

of H on GH is deﬁned as follows: for h1 ∈ H and u ∈ GH , we deﬁne uh1 by


                                          uh1 (h) = u(hh−1
                                                        1 )


for all h ∈ H. An element of G Wr H can be written as an ordered pair (h, d) with h ∈ H

and d ∈ GH and we say that GH is the base group of G Wr H.



                                               – 25 –
The Kaloujnine–Krasner embedding

The Kaloujnine–Krasner embedding allows us to embed any group extension into an

unrestricted wreath product. The ability to pass from a general extension to a split

extension in this way is a very useful technique. The result was published in 1951 in one

of a series of papers dealing with permutation groups [22]. Since we will use the details

of this embedding in our applications we include a proof.

Theorem 2.3.1 (Kaloujnine and Krasner, 1951). The unrestricted wreath product

A Wr B contains an isomorphic copy of every group that is an extension of A by B.

Proof. Let G be a group with normal subgroup N such that N is isomorphic to A and

G/N is isomorphic to B. Let T be a transversal to N in G and let τ be the natural

bijective map from B to T corresponding to the isomorphism G/N ∼
                                                               = B. Let µ : G → B
be the natural epimorphism such that N = ker µ and let α : N → A be an isomorphism.

Let D = AB be the base group of the unrestricted wreath product A Wr B. We write

elements of A Wr B as ordered pairs (b, d) with b ∈ B and d ∈ D and deﬁne a map

γ : G → A Wr B as follows: for each element g of G we set gγ = (gµ, φg ) where, for each

b ∈ B,
                                                        
                            φg (b) =   b(gµ)−1 τ g(bτ )−1 α.

It is straightforward to check that this is a well-deﬁned monomorphism.

   In the situation of Theorem 2.3.1, suppose that A is abelian. If N is torsion-free,

we may regard it as a Z[G/N ]-module and hence, since G/N ∼
                                                          = B, as a Z[B]-module.
We may also regard the base group D of the wreath product as a Z[B]-module. The

embedding γ|N of N into D is a Z[B]-module homomorphism. Thus, if N is torsion-free

as a Z[G/N ]-module, then the image of N in A Wr B is torsion-free as a Z[B]-module.

Suppose now that N has ﬁnite exponent n and that p is a prime divisor of n. We may

regard the subgroup Np of N of elements of order dividing p as an Fp [B]-module. The

embedding γ|Np of Np into the submodule of D of elements of order dividing p is an

Fp [B]-module homomorphism. Thus, if Np is torsion-free as an Fp [G/N ]-module, then

the image of Np in A Wr B is torsion-free as an Fp [B]-module.



                                         – 26 –
The restricted wreath product
                                                                        Q
The direct product of a family of groups {Gλ | λ ∈ Λ}, denoted by λ∈Λ Gλ , is the
            Q
subgroup of C λ∈Λ Gλ of functions f such that f (λ) = 1 for all but ﬁnitely many λ ∈ Λ.

The direct power of G by Λ, denoted by G(Λ) , is the direct product of groups {Gλ | λ ∈ Λ}

where Gλ ∼
         = G for each λ ∈ Λ. The restricted wreath product of G by H, denoted by
G wr H, is the semi-direct product of G(H) by H where the action of H on G(H) is deﬁned

as in the unrestricted wreath product. An element of G wr H can be written as a ordered

pair (h, d) with h ∈ H and d ∈ G(H) and we say that G(H) is the base group of G wr H.

The following lemma is a direct consequence of [3, Lemma 3].

Lemma 2.3.1 (Baumslag, 1959). Let G = U wr H, where H is torsion-free, and let A

be the base group of G. Let a be a non-trivial element of A and let g be an element of G.

If [a, g] = 1 then g is in A.

Proof. Let a = (1, d) and let g = (h, c) with h ∈ H and d, c ∈ A. Since a 6= 1, we may

choose a non-trivial element u of H such that d(u) 6= 1. We have [a, g] = (1, d(h − 1)), so

that [a, g] = 1 implies that d(uh−1 ) = dh (u) = d(u) 6= 1 and it follows that d(uhr ) = d(u)

for all r ∈ Z. This implies that {uhr |r ∈ Z} is in the support of d. If h 6= 1 then h is of

inﬁnite order and the set {uhr |r ∈ Z} is inﬁnite. But d is of ﬁnite support and hence we

must have that h = 1 and g ∈ A.

    The left-iterated restricted wreath product of the groups Gi for i = 1, . . . , n, denoted

by wrni=1 Gi , is

Verbal wreath products

A group G is a free product of the subgroups {Gλ | λ ∈ Λ} if

     morphism φ : G → H such that φ|Gλ = φλ for each λ ∈ Λ.

The O-verbal product of a family of groups is equal to their free product and the A-verbal

                                          – 28 –
The Shmel′ kin embedding

Shmel′ kin [60, Theorem 1] generalized the Magnus embedding in the following way. Let F

be a free group of countable rank with free generating set {xλ | λ ∈ Λ}, let R be a normal

subgroup of F and let xλ be the image of xλ in F/R. Let V be a set of words which

deﬁnes a variety V and let U be a free group in V with free generating set {uλ | λ ∈ Λ}.

Theorem 2.3.3 (Shmel′ kin, 1964). Let x̃λ be the image of xλ in F/V (R). An embed-

ding of F/V (R) into U wrV(F/R) is given by setting

                                    x̃λ 7→ (xλ , uλ (1)) .

   Shmelkin’s original proof [61] was computational and he later gave a brief and concep-

tual proof of the result [62]. Since the original proofs are in Russian, we include a proof

which is based on that of Romanovskii for the generalized Shmel′ kin embedding [56].

Proof. We deﬁne α : F → U wrV(F/R) to be the homomorphism given by

                                    xλ 7→ (xλ , uλ (1)) .

Let N be the base group of U wrV(F/R). Since Rα ⩽ N and N is in V, we have

V (R) ⩽ ker α. In order to prove the theorem it remains to prove the inverse inclusion.

   The group F/V (R) is an extension of R/V (R) by F/R and the Kaloujnine–Krasner

embedding (see Theorem 2.3.1) gives an embedding γ of F/V (R) into

                           (R/V (R)) Wr(F/R) = D ⋊ (F/R),

where x̃λ γ = (xλ , dλ ) with dλ ∈ D. Since U is a free group in V and D is in V, the map

β : U → D : uλ 7→ dλ is a homomorphism; β extends to a homomorphism β : N → D

which respects the action of F/R. We can deﬁne a homomorphism

               σ : U wrV(F/R) → (R/V (R)) Wr(F/R) : (f, u) 7→ (f, uβ).

By construction ασ = γ and hence ker α is contained in ker γ = V (R).

   Since the A-verbal product of a family of groups is equal to their direct product,

G wrA H is equal to G wr H and it follows that the Magnus embedding is a special case

of the Shmel′ kin embedding with V = {[x, y]}.


                                           – 29 –
   The Magnus and Shmel′ kin embeddings provide a useful technique for dealing with

free extensions of groups. The embeddings are particularly valuable owing to the greater

ease of calculation in the wreath product.



2.4      Product varieties

For varieties U and V we deﬁne the product variety UV to be the variety of all groups

that are extensions of a group in U by a group in V.


Examples of product varities

   • The variety Sd of soluble groups of derived length d is equal to the product variety

      |A ·{z
           · · A}.
          d

   • The variety Pc of polynilpotent groups with class sequence at most c = (c1 , . . . , ck )

      is equal to the product variety Nck · · · Nc1 .


   The following results are useful in determining groups which discriminate a product

variety. The ﬁrst result, due to Baumslag [5, Theorem 1], illustrates the importance of

the restricted wreath product in this context. The proof, based on an idea of Neumann,

Neumann and Neumann [43, Theorem 6.5], involves the Kaloujnine–Krasner embedding

as well as some very technical arguments.

Theorem 2.4.1 (Baumslag, 1963). If the collection of groups C discriminates U and

the collection of groups D discriminates V then the collection of groups

                             C wr D = {C wr D | C ∈ C, D ∈ D}

discriminates UV.

   In particular, if G discriminates U and H discriminates V then G wr H discriminates

UV. Next we consider when a product variety can be discriminated by a group of ﬁnite

rank [8, Theorem 3.3].

Theorem 2.4.2 (Baumslag, Neumann, Neumann and Neumann, 1964). Let

V 6= E be a variety of exponent zero and suppose that V can be discriminated by a k-


                                             – 30 –
generator group which is residually periodic. Then, for k ⩾ 2, the product variety UV is

discriminated by a k-generator group for any variety U.

   The variety Nc for c ⩾ 3 is generated by, and hence discriminated by, its (c − 1)-

generator groups (see, for exmple, [27], [24]). The variety of abelian groups is discrimina-

ted by the inﬁnite cyclic group, and the variety of nilpotent groups of class 2 is generated

by, and hence discriminated by, its 2-generator groups. It follows from Theorem 2.4.2

that the variety of polynilpotent groups with class sequence at most (c1 , . . . , ck ) is discri-

minated by its r-generator groups, where r = max{2, c1 − 1}. In particular, the variety

of soluble groups of derived length d is generated by its 2-generator groups.

   The following result, dealing with product varieties and the property of being resi-

dually a ﬁnite p-group, is an immediate corollary of a result of Baumslag [5, Theorem 3]

dealing with a more general class of residual properties.

Lemma 2.4.1 (Baumslag, 1963). Let p be a prime. If the free groups of the varieties

U and V are residually finite p-groups then the free groups of UV are residually finite

p-groups.

Proof. Let C = {Fn (U) | n ∈ N} and let D = {G ∈ V | G is a ﬁnitely generated

p-group}. The set C discriminates U and, by Theorem 2.2.1, the set D discriminates

V. Thus, by Theorem 2.4.1, the set C wr D discriminates the product variety UV. Every

group in C wr D is residually a ﬁnite p-group by a result of Gruenberg [18]; it is also ﬁnitely

generated. Thus the free groups of UV are residually ﬁnite p-groups by Theorem 2.2.1.

   It follows from this and Lemma 2.2.1 above, that free nilpotent groups, free soluble

groups and free polynilpotent groups are residually ﬁnite p-groups for every prime p.

Thus, by Theorem 2.2.3, each of these groups is discriminating.

   For product varieties we have an alternative condition for a subgroup of a relatively

free group to be relatively free. This is again a result of Baumslag [6, Corollary 1].

Theorem 2.4.3 (Baumslag, 1965). Let F be a free group in the product variety UV,

where U and V are varieties whose free groups are residually finite p-groups for the same

prime p, and let V be the set of words defining V. A subgroup G of F is free in UW if G

has a generating set whose elements generate modulo V (F ) a free group in W.


                                             – 31 –
   Mal′ cev showed in [37] that any pair of elements in a free soluble group F which

commute either belong to the last non-trivial term of the derived series of G or generate

a cyclic subgroup. He used this fact to show that the terms of the derived series of F

are deﬁnable. Shmel′ kin [59] extended Mal′ cev’s result to free polynilpotent groups in

the following way: if F is a free polynilpotent group with class sequence (c1 , . . . , ck ) then

any pair of elements which commute either generate a cyclic subgroup or belong to the

subgroup γck−1 (· · · (γc1 (F )) · · · ). This result has also been extended, again by Baumslag

(see [44, 42.52]), to a larger class of relatively free groups.

Theorem 2.4.4 (Baumslag). Let U and V be non-trivial varieties whose free groups are

residually finite p-groups for the same prime p. Let V be the set of words which define V

and suppose that the free groups of V are torsion-free. Every non-cyclic nilpotent subgroup

of a free group F in the product variety UV is in the verbal subgroup V (F ).

Proof. Let N be a non-cyclic nilpotent subgroup of F . Suppose to begin with that

N ∩ V (F ) = {1} and choose elements g, h ∈ N such that hg, hi is abelian and non-cyclic.

The elements g and h generate a free abelian group modulo V (F ) and, by Theorem 2.4.3,

the group hg, hi is a free UA group, contradicting the assumption that hg, hi is abelian.

   Suppose now that N has non-trivial intersection with V (F ) but that N 6⊆ V (F ). We

choose an element g ∈ N \ V (F ). The intersection N ∩ V (F ) is a non-trivial normal

subgroup of N and hence intersects the centre non-trivially. (This is an elementary fact,

see [53, 5.2.1].) We may choose h ∈ N ∩ V (F ) such that [g, h] = 1. Since F/V (F ) is

free in V, it is torsion-free and g has inﬁnite order modulo V (F ). Consider the group

U wr F∞ (V), where U generates U. For any ﬁnite set of non-trivial elements X in F , there

exists a homomorphism α : F → U wr F∞ (V) satisfying the following conditions: xα 6= 1

for all x ∈ X and gα is in the base group of U wr F∞ (V) if and only if g ∈ V (F ) (see

[8, Corollary 2.23]). The image of g in U wr F∞ (V) has inﬁnite order modulo the base

group. It follows, by Lemma 2.3.1, that [g, h] = 1 if and only if g ∈ V (F ), contradicting

our choice of the elements g and h.

   This result proves to be very useful in allowing us to give existential and universal

sentences deﬁning the verbal subgroup V (F ) of a free group F in a product variety UV

where the words V deﬁne the variety V.

                                             – 32 –
2.5      Universal theory

The following lemma is a well-known fact. Since we do not know of a good reference, we

include a proof in the case of groups.

    Let A ⊆ G and B ⊆ H be ﬁnite subsets. In this context we deﬁne an isomorphism to

be a bijective map ν : A → B such that, for g1 , g2 , g3 ∈ A,

  (i) g1 g2 = g3 if and only if g3 ν = g1 νg2 ν;

 (ii) g1−1 = g2 if and only if g2 ν = (g1 ν)−1 .

Lemma 2.5.1. A group G satisfies the universal theory of a group H if and only if every

finite subset of G is isomorphic to a finite subset of H.

Proof. Suppose to begin with that G |= Th∀ (H) and let A = {a1 , . . . , ar } be a ﬁnite

subset of G. Since A is a ﬁnite set, it has a ﬁnite theory which can be written as a single

quantiﬁer-free formula θ(a1 , . . . , ar ). It follows that G satisﬁes the existential sentence φ

deﬁned by

                                       ∃x1 . . . xr θ(x1 , . . . , xr ).

Since G satisﬁes the universal theory of H, we have H |= Th∃ (G) and φ holds in H; we

may choose elements b1 , . . . , br ∈ H such that H |= θ(b1 , . . . , br ). If B = {b1 , . . . , br } then

the map A → B : ai 7→ bi is an isomorphism.

    For the converse, suppose that every ﬁnite subset of G is isomorphic to a ﬁnite subset

of H and let φ be a universal sentence such that H |= φ. We may assume without loss of

generality that φ is of the form


                                       ∀x1 . . . xr θ(x1 , . . . , xr ),


where θ(x1 , . . . , xr ) is a quantiﬁer-free formula. Let a1 , . . . , ar be elements of G and let

A = {a1 , . . . , ar }. There is a ﬁnite subset B = {b1 , . . . , br } of H and an isomorphism

ν : A → B : ai 7→ bi . We have H |= θ(b1 , . . . , br ) and, since ν is an isomorphism,

G |= θ(a1 , . . . , ar ). This holds for all tuples of elements from G and it follows that G |= φ.

Thus G satisﬁes the universal theory of H.




                                                   – 33 –
    Timoshenko [66] uses this result to show that if F is a free group in a variety V and G

is a subgroup of F then F and G have the same universal theory if and only they satisfy

the same laws.

Theorem 2.5.1 (Timoshenko, 2000). Let F be a free group in a variety V such that

F is residually a finite p-group for infinitely many primes p. If the subgroup G of F

generates the same variety as F then the universal theories of G and F coincide.

Proof. It is clear, since G ⩽ F , that G satisﬁes the universal theory of F . By Lemma 2.5.1,

in order to prove that F satisﬁes the universal theory of G, it is enough to show that

every ﬁnite subset of F is isomorphic to a ﬁnite subset of G.

    By Lemma 2.2.3, the group G is discriminating and hence G discriminates V. Let S

be a ﬁnite subset of F and let S be the extension of S deﬁned by

                  S = S ∪ {g1 g2−1 | g1 , g2 ∈ S} ∪ {g1 g2 g3−1 | g1 , g2 , g3 ∈ S}.

Each element s ∈ S is the image of a word ws and if s 6= 1 then ws is not a law in V. Since

G discriminates V, there exist elements h1 , . . . , hn ∈ G such that ws (h1 , . . . , hn ) 6= 1 for

all non-trivial s ∈ S. Let SG = {ws (h1 , . . . , hn ) | s ∈ S} ⊆ G. The map α : S → SG : s 7→

ws (h1 , . . . , hn ) is the required isomorphism.

    The following result is useful in allowing us to derive an embedding from the fact that

one group is in the universal closure of another. In [66], Timoshenko proves the result for

use in a limited context; we are able to apply it more generally (see Section 9.2).

Lemma 2.5.2 (Timoshenko, 2000). Let G be a group which is finitely presented in

some variety V and let H be a group such that G ∈ ucl(H). There exists an embedding

of G into the countable Cartesian power H N of H.

Proof. Let ha1 , . . . , as | r1 (a), . . . , rt (a)i be a presentation for G in V and let g be a non-

trivial element of G, so that g is the image of a word w. We deﬁne the existential sentence

ψg by                                                                   !
                                             t
                                             ^
                             ∃ x1 . . . xs         ri (x) = 1 ∧ w(x) 6= 1
                                             i=1
where x is the s-tuple (x1 , . . . , xs ). We have G |= ψg and, since G is universally equivalent

to H, it follows that H |= ψg . We may choose elements b1 , . . . , br ∈ H such that ri (b) = 1


                                                   – 34 –
for i = 1, . . . , r and w(b) 6= 1. Then the map αg : G → H deﬁned by ai 7→ bi for i = 1, . . . , r

is a homomorphism by Von Dyck’s theorem (see [53, 2.2.1]). We enumerate the non-

identity elements of G to obtain a list g1 , g2 , . . . and deﬁne a map α : G → H N : g 7→ fg

where fg (i) = αgi (g) for i ∈ N. Then α is the desired embedding.



2.6       Ultraproducts of groups

Let G be a group. The results in this next section establish the strong relationship between

those groups in the universal closure of G and the ultrapowers of G. To begin with we

deﬁne ultraﬁlters and ultrapowers and state some standard results.


Filters

Let Λ be a non-empty set. A filter over Λ is a set D ⊆ P(Λ) such that the following

conditions hold: (i) Λ ∈ D and ∅ 6∈ D; (ii) X, Y ∈ D =⇒ X ∩ Y ∈ D; (iii) X ∈ D and

X ⊆ Y ∈ P(Λ) =⇒ Y ∈ D. An ultrafilter over Λ is a ﬁlter U =
                                                          6 P(Λ) such that, for all

X ∈ P(Λ) either X ∈ D or Λ \ X ∈ D. If F is the ﬁlter generated by some non-empty

S ⊆ Λ then F is a principal ﬁlter. A principal ultraﬁlter U is generated by a singleton.

Lemma 2.6.1. If S ⊆ P(Λ) has the finite intersection property then there exists an

ultrafilter over Λ containing S.

Proof. The proof of this lemma is an easy consequence of Zorn’s Lemma.

Lemma 2.6.2. An ultrafilter over Λ is non-principal if and only if U contains the cofinite

filter.

Proof. This is an easy exercise and we omit it.


Ultraproducts of groups
                                                                                        QC
Let {Aλ | λ ∈ Λ} be a non-empty collection of groups indexed by Λ and let A =             λ∈Λ Aλ .

Let U be a non-principal ultraﬁlter over Λ. Deﬁne an equivalence relation ∼ on A as

follows: a ∼ b if and only if {λ ∈ Λ | a(λ) = b(λ)} ∈ U. Let ã be the ∼-equivalence class
                                                                    Q
of a ∈ A. The ultraproduct of {Aλ | λ ∈ Λ} modulo U, denoted by λ∈Λ Aλ /U, is the set


                                              – 35 –
                                                           Q
of ∼-equivalence classes of A. If Aλ ∼

of A.

   The elementary properties of a family of groups, that is those properties which can

be expressed using ﬁrst-order formulae, are preserved under taking ultraproducts. This

follows from the fundamental theorem concerning ultraproducts:

Theorem 2.6.1 (Loś). Let {Aλ | λ ∈ Λ} be a non-empty collection of groups indexed by

Λ and let U be a non-principal ultrafilter over Λ. Then, for any formula φ(x1 , . . . , xk ) in

Proof. See [15, Theorem 3.1].

Theorem 2.6.2. Let φλ : Aλ → Bλ , λ ∈ Λ be a family of embeddings and let U be a

non-principal ultrafilter over Λ. There is an embedding
                                   Y                      Y

Proof. This follows from the fact that the ultraproduct is a functor; see [15, §4].

   The following result is a counterpart to Frayne’s Lemma (see [9, Lemmas 8.1.1 and

9.3.8]), which says that a structure A is elementarily equivalent to a structure B if and

only if there is an elementary embedding of A into an ultrapower of B, and the proof

follows exactly the same lines. Let G and H be groups. We show that G satisﬁes the

universal theory of H if and only if there is an embedding of G into some ultrapower

of H. By the fundamental theorem, H is elementarily equivalent to any ultrapower of

itself. Thus, if there is an embedding of G into some ultrapower H of H, then G satisﬁes

the universal theory of H and hence G satisﬁes the universal theory of H. To prove the

converse requires rather more work.

Lemma 2.6.3. Let G and H be groups. If G is countable and satisfies the universal

        THE
UNIVERSAL THEORY OF
