 WREATH PRODUCTS
                                      Chapter 3


                        PRELIMINARY RESULTS



This chapter contains a range of preliminary results which will be important in the fol-

lowing four chapters. These results split into two types: group-theoretic results about

restricted wreath products and results related to the universal theory of restricted wreath

products.

   In Section 3.1 we recall the deﬁnitions of an integral domain and an Ore domain. We

recall also that the group ring over a ﬁeld of a group, each of whose ﬁnitely generated

subgroups has inﬁnite cyclic image, is an integral domain and that, if the group ring over

a ﬁeld of a soluble group is an integral domain then it is an Ore domain.

   In Section 3.2 we recall the deﬁnition of the tensor product of two modules.

   In Section 3.3 we prove the crucial result that a ﬁnitely generated extension of an

abelian group A, which is torsion-free or of ﬁnite square-free exponent n, by a torsion-

free soluble group B can be embedded in a restricted wreath product U wr B, where U

is a ﬁnitely generated abelian group of exponent n. This relies on the result that, for

a torsion-free soluble group B, the group rings Z[B] and Fp [B], where p is prime, are

Ore domains. We also prove some results about ﬁnitely generated subgroups of restricted

wreath products U wr G, where U is a ﬁnitely generated abelian group which is torsion-

free or of ﬁnite square-free exponent n and G is a torsion-free soluble group. In particular

we show that every non-abelian nilpotent subgroup of U wr G embeds in G. We identify

U wr G with the group of matrices
                                (            !                     )
                                       u 0
                      M (G, D) =                 | u ∈ G and d ∈ D ,
                                       d 1

where D is the base group of the wreath product which we write additively. Using this

                                          – 40 –
identiﬁcation we derive some useful identities which hold in U wr G.

   The focus of Section 3.4 is on showing that certain restricted wreath products are

universally equivalent. An easy adaptation of Timoshenko’s proof that the restricted

wreath product preserves universal equivalence [65, Theorem 2] yields the result that if

A1 , A2 , B1 , and B2 are groups such that A1 |= Th∀ (A2 ) and B1 |= Th∀ (B2 ) then A1 wr B1

satisﬁes the universal theory of A2 wr B2 . We also prove that if B is an abelian group of

exponent n and G and H are torsion-free universally equivalent groups then B wr G is

universally equivalent to Cn wr H.



3.1     Ore domains

A skew-field is a ring R, not necessarily commutative, whose non-zero elements R∗ form

a group under multiplication. An element u of a ring R is a left zero-divisor if u 6= 0

and there exists v ∈ R∗ such that uv = 0. An element of R which is neither zero nor

a left zero-divisor is a left non-zero-divisor. The analogous deﬁnitions hold with “right”

in place of “left”. A non-zero ring containing no left or right zero-divisors is an integral

domain.

   The group ring R[G] of a group G is the set of all ﬁnite linear combinations of elements

from G with multiplication deﬁned by extending the multiplication on G. We may write

an element α of R[G] in the form
                                            X
                                       α=         αg g,
                                            g∈G

with each αg ∈ R and where αg = 0 for all but ﬁnitely many g ∈ G. The support of an

element α in R[G], which we denote by supp(α), is the set {g ∈ G | αg 6= 0}.

   There is a long-standing conjecture that the group ring of a torsion-free group over

a ﬁeld (or over the integers) is an integral domain. The conjecture has been proved in a

number of special cases: in particular, if G is a group such that every ﬁnitely generated

subgroup of G has inﬁnite cyclic image then Z[G] is an integral domain (Higman, see [53,

15.3.10]). We note that the same argument applies for group rings over ﬁelds.

Lemma 3.1.1. Let F be a field. If G is a group such that every non-trivial finitely

generated subgroup has an infinite cyclic image, then F [G] is an integral domain.


                                          – 41 –
Proof. Suppose that F [G] contains non-zero elements α and β with αβ = 0 and that

supp(α) = {g1 , . . . , gm } and supp(β) = {h1 , . . . , hn }. We choose α and β in such a way

that m + n is minimal, subject to the condition that αβ = 0. It is clear that m + n 6= 2.

Multiplying by group elements if necessary, we may assume that 1 ∈ supp(α) ∩ supp(β).

   Let H = hg1 , . . . , gm , h1 , . . . , hn i. Then H has a normal subgroup K such that H/K =

haKi is an inﬁnite cyclic group. We may write

                α = γ1 ar1 + · · · + γs ars    and     β = δ1 aq1 + · · · + δt aqt ,

with γi , δj ∈ F [K] where r1 < · · · < rs and q1 < · · · < qt . If s = 1 then αa−r1 = γ1 ∈ F [K]

and, since 1 ∈ supp(α), the element a−r1 is in supp(γ1 ), and hence in K. Thus, since

H/K is torsion-free, either a is in K and H = K, contradicting our assumption that H/K

is inﬁnite, or r1 = 0 and α = γ1 ∈ F [K]. Similarly, if t = 1 then β = δ1 ∈ F [K] and

if s = t = 1 then supp(α) and supp(β) are in K and H = K, once more contradicting

our assumption that H/K is inﬁnite. We may assume that either r > 1 or s > 1 and

it follows that either | supp(γ1 )| < m or | supp(δ1 )| < n. The smallest power of a which

occurs in the product αβ is ar1 +q1 , which has coeﬃcient γ1 δ1 . Since αβ = 0, we must

have γ1 δ1 = 0 and, since | supp(γ1 )| + | supp(δ1 )| < m + n, this contradicts the choice of

α and β.

   In particular, if G is a ﬁnitely generated, torsion-free nilpotent group, then G has a sub-

normal series with inﬁnite cyclic factors. Thus G satisﬁes the conditions of Lemma 3.1.1

and F [G] is an integral domain.

   For an arbitrary torsion-free soluble group G, Lemma 3.1.1 is not strong enough to

imply that the groups rings Z[G] and Fp [G], where p is prime, are integral domains. The

positive solution of the zero-divisor problem for torsion-free soluble groups is a very deep

result:

Theorem 3.1.1 (Kropholler, Linnell and Moody, [25, Theorem 1.4]). Let F be a

field and let G be a torsion-free soluble group. If G is torsion-free then F [G] is an integral

domain.

   A right Ore domain is an integral domain R satisfying the right Ore condition: for each

pair of elements r, s ∈ R∗ there exist elements u, v ∈ R∗ such that ru = sv. Analogously,


                                              – 42 –
a left Ore domain is an integral domain R satisfying the left Ore condition: for each pair

of elements r, s ∈ R∗ there exist elements u, v ∈ R∗ such that ur = vs. A ring R which is

both a left Ore domain and a right Ore domain is an Ore domain.

    The following lemma follows easily from the fact that a skew polynomial ring over a

right Ore domain is a right Ore domain [14, Proposition 0.8.4]. See also Lewin’s proof of

this result [28].

Lemma 3.1.2. Let G be a soluble group and let R be a field or the ring of integers. If

the group ring R[G] is an integral domain then R[G] is an Ore domain.

Proof. Let G be a soluble group and let R be a ﬁeld or the ring of integers. We suppose
                                                          P                   P
that the group ring R[G] is an integral domain. Let α = ni=1 ai gi and β = m     i=1 bi hi

be elements of R[G]∗ with ai , bi ∈ R and gi , hi ∈ G. Let H = hg1 , . . . , gn , h1 , . . . , hm i;

then α, β ∈ R[H]∗ . Thus it is enough to show that the group ring over R of every ﬁnitely

generated subgroup of G is an Ore domain. By symmetry we need only consider the right

Ore condition.

    Let S be a ring which is not a right Ore domain, so that there exist α, β ∈ S such that

αS ∩ βS = {0}. This implies that the elements αn β (for n = 0, 1, . . .) are right linearly

independent over S and we have an inﬁnite chain of right ideals


                                   {0} = I0 < · · · < In < · · ·


where In is the ideal generated by the elements {αi β | i = 0, . . . , n}; thus S is not right

Noetherian.

    We proceed by induction on the derived length d of G. Suppose that G is abelian and

let H be a ﬁnitely generated subgroup of G; then H is polycyclic and, by a result of P.

Hall (see [53, 15.3.3]), the ring R[H] is Noetherian.

    Suppose now that the hypothesis holds for every soluble group of derived length at

most d − 1 whose group ring over R is an integral domain and that G has derived length

d. Let H be a ﬁnitely generated subgroup of G; then the derived subgroup H ′ of H has

derived length at most d − 1. The ring R[H ′ ] is a subring of R[G] and, therefore, an

integral domain. By induction, R[H ′ ] is an Ore domain. The quotient H/H ′ is a ﬁnitely



                                              – 43 –
generated abelian group; thus it is polycyclic and has a subnormal series with inﬁnite

cyclic factors

                          H ′ = H0 ⊳ H1 ⊳ · · · ⊳ Hk−1 ⊳ Hk = H.

We proceed now by induction on i to show that R[Hi ] is an Ore domain for i = 0, . . . , k.

Suppose that R[Hi−1 ] is an Ore domain and consider R[Hi ]. The quotient Hi /Hi−1

is an inﬁnite cyclic group, Hi /Hi−1 = haHi−1 i say, and hence the ring R[Hi ] is a skew

polynomial ﬁeld in a over R[Hi−1 ]. It follows that R[Hi ] is an Ore domain [14, Proposition

0.8.4]

   A right Ore domain R can be embedded in a skew-ﬁeld F . We deﬁne an equivalence

relation ∼ on R × R∗ as follows: (r1 , s1 ) ∼ (r2 , s2 ) if there exist u, v ∈ R∗ such that

s1 u = s2 v and r1 u = r2 v. The quotient of R × R∗ by this equivalence relation, with

the natural deﬁnitions of addition and multiplication, is the skew-ﬁeld F . This is the

skew-field of right fractions of R. Analogously, a left Ore domain R can by embedded in

a skew-ﬁeld, the skew-field of left fractions of R.

   Since R ⩽ F , we have R[G] ⩽ F [G] and, if F [G] is an integral domain, then R[G] is

an integral domain. In particular, Z is an Ore domain with ﬁeld of fractions Q and, if G

is a soluble group then Z[G] is an integral domain by Theorem 3.1.1 and hence an Ore

domain by Lemma 3.1.2.

   For a discussion of the history of the zero-divisor problem see Passman’s book [47,

Chapter 13] and for a discussion of Ore domains see Cohn’s book [14, Chapter 0].



3.2      Tensor products

Let R be a ring, let M be a right R-module and let N be a left R-module. The notion of

the tensor product of R-modules is useful in allowing us to prove some important results.

Deﬁnition 3.2.1. Let A be an abelian group under addition. A map α : M × N → A is

R-balanced if the following conditions hold:

  (i) (m1 + m2 , n)α = (m1 , n)α + (m2 , n)α;

 (ii) (m, n1 + n2 )α = (m, n1 )α + (m, n2 )α;


                                           – 44 –
(iii) (mr, n)α = (m, rn)α.

Deﬁnition 3.2.2. The tensor product of M and N is an abelian group T , together with

an R-balanced map ⊗ : M × N → T with the following property: for any R-balanced map

g : M × N → L to some abelian group L, there exists a unique group homomorphism

g̃ : T → L such that the following diagram commutes:


                                               g
                               M ×N                         L


                                       ⊗               g̃

                                                T



   Let F be the additive free abelian group with free basis the set M × N and let

ι : M × N → F be the inclusion map. Let K be the subgroup generated by the set


  {(m1 + m2 , n) − (m1 , n) − (m2 , n) | m1 , m2 ∈ M, n ∈ N }

                ∪ {(m, n1 + n2 ) − (m, n1 ) − (m, n2 ) | m ∈ M, n1 , n2 ∈ N }

                                           ∪ {(mr, n) − (m, rn) | m ∈ M, n ∈ N, r ∈ R}.

Let T be the quotient F/K, let q : F → T be the quotient map and let ⊗ : M × N → T be

the composite map ⊗ = ιq. Then the pair (T, ⊗) satisﬁes the conditions of Deﬁnition 3.2.2

(see [17, Theorem 3.4.2]). Thus the tensor product of M and N exists.

   If (T1 , ⊗1 ) and (T2 , ⊗2 ) are both tensor products of M and N then, by Deﬁnition 3.2.2,

there is an isomorphism φ : T1 → T2 such that the following diagram commutes:



                                                            T2
                                             ⊗2


                                M ×N                             φ


                                             ⊗1
                                                            T1

It follows that the tensor product of M and N is unique up to isomorphism. The image
                                             N
⊗(m, n) is written m ⊗ n and T is written M R N .


                                           – 45 –
 If N is also a right R-module then there is a unique right R-module structure on
 N
M R N compatible with the map ⊗ (see [17, Theorem 3.4.3]).

   For a further discussion of tensor products see Chapter 3 of the book on algebra by

Goldhaber and Ehrlich [17].



3.3     Wreath products

In Lemmas 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 we prove two crucial embedding results.

Lemma 3.3.1. Let A and B be torsion-free groups and suppose that A is abelian. Let G

be a finitely generated group with a normal subgroup N such that N ∼
                                                                   = A and G/N ∼
                                                                               = B.
If Z[G/N ] is an Ore domain and N is torsion-free as a Z[G/N ]-module then G embeds

in U wr B, for some finitely generated torsion-free abelian group U .

Proof. The group G is an extension of A by B and therefore G embeds in the unrestricted

wreath product A Wr B by the Kaloujnine–Krasner embedding (see Theorem 2.3.1). Let

K be the image of G under this embedding and let H be the group generated by K and B.

Then H = D ⋊ B for some subgroup D which is ﬁnitely generated as a normal subgroup

of H and which is in the base group of A Wr B. We may regard D as a Z[B]-module and

we let T be the set of Z[B]-torsion elements of D. Since Z[B] is an Ore domain, T is a

submodule of D. By the deﬁnition of the Kaloujnine–Krasner embedding, only elements

of N are mapped into D, and hence the intersection of D and K is in the image of N . As

discussed in Section 2.3, the image of N in A Wr B is torsion-free as a Z[B]-module and

hence K ∩ T is trivial; it follows that G can be embedded in (D/T ) ⋊ B.

   The quotient D/T is ﬁnitely generated as a right Z[B]-module. Let Q be the skew-ﬁeld

of right fractions of Z[B], which exists since Z[B] is a right Ore domain. Since D/T is

torsion-free as a right Z[B]-module, it can be embedded in the ﬁnitely generated Q-vector
                  N
space V = D/T Z[B] Q by [14, Corollary to Proposition 0.6.1] for which we may choose

a basis e1 , . . . , er . If d1 , . . . , dk generate D/T as a right Z[B]-module then, for each i,
                                                         P
there exist elements aij ∈ Q such that di = ri=1 ej aij . Since Z[B] is left Ore, we can

ﬁnd a common left denominator b ∈ Z[B]∗ for the elements aij : let aij = b−1 bij with
                   P
bij ∈ Z[B] and di = ri=1 (ei b−1 )bij . The quotient module D/T can be embedded in the


                                             – 46 –
ﬁnitely generated free right Z[B]-module M with free generators e1 b−1 , . . . , er b−1 .

   It follows that G embeds in the semi-direct product M ⋊ B, which is the restricted

wreath product of a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free abelian group and the group B.

Lemma 3.3.2. Let A be an abelian group of finite square-free exponent n and let B be

a torsion-free group. Let G be a finitely generated group with a normal subgroup N such

that N ∼
       = A and G/N ∼
                   = B. For each prime divisor p of n, suppose that Fp [G/N ] is
an Ore domain and that the submodule of N of elements of order p is torsion-free as an

Fp [G/N ]-module. Then G embeds in U wr B, for some finitely generated abelian group U

of exponent n.

Proof. By the same argument as in Lemma 3.3.1, the group G embeds in the subgroup

H = D ⋊ B of A Wr B for some subgroup D which is ﬁnitely generated as a normal

subgroup of H and which is in the base group of A Wr B. Let n = p1 · · · pk where p1 , . . . , pk

are distinct primes and let Di be the normal subgroup of D consisting of elements of order

pi so that D = D1 × · · · × Dk . We may regard D as an Rn [B]-module and each Di as an

Fpi [B]-module. By the deﬁnition of the Kaloujnine–Krasner embedding, only elements

of N are mapped into D, and hence the intersection of D and K is in the image of N .

Now, N = N1 × · · · × Nk , where Ni is of exponent pi and is torsion-free as an Fpi [G/N ]-

module. As discussed in Section 2.3 we may regard the image of Ni in A Wr B as a

torsion-free Fpi [B]-module for i = 1, . . . , k. Let Ti be the set of Fpi [B]-torsion elements

of Di . Since Fpi [B] is an Ore domain, the set Ti is an Fpi [B]-submodule of Di . Moreover,

K ∩ (T1 × · · · × Tk ) is trivial. Hence G can be embedded in

                                                             
                                (D1 /T1 ) × · · · × (Dk /Tk ) ⋊ B


and Di /Ti is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free Fpi [B]-module.

   By the same argument as in Lemma 3.3.1, the quotient module Di /Ti can be embedded

in a ﬁnitely generated free Fpi [B]-module Mi . Suppose that Mi is freely generated as an

Fpi [B]-module by ri elements and let r = max{r1 , . . . , rk }. For each i, we may embed Mi

in a free Fpi [B]-module M i of rank r and M = M 1 × · · · × M k is a free Rn [B]-module

of rank r. Then (D1 /T1 ) × · · · × (Dk /Tk ) embeds in M and G embeds in M ⋊ B which



                                             – 47 –
is the restricted wreath product of a ﬁnitely generated abelian group of exponent n and

the group B.

   Suppose for the remainder of this section that n is a square-free positive integer or

zero and that c = (c1 , . . . , cl ) is a tuple of positive integers. Recall from Chapter 2 the

deﬁnition of words sci (x). A group G is in Pci if and only if the verbal subgroup sci (G)

is trivial. We prove some results about subgroups of restricted wreath products.

Lemma 3.3.3. Let U be a finitely generated abelian group of exponent n and let P be a

finitely generated torsion-free group in Pc . If G is a finitely generated subgroup of U wr P

and G is in Pc then either G embeds in P or G embeds in V wr Q, where V is a finitely

generated abelian group of exponent n and Q is a finitely generated subgroup of P such

that Q ∈ Pcl−1 .

Proof. Let A be the base group of the restricted wreath product U wr P , so that U wr P =

A ⋊ P . We may write elements as pairs (u, d) with u ∈ P and d ∈ A. Let φ : U wr P →

P : (u, d) 7→ u be the canonical map and let θ := φ|G . There are two cases to consider:

  (i) im θ ∈ Pcl−1 ;

 (ii) im θ ∈ Pc \ Pcl−1 .

Let Q = im θ and let N = ker θ = G ∩ A, so that Q ∼
                                                  = G/N .


Case (i): Suppose to begin with that n = 0 and consider the action of Z[Q] on N : since A

      is torsion-free as a Z[P ]-module, the submodule N is torsion-free as a Z[Q]-module.

      The group G is an extension of N by Q satisfying the conditions of Lemma 3.3.1

      and it follows that G embeds in V wr Q where V is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free

      abelian group.

      Suppose now that n 6= 0 and let p be a prime divisor of n. The submodule of A

      of elements of order p is torsion-free as an Fp [P ]-module and hence the submodule

      of N of elements of order p is torsion-free as an Fp [Q]-module. The group G is an

      extension of N by Q satisfying the conditions of Lemma 3.3.2 and it follows that G

      embeds in V wr Q where V is a ﬁnitely generated abelian group of exponent n.


                                            – 48 –
Case (ii): Since Q 6∈ Pcl−1 , the group G contains an element g such that g ∈ scl−1 (G)

      and g 6∈ N . Suppose for a contradiction that N is non-trivial, so that there is

      some h′ ∈ N with h′ 6= 1. The element [g, h′ ] is in N ∩ scl−1 (G) since h′ ∈ N ⊳ G

      and g ∈ scl−1 (G) ⊳ G. If [g, h′ ] = 1 then, by Lemma 2.3.1, either h′ = 1 or

      g ∈ A ∩ G = N contradicting our assumptions. Thus h = [g, h′ ] is a non-trivial

      element of N ∩ scl−1 (G). The group scl−1 (G) is nilpotent of class cl and contains

      both g and h. Thus [h, g, . . . , g ] = 1 and, by repeated applications of Lemma 2.3.1,
                             | {z }
                                 cl
      either h = 1 or g ∈ A ∩ G = N contradicting our choice of the elements h and g.

      Hence N = ker θ is trivial and θ is an embedding of G into P .

   The following is a corollary of Lemma 3.3.3.

Lemma 3.3.4. Let U be a finitely generated abelian group of exponent n and let P be a

finitely generated torsion-free group in Pc . If G is a finitely generated subgroup of U wr P

and G is in Pci for some i ⩽ l, then either G embeds in P or G embeds in V wr Q, where

V is a finitely generated abelian group of exponent n and Q is a finitely generated subgroup

of P such that Q ∈ Pci−1 .

Proof. Suppose that G does not embed in P . By Lemma 3.3.3, the group G embeds in

V1 wr Q1 , where V1 is a ﬁnitely generated abelian group of exponent n and Q1 is a ﬁnitely

generated subgroup of P such that Q1 ∈ Pcl−1 . Since G does not embed in P , it does

not embed in Q1 and, by repeated applications of Lemma 3.3.3, it follows that G embeds

in V wr Q where V is a ﬁnitely generated abelian group of exponent n and Q is a ﬁnitely

generated subgroup of P such that Q ∈ Pci .

   We now consider what can be said about the nilpotent subgroups of restricted wreath

products U wr H. The next result is particularly useful when H is itself nilpotent.

Lemma 3.3.5. If U is an abelian group of exponent n and H is a torsion-free group then

a finitely generated nilpotent subgroup of U wr H, which is not contained in the base group

of the wreath product, can be embedded into H.

Proof. Let A be the base group of U wr H, so that U wr H = A ⋊ H. Again we write

elements as pairs (u, d) with u ∈ H and d ∈ A. Let φ : U wr H → H : (u, d) 7→ u be the


                                           – 49 –
canonical map and let θ := φ|G . If ker θ = 1 then θ is an embedding of G into H. Suppose

now that ker θ 6= 1. Let N = ker θ = A ∩ G and let y be a non-trivial element of N .

The group G is nilpotent and hence has non-trivial centre; choose z ∈ Z(G) \ {1}. Since

y 6= 1, this implies that z is in N by Lemma 2.3.1. Now let x be an arbitrary element of

G. Then [z, x] = 1 and, again by Lemma 2.3.1, we have x ∈ N . Thus G is contained in

N ⩽ A, the base group of U wr H.

3.4     Universal theory

We begin by noting that Timoshenko’s proof that the restricted wreath product preserves

universal equivalence [65, Theorem 2] can easily be adapted to give the following result.

                                            – 53 –
                                     Chapter 4


FREE GROUPS IN THE VARIETY An A WHERE n IS A

               SQUARE-FREE POSITIVE INTEGER



Chapuis [12] characterizes those groups which satisfy the universal theory of a non-cyclic,

free metabelian group from three distinct points of view:

   • in terms of the module-theoretic properties of the Fitting subgroup;

   • as those groups satisfying a certain collection of universal sentences;

   • in terms of the embeddability of ﬁnitely generated subgroups in certain restricted

     wreath products.

As well as giving an explicit description of the universal theory of a non-cyclic free me-

tabelian group, this characterization provides a proof of the decidability of the universal

theory of a non-cyclic, free metabelian group which avoids the combinatorial arguments

of his original proof in [11]. Chapuis calls groups universally equivalent to a non-cyclic,

free metabelian group ∀-free metabelian. He gives a number of applications of his main

theorem including a characterization of ∀-free metabelian groups in terms of residual pro-

perties, a proof that parafree metabelian groups are ∀-free metabelian and a study of

2-generator ∀-free metabelian groups. In particular, he shows that there are precisely two

non-isomorphic 2-generator ∀-free metabelian groups, namely the free metabelian group

of rank 2 and the restricted wreath product of two inﬁnite cyclic groups.

   In this chapter we obtain similar results to those of Chapuis in the case of free groups

in the variety An A where n is a square-free positive integer. Our proofs also are similar

to those of Chapuis, the main new ingredients being some of those results proved in


                                          – 54 –
Chapter 3. We characterize those groups contained in the universal closure of a non-

cyclic free group in An A and use this characterization to prove that the universal theory

of a non-cyclic free group in this variety is decidable. We prove that a non-abelian

ﬁnitely generated group G is universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in Ap A

for a prime p if and only if G is ℵ0 -approximable by groups universally equivalent to

F2 (Ap A). Moreover we show that there are precisely two non-isomorphic 2-generator

groups universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in An A.



4.1     Statement of theorem

In his paper [12], Chapuis deﬁnes the notion of ρ-groups in order to capture some of the

module-theoretic properties of the Fitting subgroup of a non-cyclic free metabelian group.

We shall require a similar notion for our study of groups satisfying the universal theory

of a non-cyclic free group in An A.

Deﬁnition 4.1.1. (σn -groups). A group G is a σn -group if it satisﬁes the following

conditions:

  1. G is metabelian;

  2. Fitt(G) is abelian, of exponent dividing n and isolated in G;

  3. For each prime divisor p of n, the submodule of Fitt(G) of elements of order p is

      torsion-free as an Fp [G/ Fitt(G)]-module;

  4. Every abelian subgroup of G is either torsion-free or of exponent dividing n.


In Section 4.2 below we deﬁne the collection Un of universal sentences.

Theorem 4.1.1. If G is a group then the following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G satisfies the universal theory of a non-cyclic free group in An A;

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Un ;

 (3) G is a σn -group or G is torsion-free abelian;



                                          – 55 –
                                                                                                 (r)
 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in Cn wr Z(s) for some

       r, s ∈ N.


We show that, for a positive integer m, any two non-cyclic free groups in Am A have the

same universal theory. Thus it makes sense to consider the universal theory of a non-cyclic

free group in Am A. In order to do this we ﬁrst show that every non-cyclic free group in

Am A is universally equivalent to the restricted wreath product Cm wr Z.

tricted wreath product Cm wr Z.

            = Cm wr Z.

Corollary 4.1.1. A non-cyclic free group in Am A is universally equivalent to Cm wr Z.

Proof. Let F be a non-cyclic free group in Am A. It contains a copy of F2 (Am A) which

in turn contains a copy of Cm wr Z by Lemma 4.1.2. Thus Cm wr Z satisﬁes the universal

theory of F . By Lemma 4.1.1, the group F satisﬁes the universal theory of Cm wr Z. It

follows that F is universally equivalent to Cm wr Z.

   It also follows immediately that

Corollary 4.1.2. Any two non-cyclic free groups in Am A have the same universal theory.



4.2     The sentences

We begin with some useful one-variable formulae. We deﬁne a universal formula


                                      ﬁtt∀ (x) : ∀ t ([x, xt ] = 1)


and an existential formula


                         ﬁtt∃ (x) : ∃ t1 t2 ([t1 , t2 , x] = 1 ∧ [t1 , t2 ] 6= 1) .


The signiﬁcance of the formulae ﬁtt∀ (x) and ﬁtt∃ (x) is as follows: if G is a model of Un

then Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G) and if G is a non-abelian model of Un then Fitt(G) ⊆ ﬁtt∃ (G)

(see Lemma 4.3.1 below).

   For each positive integer m and each prime p, we denote by Im,p the set of partitions

of {1, . . . , m} into sets X of size a multiple of p.

   Let Un be the union of the following six sets of universal sentences together with the

sentence φgp as deﬁned on page 14:




                                                 – 57 –

    A group G satisﬁes φ1 if and only if G is metabelian.

(2) The countable collection of sentences {φn2 (m) | m ∈ N}, where φn2 (m) is deﬁned by
            

    either torsion-free or of exponent n.

                       ∀xy (([x, y, x] = 1 ∧ [x, y, y] = 1) → [x, y] = 1) .

    If a group G satisﬁes φ3 then every nilpotent subgroup of G is abelian.

    Let G be a non-abelian metabelian group such that every nilpotent subgroup of G

    Let G be a non-abelian metabelian group such that every nilpotent subgroup of G

   Each of the sentences in Un contains only the universal quantiﬁer ∀ when written in

prenex normal form. In certain cases we have given the sentences in a more transparently

comprehensible form than the prenex normal form.

Lemma 4.2.1.

                                       Cn wr Z |= Un

Proof. By Lemma 2.3.1, we have ﬁtt∃ (Cn wr Z) = Fitt(Cn wr Z) and it is clear that

ﬁtt∀ (Cn wr Z) = Fitt(Cn wr Z). The base group D of Cn wr Z is a direct product of

groups Di of exponent pi , where the pi are the prime divisors of n. The ring Fpi [Z] is an

integral domain (for example by Lemma 3.1.1) and, since Di is a free Fpi [Z]-module, it is

torsion-free. It follows easily from these facts that Cn wr Z |= Un .



4.3     σn-groups

In this section we establish the relationship between the σn -groups deﬁned in Section 4.1

and the sentences Un deﬁned in the previous section. This relationship plays a key role

in our proof of Theorem 4.1.1.

   In Lemma 4.3.1 we explain the signiﬁcance of the universal formula ﬁtt∀ (x) and the

existential formula ﬁtt∃ (x). These formulae are important in allowing us to describe,

using universal sentences, the Fitting subgroup Fitt(G) of a group G and the quotient

group G/ Fitt(G).



                                           – 59 –
Lemma 4.3.1. Let G be a group such that G |= Un ; then Fitt(G) is abelian and Fitt(G) =

ﬁtt∀ (G). If G is not abelian then g ∈ Fitt(G) implies G |= ﬁtt∃ (g).

Proof. By Fitting’s theorem, every ﬁnitely generated subgroup of Fitt(G) is nilpotent.

The validity of the sentence φ3 in G implies that every nilpotent subgroup of G is abelian

and it follows that Fitt(G) is abelian. If g is an element of Fitt(G) then the normal closure

in G of g is in Fitt(G) which is abelian. Thus [gh , g] = 1 for all h ∈ G and g ∈ ﬁtt∀ (G).

Now let g be an element of ﬁtt∀ (G), so that g commutes with all its conjugates in G. The

normal closure in G of g is abelian and g ∈ Fitt(G).

   Suppose now that G is not abelian and let g be an element of Fitt(G). Since G is

metabelian, G′ is an abelian normal subgroup of G and G′ ⩽ Fitt(G). Since G is not

abelian, there exist elements h1 , h2 ∈ G such that [h1 , h2 ] 6= 1. The elements [h1 , h2 ] and

g are in Fitt(G) which is abelian and hence [h1 , h2 , g] = 1. Therefore g ∈ Fitt(G) implies

G |= ﬁtt∃ (g).

   In Lemmas 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 we show that, for a non-abelian group G, the statements

that G is a σn -group and that G satisﬁes the sentences Un are equivalent.

Lemma 4.3.2. If G is a non-abelian group such that G |= Un then G is a σn -group.

Proof. The validity of the sentence φ1 in G implies that G is metabelian. Since G |= φn4

and G |= φ5 (m) for all m ∈ N, it follows that Fitt(G) is of exponent n and isolated in G.

Let p be a prime divisor of n and let g be an element of Fitt(G) of order p. The sentences

φp6 (m) for all m ∈ N hold in G; if gα = 1 for some α ∈ Fp [G/ Fitt(G)] then α = 0.

Thus the submodule of Fitt(G) of elements of order p is torsion-free as an Fp [G/ Fitt(G)]-

module. Finally the validity of the sentence φn2 (m) for all m ∈ N implies that every

abelian subgroup of G is either torsion-free or of exponent n.

Lemma 4.3.3. If G is a σn -group then G |= Un .

Proof. Let G be a σn -group. It is clear that G satisﬁes the sentences φ1 and φn2 (m) for

all m ∈ N. Let g be an element of G such that G |= ﬁtt∃ (g). Then there exist elements

h1 , h2 ∈ G such that h = [h1 , h2 ] 6= 1 and [h, g] = 1. Since G is metabelian, G′ ⩽ Fitt(G)

and the element h is in Fitt(G). Suppose that h is of order m (where m divides n) and


                                            – 60 –
                                                m
let p be a prime divisor of m. Then h′ = h p is a non-trivial element of the submodule

Np of Fitt(G) of elements of order dividing p. Moreover, if [h, g] = 1 then


                                    h′(−1+g) = [h′ , g] = 1.


Thus, since Np is torsion-free as an Fp [G/ Fitt(G)]-module, the image of g in G/ Fitt(G) is

trivial and g is in Fitt(G). Hence ﬁtt∃ (G) ⊆ Fitt(G). Moreover, since Fitt(G) is abelian,

ﬁtt∀ (G) = Fitt(G). It follows easily that the sentences φn4 , φ5 (m) for all m ∈ N and φp6 (m)

for all prime divisors p of n and all m ∈ N hold in G. It remains to show that G |= φ3 .

Let g and h be elements of G such that [g, h, g] = 1 and [g, h, h] = 1. The subgroup

Fitt(G) is abelian and so if g and h are elements of Fitt(G) then [g, h] = 1. We suppose,

for a contradiction, that [g, h] 6= 1 and we may assume, without loss of generality, that g

is not in Fitt(G). If [g, h, g] = 1 then [g, h]−1+g = 1 and −1 + g is a non-trivial element of

Fp [G/ Fitt(G)] for some prime divisor p of n. By the same argument as before, with [g, h]

in place of h, we show that g is an element of Fitt(G), contradicting our assumptions.

Thus G |= φ3 .



4.4     Proof of theorem

For the reader’s convenience we restate the theorem which will be proved in this section.

Recall that n is a square-free positive integer.

Theorem 4.1.1 If G is a group then the following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G satisfies the universal theory of a non-cyclic group free in An A;

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Un ;

 (3) G is a σn -group or G is torsion-free abelian;

                                                                          (r)
 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in Cn wr Z(s) for some

      r, s ∈ N.

Proof. We prove the implications (1) =⇒ (2) ⇐⇒ (3) =⇒ (4) =⇒ (1).




                                            – 61 –
(1) =⇒ (2). Let F be a non-cyclic free group in An A. By Corollary 4.1.1, the group

     F is universally equivalent to Cn wr Z. Thus G |= Th∀ (F ) = Th∀ (Cn wr Z). By

     Lemma 4.2.1, we have Cn wr Z |= Un and hence G |= Un .

(2) ⇐⇒ (3). Suppose to begin with that G is abelian. Since G satisﬁes φn2 (m) for all

     m ∈ N, either G is torsion-free or G is of exponent dividing n. In the latter case

     G is a σn -group. This, together with Lemma 4.3.3, implies the equivalence of (2)

     and (3) when G is abelian. If G is non-abelian then the equivalence of (2) and (3)

     follows immediately from the results of Section 4.3.

(3) =⇒ (4). Let G be a σn -group and let G1 be a ﬁnitely generated subgroup of G. Since

     G satisﬁes Un which is a universal set of sentences, every subgroup of G satisﬁes

     Un ; in particular, we have G1 |= Un . The validity in G of the sentences φn2 (m) for

     m ∈ N implies that if G1 is abelian then it is either torsion-free or of exponent

     dividing n. In the former case G1 embeds in some power of Z and in the latter case

     G1 = Cn1 × · · · × Cnr where Cnj is a cyclic group of exponent nj and nj divides n.

     The cyclic group Cnj embeds in Cn for each j and hence G1 embeds in the direct

     product of r copies of Cn .

     Suppose now that G1 is non-abelian, so that G1 is a σn -group by Lemma 4.3.2.

     Then G1 is an extension of Fitt(G1 ) by G1 = G1 / Fitt(G1 ) satisfying the conditions

     of Lemma 3.3.2, and hence G1 embeds in V wr G1 , where V is a ﬁnitely generated

     abelian group of exponent dividing n. As in the abelian case above, V embeds in
       (r)
     Cn      for some positive integer r and, since G1 is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free

     abelian group, it isomorphic to Z(s) for some positive integer s. It follows that G1
                    (r)
     embeds in Cn wr Z(s) .

(4) =⇒ (1). Let F be a non-cyclic free group in An A and let φ be in Th∀ (F ). We may

     suppose that φ is of the form


                                     ∀x1 . . . xk ϕ(x1 , . . . , xk )


     where ϕ(x1 , . . . , xk ) is quantiﬁer-free. We let g1 . . . , gk be elements of G and let
                                                     (r)
     G1 = hg1 , . . . , gk i, so that G1 embeds in Cn wr Z(s) for some positive integers r and


                                            – 62 –
                                                     (r)
      s. By Lemmas 3.4.2 and 4.1.1, we have Cn wr Z(s) |= Th∀ (Cn wr Z) = Th∀ (F );

      in particular, G1 satisﬁes φ and ϕ(g1 , . . . , gk ) holds. This is true for all k-tuples

      g1 , . . . , gk ∈ G and hence G satisﬁes φ. It follows that G |= Th∀ (F ) and G ∈

      ucl(F ).



4.5     Some consequences of the theorem

In this section we consider some of the consequences of Theorem 4.1.1. Let F be a non-

cyclic free group in An A. We establish necessary and suﬃcient conditions for a group

in ucl(F ) to be universally equivalent to F and we use these conditions to prove that

the universal theory of F is decidable. We go on to construct lattice diagrams of those

universally closed classes of groups in ucl(F ) for selected values of n. We also construct

such a lattice diagram for the universal closure of a non-cyclic free metabelian group;

Chapuis did not do so in his paper [12]. As a further consequence of Theorem 4.1.1, we

prove that a non-abelian ﬁnitely generated group G is universally equivalent to a non-

cyclic free group in Ap A for a prime p if and only if G is ℵ0 -approximable by groups

universally equivalent to F2 (Ap A). Finally we determine the isomorphism classes of 2-

generator groups universally equivalent to F .

Corollary 4.5.1. A group G is universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in An A

if and only if it is non-abelian, contains an element of order n and satisfies the collection

Un of universal sentences.

Proof. Let G be a non-abelian group satisfying Un and containing an element of order

n. Theorem 4.1.1 implies that G is a σn -group. Let g be an element of G \ Fitt(G) and

let h be an element of G such that o(h) = n. Then h is a non-trivial element of Fitt(G)
                                                                                    t
and the annihilator of h in Rn [G/ Fitt(G)] is trivial. For t ∈ Z, let Ht = hhg i and let

H = hHt | t ∈ Zi. Then H is a direct product of the Ht and each Ht is isomorphic to Cn .

By deﬁnition H ⊳ hg, hi and, since A is isolated in G, the intersection H ∩ hgi is trivial.

Thus hg, hi is the semidirect product of H by hgi and hg, hi ∼
                                                             = Cn wr Z. It follows that G
is universally equivalent to Cn wr Z and hence to Fr (An A) for r ⩾ 2 by Corollary 4.1.1.

   Suppose now that G is universally equivalent to a non-cyclic group F free in An A.


                                            – 63 –
Theorem 4.1.1 implies that G |= Un . Let θ and θn be existential sentences deﬁned as

follows:

                              θ : ∃xy ([x, y] 6= 1),
                                                  k
                                                                  !
                                                  ^
                                         n              n/pi
                             θn : ∃x   x =1∧            x      6= 1
                                                  i=1

where n = p1 · · · pk and each pi is prime. We have Cn wr Z |= θ and Cn wr Z |= θn . Thus,

since F is universally equivalent to Cn wr Z and G is universally equivalent to F , it follows

that G |= θ and G |= θn . Hence G is non-abelian and contains an element of order n.

   If n is a prime p then the condition that G contains an elements of order p follows from

the fact that G is non-abelian: the subgroup G′ is non-trivial and contained in Fitt(G);

since Fitt(G) has exponent dividing p, it follows that any non-trivial element of G′ is of

order p.

Corollary 4.5.2. A group G is universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in Ap A,

where p is prime, if and only if it is non-abelian and satisfies the collection of universal

sentences Up .

   The necessary and suﬃcient conditions given in Corollary 4.5.1 for a group to be

universally equivalent to a non-cyclic group F free in An A yield a recursive collection of

universal and existential sentences which completely distinguish those groups universally

equivalent to F . Using this result we show that F has decidable universal theory.

Corollary 4.5.3. The universal theory of a non-cyclic free group in An A is decidable.

Proof. Let Un be the recursive set of sentences Un ∪ {θ, θn }. By Lemma 4.5.1, we have

G |= Un if and only if G is universally equivalent to F = Fr (An A) for r ⩾ 2. Let φ

be a universal sentence; by the completeness theorem, Un ⊢ φ or Un ⊢ ¬φ. We have

φ ∈ Th∀ (F ) if and only if Un ⊢ φ and φ 6∈ Th∀ (F ) if and only if Un ⊢ ¬φ. Thus, since Un

is recursive, the universal theory of F is decidable.

   The results of Chapuis [12] show that a group is universally equivalent to a non-cyclic

free metabelian group F if and only if it is non-abelian and contained in the universal

closure of F . Moreover, a torsion-free abelian group A is universally equivalent to Z if


                                             – 64 –
and only if it is non-trivial [16, Lemma 1]. Using these facts we can construct a lattice

diagram of the universally closed classes of groups in the universal closure of a non-cyclic

free metabelian group (see Figure 4.1). Since ﬁnite groups of diﬀerent orders can be

distinguished using universal sentences1 , the picture becomes more complex when the

bottom group is of ﬁnite exponent (see Figures 4.2 and 4.3). Whereas all non-trivial

torsion-free abelian groups are universally equivalent, abelian groups of ﬁnite exponent,

with ﬁnite generating sets of diﬀering size, are not. When dealing with groups whose

Fitting subgroup has non-prime exponent, we also have non-abelian universally closed

classes of groups properly contained in the universal closure of a non-cyclic free group in

An A. These are classes of groups which do not contain an element of order n.

      In Figure 4.3 we have three sublattices Lp , Lq and Lpq , where p and q are distinct

primes. These are the lattices of universally closed classes of abelian groups of exponent

dividing p, q and pq respectively, such that each class in the lattice contains a group of

exponent p, q and pq respectively. The lattice Lp also occurs as a sublattice in Figure 4.2.

For a more explicit depiction of these lattices showing all universal closures of abelian

groups of exponent dividing pq see Figure 4.4. We note that each class in Lp and each

class in Lq is contained in some class in Lpq . In Figure 4.3 we have omitted some of

the points in the sublattice of abelian groups. These points represent the union of two

or more universal closures of groups, at least one of which is contained in one of the

sublattices Lp , Lq and Lpq . For example, we have omitted the class of groups which are

abelian and either of order dividing p or of order dividing q. This class is the union of

ucl(Cp ) and ucl(Cq ). These omissions simplify the presentation of the lattice greatly and

do not have a signiﬁcant impact on the information it contains. The two occurrences

in Figure 4.3 of the following universally closed classes of groups should be thought of

as single points in the lattice: the class of groups with Fitting subgroup of exponent p

or q and the universal closure of Z. They have been duplicated in order to simplify the

presentation of the lattice.

                                            – 68 –
    Next we consider the relationship between universal equivalence and ℵ0 -approximab-

ility. Let X be a non-trivial class of groups and let r be a positive integer. A group G

is r-approximable by X-groups if, for all non-trivial g1 , . . . , gr ∈ G, there exists a group

H ∈ X and a homomorphism f : G → H such that f (gi ) 6= 1 for i = 1, . . . , n. A group

G is ℵ0 -approximable by X-groups if it is r-approximable by X-groups for all r ∈ N.

In [49] Remeslennikov showed that a ﬁnitely generated non-abelian group is universally

equivalent to a non-cyclic free group if and only if it is ℵ0 -approximable by non-cyclic free

groups and, in [12, Section 5], Chapuis showed that the same is true for free metabelian

groups: a ﬁnitely generated non-abelian group is ∀-free metabelian if and only if it is

ℵ0 -approximable by non-cyclic free metabelian groups. By Corollary 4.5.2, a non-abelian

group which satisﬁes the universal theory of a non-cyclic free group in Ap A, where p is

prime, is universally equivalent to it. We use this fact to prove a similar result about

ℵ0 -approximability in the case of free groups in Ap A.

Corollary 4.5.4. Let X be a non-empty class of groups universally equivalent to a non-

cyclic free group in Ap A, where p is prime. A finitely generated non-abelian group is

universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in Ap A if and only if it is ℵ0 -approximable

by X-groups.

Proof. Let X be a non-empty class of groups universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free

group in Ap A, where p is prime, and let G be a ﬁnitely generated non-abelian group.

    We suppose initially that G is universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in Ap A,

so that G is in Ap A. Finitely generated metabelian groups have the maximal condition

on normal subgroups (P. Hall, see [53, 15.3.1]) and hence G has a ﬁnite presentation

ha1 , . . . , as | r1 (a), . . . , rt (a)i in Ap A. Let g1 , . . . , gr be non-trivial elements of G, so that

gi = gi (a) for i = 1, . . . , r. We consider the existential sentence ψ deﬁned by
                                            t              r
                                                                        !
                                            ^              ^
                              ∃ x1 . . . xs   ri (x) = 1 ∧   gi (x) 6= 1
                                            i=1               i=1

where x is the s-tuple (x1 , . . . , xs ). Each group in X is universally equivalent to a non-

cyclic free group in Ap A and hence is universally equivalent to G. Since G |= ψ, it follows

that H |= ψ for each group H ∈ X. Fix H ∈ X and choose b1 , . . . , bs ∈ H such that

ri (b) = 1 for i = 1, . . . , t and gi (b) 6= 1 for i = 1, . . . , r. Then the map f : G → H deﬁned


                                                  – 69 –
by ai 7→ bi for i = 1, . . . , s is the required homomorphism by Von Dyck’s Theorem (see

[53, 2.2.1]).

    Suppose now that G is ℵ0 -approximable by X-groups. By Corollary 4.5.2, it is suf-

ﬁcient to show that G satisﬁes the universal theory of a non-cyclic free group in Ap A.

Equivalently, we show that a non-cyclic free group F in Ap A satisﬁes the existential theory

of G. We let φ be a sentence in Th∃ (G) and we assume without loss of generality that φ

is of the form                                                                !
                                         s
                                         ^                    t
                                                              ^
                          ∃x1 . . . xr         ui (x) = 1 ∧         wj (x) 6= 1
                                         i=1                  j=1

where x is the r-tuple (x1 , . . . , xr ). Since G satisﬁes φ, we may choose g1 , . . . , gr ∈ G such

that ui (g) = 1 for i = 1, . . . , s and wj (g) 6= 1 for j = 1, . . . , t. There is a group H ∈ X

and a homomorphism f : G → H such that wj (h) = f (wj (g)) 6= 1 for j = 1, . . . , t where

h is the r-tuple (h1 , . . . , hr ) and hi = f (gi ) for i = 1, . . . , r. Since f is a homomorphism,

ui (h) = f (ui (g)) = 1 for i = 1, . . . , s. Hence H satisﬁes φ and it follows, since H is

universally equivalent to F , that F satisﬁes φ.

    In particular we may choose X = {F2 (Ap A)}. Thus a ﬁnitely generated non-abelian

group G is universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in Ap A if and only if it is

ℵ0 -approximable by F2 (Ap A).

    The ﬁnal result in this section concerns 2-generator groups universally equivalent to a

free group in An A. Our proof requires the following well-known result (see, for example,

[12, Lemma 5.4]).

Lemma 4.5.1. If G is a 2-generator group containing a normal subgroup N such that

G/N ∼
    = Z then there exist elements u, v ∈ G such that G = hu, vi with v ∈ N \ {1}.

Proof. Since G/N is cyclic we can choose u ∈ G which generates G modulo N . If H =

hx, yi then x = ur c1 and y = us c2 for some integers r and s and some elements c1 , c2 ∈ N .

We choose x and y in such a way as to minimise max{|r|, |s|}. Replacing x with x−1

and y with y −1 as required, we may assume without loss of generality that both r and s

are non-negative. If r = 0 or s = 0 then we have the desired result. Suppose therefore

that r > 0 and s > 0 and let y1 = x2 x−1
                                      1 . Clearly G is generated by x and y1 and




                                                  – 70 –
y1 = us−r c3 with c3 ∈ N . If r = s then y1 ∈ N and we have the desired result. Otherwise

max{|r|, |s − r|} < max{|r|, |s|} contradicting the choice of x and y.

   We are now able to determine explicitly those 2 generator groups universally equivalent

to a free group in An A.

Corollary 4.5.5. A 2-generator group universally equivalent to a free group in An A is

isomorphic to either F2 (An A) or Cn wr Z.

Proof. Let H = hg, hi be a 2-generator group universally equivalent to a free group in

An A. Let A = Fitt(H). We have two cases:

  (i) the elements g and h are linearly independent modulo A;

 (ii) there exist r, s ∈ N such that gr hs = 1 modulo A.


Case (i): Let F = F2 (An A) = hx, yi. Since H ∈ An A, there exists an epimorphism

     f : F → H with f (x) = g and f (y) = h. Suppose that the kernel of f is non-trivial

     and let u ∈ F \ {1} such that f (u) = 1. We can write u as u = xr y s modulo

     F ′ . Thus, since H ′ ⩽ A, we have 1 = f (u) = gr hs modulo A. By our hypothesis

     this implies that r = s = 0 and u ∈ F ′ . The element [x, y] generates F ′ as an

     Rn [F/F ′ ]-module and

                                              Chapter 5


          LEFT-ITERATED WREATH PRODUCTS OF

                     TORSION-FREE ABELIAN GROUPS



Chapuis [11] proved using combinatorial arguments that a left-iterated restricted wreath

product of torsion-free abelian groups has decidable universal theory. It is worth noting

that, in contrast to the metabelian case, a non-cyclic free soluble group of derived length

d ⩾ 3 is not universally equivalent to the left-iterated wreath product of d non-trivial

torsion-free abelian groups; for d = 3 this can be seen as follows:

Remark 5.0.1. ([11, Remark 2.6]) The group wr3i=1 Ai where Ai is a torsion-free

abelian group can be distinguished from the group F2 (S3 ) by the sentence θ deﬁned by
                                           
  ∃xy1 y2 z1 z2 z3     [x, xz1 ], [x, xz1 ]z2 6= 1∧
                                                                                                            
                                                     [y1 , y2 ], [y1 , y2 ]z3 =6 1 ∧ [y1 , y2 ], [y1 , y2 ]x = 1 .

   For completeness we include a proof of this remark.

Proof. Suppose for a contradiction that F = F2 (S3 ) satisﬁes θ, so that there exist ele-

ments a ∈ F \ F ′ and b = [b1 , b2 ] ∈ F ′ \ F ′′ such that [b, ba ] = 1. By Theorem 2.4.4, every

pair of commuting elements in F which are not in F ′′ are in a cyclic subgroup. Thus

there exist non-zero integers r and s such that br = (ba )s . From the Magnus embedding,

we see that F ′ /F ′′ is torsion-free as a Z[F/F ′ ] module and it follows that b is in F ′′ or

a is in F ′ , contradicting our assumptions. Thus no such elements exist and we have the

required contradiction.

   A non-trivial torsion-free abelian group is universally equivalent to the inﬁnite cy-

clic group Z [16, Lemma 1]. Since the restricted wreath product construction preserves


                                                       – 73 –
universal equivalence [65, Theorem 2], a left-iterated wreath product of three non-trivial

torsion-free abelian groups is universally equivalent to Z wr(Z wr Z). It is straightforward

to choose elements of Z wr(Z wr Z) which demonstrate that Z wr(Z wr Z) |= θ.

   Chapuis [12] comments that it would be interesting to obtain an explicit description

of the universal theory of a left-iterated wreath product of torsion-free abelian groups.

In this chapter we characterize those groups which satisfy the universal theory of a left-

iterated wreath product of d non-trivial torsion-free abelian groups in two ways:

   • in terms of the module-theoretic properties of the Fitting subgroup;

   • in terms of the embeddability of ﬁnitely generated subgroups in certain left-iterated

      restricted wreath products.

We also recursively deﬁne a collection of universal sentences such that a group, which

is not soluble of derived length d − 1, satisﬁes the universal theory of a left-iterated

wreath product of d non-trivial torsion-free abelian groups if and only if it satisﬁes these

sentences.



5.1     Statement of theorems

The following deﬁnition is motivated by Chapuis’ deﬁnition of ρ-groups in [12]. Our

deﬁnition of ρ2 -groups is equivalent to that of ρ-groups.

Deﬁnition 5.1.1. (ρd -groups). A group G is a ρ1 -group if it is torsion-free and abelian.

For d ⩾ 2, a group G is a ρd -group if the following conditions hold:

  1. G is torsion-free and soluble of derived length at most d;

  2. Every nilpotent subgroup of G is abelian;

  3. Fitt(G) is torsion-free as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module;

  4. G/ Fitt(G) is a ρd−1 -group.


In Section 5.2 below we deﬁne the collection Wd of universal sentences.



                                          – 74 –
Theorem 5.1.1. Let S be a left-iterated wreath product of d non-trivial torsion-free abe-

lian groups. If G is a group which is not in Sd−1 then the following conditions are

equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(S);

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Wd ;

 (3) G is a ρd -group;

 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some

      r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N.


Theorem 5.1.2. Let S be a left-iterated wreath product of d non-trivial torsion-free abe-

lian groups. If G is a finitely generated group then the following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(S);

 (2) G can be embedded in wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N;

 (3) G is a ρd -group.


   We note to begin with that S is universally equivalent to Gd = wrdi=1 Ai where each Ai

is an inﬁnite cyclic group: this is an immediate consequence of the fact that a torsion-free

abelian group is universally equivalent to Z [16, Lemma 1] and the fact that the restricted

wreath product preserves universal equivalence [65, Theorem 2].



5.2     The sentences

Let Gd = wrdi=1 Ai be the left-iterated wreath product of d copies of the inﬁnite cyclic

group. We deﬁne recursively a set of universal sentences Wd which hold in Gd . Recall

from page 22 the deﬁnition of the words si (x). We begin with some useful one-variable

formulae.

   We deﬁne a universal formula

The signiﬁcance of the formulae ﬁtt∀ (x) and ﬁtt∃d (x) is as follows: if G is a model of Wd

then Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G), and if G 6∈ Sd−1 is a model of Wd then Fitt(G) ⊆ ﬁtt∃d (G) (see

Lemma 5.3.1 below).

   For a ﬁnite sequence e = (e1 , . . . , em ) on {−1, 1} let Ie be the set of partitions of

   Each of the sentences in Wd contains only the universal quantiﬁer ∀ when written in

Lemma 5.2.1. If Gd = wrdi=1 Ai , where Ai ∼
                                          = Z for i = 1, . . . , d, then

                                          Gd |= Wd .

Proof. We proceed by induction on d. For d = 1, the group G1 = Z is a torsion-free

abelian group and hence G1 |= W1 .

   Suppose that Gd−1 |= Wd−1 . It is easy to see that, for each positive integer k, there

is a homomorphism from every ﬁnitely generated subgroup of Gk to an inﬁnite cyclic

group. By Lemma 3.1.1, the ring Z[Gd−1 ] is an integral domain and the base group

D of the wreath product Gd = Z wr Gd−1 is torsion-free as a Z[Gd−1 ]-module. Recall

that Gd is isomorphic to M (Gd−1 , D) as deﬁned in Section 3.3. It is easy to show,

using the identities (3.3.1)–(3.3.4), that M (Gd−1 , D) satisﬁes W′d for each positive integer

d. It remains to show that Gd |= W∗d−1 . The identities (3.3.1)–(3.3.4) also show that

ﬁtt∀ (Gd ) = D = ﬁtt∃d (Gd ). The result follows immediately from this and the fact that

Gd /D ∼
      = Gd−1 |= Wd−1 .



5.3     ρd -groups

In this section we establish the relationship between the ρd -groups deﬁned in Section 5.1

and the sentences Wd deﬁned in the previous section. This relationship plays a key role

in our proof of Theorem 5.1.1.

   In Lemma 5.3.1 we explain the signiﬁcance of the universal formula ﬁtt∀ (x) and the

existential formula ﬁtt∃d (x). These formulae are important in allowing us to describe,

using universal sentences, the Fitting subgroup Fitt(G) of a group G and the quotient

group G/ Fitt(G).

Lemma 5.3.1. If G 6∈ Sd−1 satisfies the sentences Wd then Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G) and

Fitt(G) ⊆ ﬁtt∃d (G).

Proof. By the same argument as in Lemma 4.3.1, we have Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G).

   Let g be an element of Fitt(G). Since G is soluble of derived length d, the subgroup

G(d−1) ⊳ G is abelian, and hence G(d−1) ⩽ Fitt(G). Since G is not in Sd−1 , there exist

h1 , . . . , h2d−1 ∈ G such that h = sd−1 (h1 , . . . , h2d−1 ) 6= 1. The elements h and g are in

Fitt(G), which is abelian, and so [h, g] = 1. Hence Fitt(G) ⊆ ﬁtt∃d (G).


                                             – 78 –
   In Lemmas 5.3.2 and 5.3.3 we show that, for a group G 6∈ Sd−1 , the statements that

G is a ρd -group and that G satisﬁes the sentences Wd are equivalent.

Lemma 5.3.2. If G 6∈ Sd−1 satisfies the sentences Wd then G is a ρd -group.

Proof. We proceed by induction on d. If G |= W1 then G is a torsion-free abelian group

and hence a ρ1 -group. Suppose now that, whenever G 6∈ Sd−2 satisﬁes the sentences

Wd−1 , the group G is a ρd−1 -group. Let G 6∈ Sd−1 satisfy the sentences Wd . The validity

of the sentences φd1 and φ2 (m) for all m ∈ N implies that G is a torsion-free soluble

group of derived length at most d. Since Fitt(G) ⊆ ﬁtt∃d (G) and Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G), the

truth of the sentence φd4 (e) for every ﬁnite sequences e on {−1, 1} implies that Fitt(G) is

torsion-free as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module. The validity of the sentences W∗d−1 implies that

G/ Fitt(G) |= Wd−1 . Since G is not in Sd−1 , the quotient G/ Fitt(G) is not in Sd−2 and

it follows by induction that G/ Fitt(G) is a ρd−1 -group.

Lemma 5.3.3. If G is a ρd -group then G |= Wd .

Proof. Once more we proceed by induction on d. A ρ1 -group is torsion-free and abelian

and hence satisﬁes the sentences W1 . Suppose that, whenever G is a ρd−1 -group, G

satisﬁes Wd−1 , and let G be a ρd -group. By the deﬁnition of a ρd -group, G is torsion-free

soluble of derived length at most d and every nilpotent subgroup of G is abelian. Hence

the sentences φd1 , φ2 (m) for all m ∈ N, and φ3 hold in G. Since every nilpotent subgroup

of G is abelian it follows that Fitt(G) is abelian, and Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G).

   If g is an element of ﬁtt∃d (G) then there exist elements h1 , . . . , h2d−1 ∈ G such that


                                h = sd−1 (h1 , . . . , h2d−1 ) 6= 1


and [h, g] = 1. The element h is in G(d−1) and G(d−1) ⩽ Fitt(G) which is torsion-free

as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module. Since h 6= 1, the equality 1 = [h, g] = h(−1+g) implies that

g ∈ Fitt(G), and hence ﬁtt∃d (G) ⊆ Fitt(G). It follows that G |= φd4 (e) for every ﬁnite

sequence e on {−1, 1}.

   The quotient G/ Fitt(G) is a ρd−1 -group and hence, by induction, G/ Fitt(G) |= Wd−1 .

Since ﬁtt∀ (G) = Fitt(G) ⊇ ﬁtt∃ (G), this implies that G |= W∗d−1 .




                                             – 79 –
5.4     Proof of theorems

In this section we prove the results stated in Section 5.1. For the reader’s convenience we

restate each theorem before proving it.

Theorem 5.1.1 Let S be a left-iterated wreath product of d non-trivial torsion-free abelian

groups. If G is a group which is not in Sd−1 then the following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(S);

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Wd ;

 (3) G is a ρd -group;

 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some

      r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N.

Proof. We prove the implications (1) =⇒ (2) ⇐⇒ (3) =⇒ (4) =⇒ (1).


(1) =⇒ (2). The group S is universally equivalent to Gd = wrdi=1 Ai where each Ai is

      an inﬁnite cyclic group; thus G is in ucl(S) = ucl(Gd ). By Lemma 5.2.1, we have

      Gd |= Wd and hence G |= Wd .

(2) ⇐⇒ (3). The equivalence of (2) and (3) follows immediately from the results of

      Section 5.3.

(3) =⇒ (4). We proceed by induction on d. The group G is a ρ1 -group if and only if it

      is torsion-free and abelian. Hence any ﬁnitely generated subgroup of G embeds in

      Z(r) for some r ∈ N.

      Let G be a ρd -group, so that G |= Wd , and suppose that the hypothesis holds for

      ρd−1 -groups. Since G is not in Sd−1 , there exist elements g1 , . . . , g2d−1 ∈ G such

      that sd−1 (g1 , . . . , g2d−1 ) 6= 1. Let H be a ﬁnitely generated subgroup of G and let

      H1 = hH, g1 , . . . , g2d−1 i. Since Wd is a set of universal sentences, every subgroup

      of G satisﬁes Wd ; in particular, H1 |= Wd and H1 is a ρd -group by Lemma 5.3.2.

      The quotient H 1 = H1 / Fitt(H1 ) is ρd−1 -group and, by induction, H 1 embeds in

      K = wrm
            i=2 Z
                  (ri ) for some r , . . . , r
                                  2           m ∈ N. By the argument used in Lemma 5.2.1,




                                           – 80 –
      the ring Z[K], and hence the ring Z[H 1 ], are integral domains; thus Z[H 1 ] is an Ore

      domain by Lemma 3.1.2. The group H1 is an extension of Fitt(H1 ) by H 1 satisfying

      the conditions of Lemma 3.3.1; thus H1 embeds in U wr H 1 , where U is a ﬁnitely

      generated torsion-free abelian group. It follows that H1 embeds in Z(r1 ) wr H 1 for

      some r1 ∈ N, which in turn embeds in Z(r1 ) wr K. Finally, since H ⩽ H1 , it follows

      that H embeds in Z(r1 ) wr K as required.

(4) =⇒ (1). Let φ be in Th∀ (S) and suppose without loss of generality that φ is of the

      form

                                      ∀x1 . . . xm ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ),

      where ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ) is quantiﬁer-free. We let g1 . . . , gm be elements of G and let

      H = hg1 , . . . , gm i, so that H embeds in wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N. Since

      This is true for all m-tuples in G and hence G satisﬁes φ. Thus G |= Th∀ (Gd ) and

      G ∈ ucl(Gd ).

Theorem 5.1.2 Let S be a left-iterated wreath product of d non-trivial torsion-free abelian

groups. If G is a finitely generated group then the following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(S);

 (2) G can be embedded in wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N;

 (3) G is a ρm -group for some m ⩽ d.


Proof. (1) ⇐⇒ (2). If G embeds in W = wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N then W is

     universally equivalent to S and hence G |= Th∀ (S); thus G ∈ ucl(S).

     If G is in ucl(S) then G embeds in some ultrapower G of S by Lemma 2.6.3 and G

     is elementarily equivalent to S by Loś’ Theorem (see Theorem 2.6.1); thus G is not

     in Sd−1 . It follows from Theorem 5.1.1 that every ﬁnitely generated subgroup of

     G, and in particular G, can be embedded in a restricted wreath product wrdi=1 Z(ri )

     for some r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N.

(2) ⇐⇒ (3). Suppose that G embeds in wrdi=1 Z(ri ) for some r1 , . . . , rd ∈ N and let m ⩽ d

     be the least integer such that G is in Sm . By Lemma 5.4.1, the group G embeds

     in wrm
          i=1 Z
                (si ) for some s , . . . , s ∈ N and hence Theorem 5.1.1 implies that G is a
                                1           m

     ρm -group.

     Now let G be a ρm -group for some m ⩽ d. The quotient G = G/ Fitt(G) is a

     ρm−1 -group and G is an extension of Fitt(G) by G. As in the proof of Theorem

     5.1.1, the group G can be embedded in a restricted wreath product as required.




                                            – 82 –
                                      Chapter 6


RESTRICTED WREATH PRODUCTS OF AN ABELIAN

GROUP OF SQUARE-FREE OR ZERO EXPONENT BY

            A TORSION-FREE NILPOTENT GROUP



The universal theory of nilpotent groups is a diﬃcult subject: Roman′ kov [55] proved that

the decidability of the universal theory of a free nilpotent group of class 2 and rank 2 is

equivalent to the decidability of the universal theory of the ﬁeld of rationals. As discussed

in Chapter 1, the latter is a very hard open problem which seems likely to have a negative

answer.

   Let U wr H be a restricted wreath product of an abelian group U , which is either

torsion-free or of ﬁnite square-free exponent, by a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free nilpotent

group H. In this chapter we consider the universal theory of such a wreath product

modulo the “diﬃcult” universal theory of the group H. We characterize those groups

which satisfy the universal theory of U wr H from three distinct points of view:

   • in terms of the module-theoretic properties of the Fitting subgroup and the universal

     theory of the quotient group by the Fitting subgroup;

   • as those groups satisfying a certain collection of universal sentences;

   • in terms of the embeddability of the ﬁnitely generated subgroups in certain restricted

     wreath products.

This characterization provides a method of proving that U wr H has decidable univer-

sal theory, provided that there exists a recursive collection of sentences describing the

universal and existential theory of H. In [11] Chapuis proved that if H has decidable


                                           – 83 –
universal theory and U is torsion-free then U wr H has decidable universal theory. Our

method, which uses ultraproducts, avoids the combinatorial arguments of his proof. Our

method also has the advantage that it is applicable when the bottom group U is of ﬁnite

square-free exponent as well as when U is torsion-free. Our results here extend those of

Chapuis in [12] for the restricted wreath product Z wr Z.

   Finally in this chapter we consider some examples where we can explicitly determine

when a group in the universal closure of H is universally equivalent to H, and hence

when a group in the universal closure of U wr H is universally equivalent to U wr H. For

example, if H = F2 (N2 ) then, for G ∈ ucl(H), the group G is universally equivalent to

H if and only if G contains a non-abelian nilpotent subgroup. Using this information we

are able to construct the lattice of universally closed classes contained in ucl(U wr H).

   Throughout the remainder of this chapter let n be a positive square-free integer or

zero and let c be a non-negative integer.



6.1     Statement of theorem

We begin by deﬁning the notion of a ρn,H -group for a torsion-free nilpotent group H of

class c. When H = Z this reduces to the notion of ρ-groups in the terminology of [12]

when n = 0 and to the notion of σn -groups in the terminology of Chapter 4 when n 6= 0.

Deﬁnition 6.1.1. (ρn,H -groups). Let H be a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free nilpotent

group of class c. If c = 0 then a group G is a ρn,H -group if G is abelian and of exponent

n. If c ⩾ 1 then a group G is a ρn,H -group if the following conditions hold:

  1. γc+1 (G) is abelian;

  2. Fitt(G) is abelian and

      (a) if n = 0 then G is torsion-free;

      (b) if n 6= 0 then Fitt(G) is of exponent dividing n;

  3. G/ Fitt(G) satisﬁes the universal theory of H;

  4. If G1 is a nilpotent subgroup of G then either G1 is abelian of exponent n or G1

      satisﬁes the universal theory of H;


                                             – 84 –
  5. (a) If n = 0 then Fitt(G) is torsion-free as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module;

      (b) If n 6= 0 then, for each prime divisor p of n, the submodule of Fitt(G) of

              elements of order p is torsion-free as an Fp [G/ Fitt(G)]-module.


In Section 6.2 below we shall deﬁne the collection Wn,H of universal sentences.

Theorem 6.1.1. Let H be a torsion-free nilpotent group of class c and let U be a non-

trivial abelian group of exponent n. If G is a group then the following conditions are

equivalent:

                   
 (1) G ∈ ucl U wr H ;

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Wn,H ;

 (3) G is a ρn,H -group or G |= Th∀ (H);

                                                                                           (r)
 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in Cn wr K for some r ∈ N

      and some K such that K |= Th∀ (H).

   The required sets of sentences have become much more complicated than in previous

Lemma 6.2.1. If H is a finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent group of class c then

                                             Cn wr H |= Wn,c .


                                                  – 88 –
Proof. Let D be the base group of the wreath product. It follows from Lemma 2.3.1 that

ﬁtt∃ (Cn wr H) = Fitt(Cn wr H) = D and it is trivial to show that ﬁtt∀ (Cn wr H) = D.

   Since H is a ﬁnitely generated, torsion-free, nilpotent group, the group rings Z[H] and

Fp [H], where p is a prime, are integral domains by Lemma 3.1.1. If n = 0 then, since D

is a free Z[H]-module, D is torsion-free as a Z[H]-module. If n 6= 0 then, since D is an

abelian group of square-free exponent n, the base group D is a direct product of groups

Dp of exponent p, where each p is a prime divisor of n. Since D is a free Rn [H]-module,

Dp is a free Fp [H]-module, for each prime p, and hence Dp is torsion-free as an Fp [H]-

module. It is easy to show, using the identities (3.3.1)–(3.3.4), that M (H, D) satisﬁes

Wn,c .

with the sentence φ12 which allows us to use a slightly diﬀerent existential formula for the

6.3      The universal closure of Cn wr H

Fix a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free nilpotent group H of class c ⩾ 1 and suppose throu-

ghout this section that G is a group in which the universal sentences Wn,H hold. Our

aim is to describe some of the properties of G that follow from this supposition.

    In Lemmas 6.3.1, 6.3.2 and 6.3.3 we establish the signiﬁcance of the universal formula

ﬁtt∀ (x) and the existential formula ﬁtt∃c (x). These formulae are important in allowing

us to describe, using universal sentences, the Fitting subgroup Fitt(G) and the quotient

group G/ Fitt(G).

Lemma 6.3.1. The Fitting subgroup of G is nilpotent of class at most c.

Proof. By Fitting’s theorem, every ﬁnitely generated subgroup of Fitt(G) is nilpotent.

The validity in G of the sentence φc2 implies that every nilpotent subgroup has class at

most c and it follows that Fitt(G) is nilpotent of class at most c.

Lemma 6.3.2. If G is a non-nilpotent group and g ∈ Fitt(G) then G satisfies ﬁtt∃c (g).

Proof. Let g be an element of Fitt(G). Since G is not nilpotent, we may choose elements

h1 , . . . , hc+1 ∈ G such that h = [h1 , . . . , hc+1 ] 6= 1. Since γc+1 (G) is an abelian normal

subgroup of G, it follows that h is in Fitt(G). Thus hg, hi ⩽ Fitt(G) is nilpotent of class

at most c and [h, g, . . . , g ] = 1.
                  | {z }
                         c



                                              – 92 –
Lemma 6.3.3. If G is a non-nilpotent group then Fitt(G) is abelian and Fitt(G) =

ﬁtt∀ (G).

Proof. Let g and h be elements of Fitt(G). By Lemma 6.3.2, we have G |= ﬁtt∃c (g) and

G |= ﬁtt∃c (h). Thus, since G |= φc4 , the elements g and h commute and Fitt(G) is abelian.

    If g is an element of Fitt(G) then the normal closure in G of g is in Fitt(G), which

is abelian, and so g ∈ ﬁtt∀ (G). If g is in ﬁtt∀ (G) then the normal closure in G of g is

abelian and so g ∈ Fitt(G). Thus Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G).

    We next describe the nilpotent subgroups of G. Although every nilpotent normal

subgroup of G is abelian, G may contain non-abelian nilpotent subgroups. All such

non-abelian nilpotent subgroups satisfy the universal theory of H.

Lemma 6.3.4. If G1 is a nilpotent subgroup of G then either G1 is abelian of exponent

dividing n or G1 |= UH .

Proof. Suppose to begin with that n = 0. Let ψ be a sentence in UH ; we may assume wi-

thout loss of generality that ψ is of the form ∀x1 . . . xm ϕ(x1 , . . . xm ), where ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm )

is quantiﬁer-free. If g1 , . . . , gm are elements of G1 then, since G1 is nilpotent of class at
                      c (g , . . . , g ). It follows, since G |= ψ + , that ϕ(g , . . . , g ) holds.
most c, we have G |= βm   1           m                           n            1           m

This is true for all m-tuples in G1 and hence G1 |= ψ.

    Suppose now that n 6= 0 and that G1 is not abelian of exponent dividing n, so that

G1 contains elements h1 and h2 such that [h1 , h2 ] 6= 1 or hn1 6= 1 or hn2 6= 1. Let ψ

be a sentence in UH ; we may suppose without loss of generality that ψ is of the form

∀x1 . . . xm ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ) where ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ) is quantiﬁer-free. If g1 , . . . , gm are elements

of G1 then, since G1 is nilpotent of class at most c, we have

                                          c
                                    G |= βm+2 (g1 , . . . , gm , h1 , h2 ).


It follows, since G |= ψn+ , that ϕ(g1 , . . . , gm ) holds. This is true for all m-tuples in G1

and hence G1 |= ψ.

    In Lemma 6.3.5 we describe the universal theory of the quotient of G by its Fitting

subgroup when G is not nilpotent. Clearly when G is nilpotent this quotient is trivial.

6.4      ρn,H -groups

Fix a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free nilpotent group H of class c. In this section we

establish the relationship between the ρn,H -groups deﬁned in Section 6.1 and the sentences

Wn,H . This relationship plays a key role in our proof of Theorem 6.1.1.

Lemma 6.4.1. If G is a non-nilpotent group such that G |= Wn,H then G is a ρn,H -group.



Proof. There does not exist a non-nilpotent group such that G |= Wn,H where H is trivial;

thus we may assume that c ⩾ 1. The validity in G of the sentences φc1 and φc2 implies

that γc+1 (G) is abelian and that every nilpotent subgroup of G is nilpotent of class at

most c. By Lemmas 6.3.3 and 6.3.2, the subgroup Fitt(G) is abelian, ﬁtt∀ (G) = Fitt(G)

and Fitt(G) ⊆ ﬁtt∃c (G). If n = 0, the truth of the sentences φ03 (m) for all m ∈ N

implies that G is torsion-free and, if n 6= 0, the truth of the sentence φn,c
                                                                          3 implies that

Fitt(G) is of exponent dividing n. By Lemma 6.3.5, we have G/ Fitt(G) |= UH and hence

G/ Fitt(G) |= Th∀ (H). If G1 is a nilpotent subgroup of G then G1 |= UH by Lemma 6.3.4

and it follows that G1 satisﬁes the universal theory of H.

    Since G/ Fitt(G) satisﬁes the universal theory of H, it is a torsion-free nilpotent

group and hence the group rings Z[G/ Fitt(G)] and Fp [G/ Fitt(G)], where p is prime,


                                                    – 94 –
are integral domains by Lemma 3.1.1. If n = 0, the truth of the sentences φ0,c
                                                                           5 (e) for

every ﬁnite sequence e on {−1, 1} implies that if gα = 1 for some α ∈ Z[G/ Fitt(G)]

then α = 0. Thus Fitt(G) is torsion-free as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module. Suppose now that

n 6= 0 and let g be a non-trivial element of Fitt(G) of order p, where p is a prime divisor

of n. Since G |= φp,c                      α
                  5 (m) for all m ∈ N, if g = 1 for some α ∈ Fp [G/ Fitt(G)] then

α = 0. Thus the submodule of Fitt(G) of elements of order dividing p is torsion-free as

an Fp [G/ Fitt(G)]-module.

Lemma 6.4.2. If G is a ρn,H -group then G satisfies Wn,c .

Proof. If c = 0 then a ρn,H -group G is an abelian group of exponent n and hence G |=

the sentence φc2 holds in G. Hence every nilpotent subgroup of G has class at most c.

    Since G has abelian Fitting subgroup, Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G). In order to show that G

Note that, since γc+1 (G) is an abelian normal subgroup of G, it is contained in Fitt(G).
