                                                      – 96 –
6.5     Proof of theorem

For the reader’s convenience we restate the theorem which will be proved in this section.

Recall that n is a square-free positive integer or zero.

Theorem 6.1.1 Let H be a finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent group of class c and

let U be a non-trivial abelian group of exponent n. If G is a group then the following

conditions are equivalent:
                   
 (1) G ∈ ucl U wr H ;

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Wn,H ;

 (3) G is a ρn,H -group or G |= Th∀ (H);

                                                                 (r)
 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in Cn wr K for some r ∈ N

      and some K such that K |= Th∀ (H).

Proof. We prove the implications (1) =⇒ (2) ⇐⇒ (3) =⇒ (4) =⇒ (1).

(1) =⇒ (2). The group G is in ucl(U wr H) and so G |= Th∀ (U wr H). By Lemmas 3.4.1

      and 3.4.2, we have U wr H |= Th∀ (Cn wr H); thus G |= Th∀ (Cn wr H) and it follows,

      by Lemma 6.2.4, that G |= Wn,H .

(2) ⇐⇒ (3). If G is nilpotent and G |= Wn,H then either G is abelian of exponent n

      or G |= Th∀ (H) by Lemma 6.3.4 and in the former case G is a ρn,H -group. Since

      H is a subgroup of Cn wr H, we have Wn,H ⊆ Th∀ (Cn wr H) ⊆ Th∀ (H); thus

      if G |= Th∀ (H) then G |= Wn,H . The equivalence of (2) and (3) now follows

      immediately from the results of Section 6.4.

(3) =⇒ (4). If G satisﬁes Th∀ (H) then every ﬁnitely generated subgroup G1 ⩽ G also

      satisﬁes Th∀ (H). If G is a ρn,H -group and G1 is a ﬁnitely generated nilpotent

      subgroup of G then G1 |= Th∀ (H) or G is abelian of exponent dividing n. In the

      former case G1 ⩽ Cn wr G1 as required and in the latter case G1 = Cn1 × · · · × Cnr

      where each nj is a divisor of n (see [53, 4.2.6]). Each cyclic group Cnj embeds in

      Cn and hence G1 embeds in the direct product of r copies of Cn . It follows that G1
                   (r)
      embeds in Cn wr H for some positive integer r.


                                           – 97 –
      Now suppose that G is a ρn,H -group, so that G |= Wn,H by Lemma 6.4.5, and that

      G1 is a ﬁnitely generated non-nilpotent subgroup of G. Since the sentences Wn,H

      are universal, every subgroup of G satisﬁes Wn,H ; in particular, G1 |= Wn,H and,

      since G1 is not nilpotent, G1 is a ρn,H -group by Lemma 6.4.1. The quotient group

      G1 = G1 / Fitt(G1 ) satisﬁes the universal theory of H; thus G1 is a ﬁnitely generated

      torsion-free nilpotent group and hence the group rings Z[G1 ] and Fp [G1 ], where p

      is a prime, are Ore domains by Lemma 3.1.2.

      If n = 0, the group G1 is an extension of Fitt(G1 ) by G1 satisfying the conditions of

      Lemma 3.3.1 and G1 embeds in U wr G1 , where U is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free

      abelian group. It follows that G1 embeds in Z(r) wr G1 for some r ∈ N. If n 6= 0,

      the group G1 is an extension of Fitt(G1 ) by G1 satisfying the conditions of Lemma

      3.3.2 and G1 embeds in U wr G1 , where U is some ﬁnitely generated abelian group
                                                                 (r)
      of exponent dividing n. As above, U embeds in Cn for some r ∈ N and hence G1
                    (r)
      embeds in Cn wr G1 . In both cases we have G1 |= Th∀ (H) as required.

                                  
(4) =⇒ (1). Let φ be in Th∀ U wr H and suppose without loss of generality that φ is

      of the form

                                     ∀x1 . . . xm ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ),

      where ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ) is quantiﬁer-free. We let g1 . . . , gm be elements of G and let
                                                         (r)
      G1 = hg1 , . . . , gm i, so that G1 embeds in Cn wr K for some r ∈ N and some K

      such that K |= Th∀ (H). By Lemmas 3.4.2 and 3.4.1, the restricted wreath product
       (r)                                                                   (r)
      Cn wr K satisﬁes the universal theory of U wr H; in particular, Cn wr K |= φ and

      ϕ(g1 , . . . , gm ) holds. This is true for all m-tuples in G and hence G |= φ. Thus G
                                                          
      satisﬁes Th∀ U wr H and G is in ucl U wr H .



6.6     Universal equivalence and decidability

Fix a torsion-free nilpotent group H of class c ⩾ 1. Our aims in this section are to

give conditions for a group to be universally equivalent to Cn wr H and to show that

the universal theory of this group is decidable. We start by proving that if G is a non-

nilpotent group which satisﬁes the sentences Wn,H , and G contains a subgroup universally


                                             – 98 –
equivalent to H and an element of order n, then G is universally equivalent to Cn wr H.

Lemma 6.6.1. Suppose that c ⩾ 2. If G is a non-nilpotent group such that G |= Wn,H

and G1 is a non-abelian nilpotent subgroup of G then G1 ∩ Fitt(G) = {1}.

Proof. By Lemma 3.3.5, if G1 is a non-abelian nilpotent subgroup of Cn wr H then the

canonical map θ : Cn wr H → H embeds G1 in H. The kernel of θ|G1 is G1 ∩Fitt(Cn wr H).

Since θ|G1 is an embedding, this kernel is trivial and hence G1 has trivial intersection with

Fitt(Cn wr H). This can be expressed in a universal sentence
                                                                        
                   ∀xyz     β3c (x, y, z) ∧ [y, z] 6= 1 ∧ ﬁtt∃c (x) → x = 1 .


The group G satisﬁes the sentences Wn,H , which implies, by Theorem 6.1.1, that G

satisﬁes the universal theory of Cn wr H. In particular,
                                                                             
                G |= ∀xyz        β3c (x, y, z) ∧ [y, z] 6= 1 ∧ ﬁtt∃c (x) → x = 1 .

It follows from this that any non-abelian nilpotent subgroup of G has trivial intersection

with Fitt(G).

Lemma 6.6.2. Let G be a non-nilpotent group such that G |= Wn,H . Suppose that G

contains a subgroup universally equivalent to H. For n 6= 0, suppose in addition that G

contains an element of order n. Then G is universally equivalent to Cn wr H.

Proof. For c = 1, the result follows from [12, Lemma 4.9] if n = 0 and from Lemma 4.5.1

if n 6= 0. We suppose that c ⩾ 2.

   Let K be a subgroup of G such that K is universally equivalent to H. The group G

is not nilpotent and, since c ⩾ 2, the group K is not abelian. We apply Lemma 6.6.1 to

obtain K ∩ Fitt(G) = {1}. If n = 0, we choose h to be a non-trivial element of Fitt(G)

and, if n 6= 0, we choose h ∈ G such that o(h) = n; again h is a non-trivial element of

Fitt(G). For each g ∈ K, we let Hg = hhg i and L = hHg | g ∈ Ki. If n = 0 then, since

Fitt(G) is torsion-free as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module and K ∩ Fitt(G) = {1}, the group L is

a direct product of the cyclic groups Hg . If n 6= 0 then, since o(h) = n, the element h has

trivial annihilator in Rn [G/ Fitt(G)] and L is again a direct product of the groups Hg . In

both cases L is abelian and, by deﬁnition, L⊳hK, hi. Also K ∩L ⩽ K ∩Fitt(G) = {1} and


                                              – 99 –
hence hK, hi = L ⋊ K ∼
                     = Cn wr K. Since hK, hi ⩽ G, it follows that G |= Th∃ (Cn wr K) =
Th∃ (Cn wr H). Thus G |= Th∀ (Cn wr H) ∪ Th∃ (Cn wr H) and G is universally equivalent

to Cn wr H.

    If n is a prime p then the condition that G contains an elements of order p follows

from the fact that G is not nilpotent: the subgroup γc+1 (G) is non-trivial and contained

in Fitt(G); since Fitt(G) has exponent dividing p, it follows that any non-trivial element

of γc+1 (G) is of order p.

    Let G be a group. We introduce existential sentences θm and πm for each m ⩾ 0. The

sentence θ0 says that G is non-trivial, and G satisﬁes θm for m ⩾ 1 if G is not nilpotent

of class m:


                       θ0 : ∃x (x 6= 1),

                      θm : ∃x1 . . . xm+1 ([x1 , . . . , xm+1 ] 6= 1)            for m ⩾ 1.


The sentence π0 is true in any group and G satisﬁes πm for m ⩾ 1 if G contains an element

of order m:

    Let VH ⊆ Th∃ (H) be a set of existential sentences such that a group K ∈ ucl(H)

Lemma 6.6.3. If G is a finitely generated group such that G |= Wn,H ∪ V+

Proof. If H is non-trivial and abelian then, by the results of Chapuis [12, Lemma 4.9]

follows. Suppose therefore that H is not abelian, so that c ⩾ 2.

     For each ﬁnite subset Y of VH , we have G |= ψY ; thus we may choose elements

g11 , . . . , grkr ∈ G which satisfy this sentence. The subgroup KY = hg11 , . . . , grkr i is

   Let K = KY /U. Since each KY is nilpotent, K is nilpotent by Loś’ Theorem (see

   For each Y ∈ Υ, let GY be an isomorphic copy of G. Since KY embeds in GY for each
                                             Q
Y ∈ Υ, the ultraproduct K embeds in G1 =       GY /U (see Theorem 2.6.2). It follows

from Loś’ Theorem that taking ultrapowers preserves elementary equivalence, and hence

G1 is elementarily equivalent to G. The group K satisﬁes the existential theory of H;

in particular, since H is non-abelian, K is a non-abelian nilpotent subgroup of G1 and

hence K |= UH by Lemma 6.3.4. Thus K |= UH ∪ VH and K is universally equivalent to

H.

     If VH is ﬁnite, let G1 = G and let K = KY , where Y = VH . Certainly, G1 is

elementarily equivalent to G and K is universally equivalent to H.

     The group G1 satisﬁes the elementary theory of G and G |= Wn,H ∪ V+
                                                                       H ∪ {θc , πn };




                                            – 101 –
thus G1 satisﬁes the sentences Wn,H ∪ V+
                                       H ∪ {θc , πn }. The validity in G1 of the sentence θc

implies that G1 is not nilpotent of class c and hence that G1 is not nilpotent. The validity

in G1 of the sentence πn implies that G1 contains an element of order n. Moreover, the

subgroup K of G1 is universally equivalent to H. Thus G1 is universally equivalent to

Cn wr H by Lemma 6.6.2 and, since G is elementarily equivalent to G1 , it follows that G

is universally equivalent to Cn wr H.

Corollary 6.6.1. Suppose that H is non-trivial and that there exist a recursive set of

universal sentences UH and a recursive set of existential sentences VH such that a group

K is universally equivalent to H if and only if K |= UH ∪ VH . Then, for any abelian

group U of exponent n, the group U wr H has decidable universal theory.

Proof. Let Wn,H be the recursive collection of sentences Wn,H ∪ V+
                                                                 H ∪ {θc , πn }. By

Lemma 6.6.3, a group G satisﬁes Wn,H if and only if G is universally equivalent to

Cn wr H. Let φ be a universal sentence; by the completeness theorem, Wn,H ⊢ φ or
                                                                              
Wn,H ⊢ ¬φ. Hence φ ∈ Th∀ U wr H if and only if Wn,H ⊢ φ, and φ 6∈ Th∀ U wr H

if and only if Wn,H ⊢ ¬φ. Since Wn,H is recursive, the universal theory of U wr H is

decidable.



6.7     Free nilpotent groups

In this section we consider necessary and suﬃcient conditions for a group in the universal

closure of a free nilpotent group to be universally equivalent to it. We present examples

of torsion-free nilpotent groups H for which we can write down explicitly a collection of

sentences VH such that if K ∈ ucl(H) then K is universally equivalent to H if and only

if K |= VH . Proposition 6.7.1 gives conditions for a group in ucl(F ), where F is a free

nilpotent group of rank 2, to be universally equivalent to F .

Proposition 6.7.1. If G is in ucl(F2 (Nc )) then G is universally equivalent to F2 (Nc ) if

and only if G contains a 2-generator subgroup which is not in Nc−1 .

Proof. Let H = F2 (Nc ) and let g and h be elements of G such that hg, hi 6∈ Nc−1 . A

ﬁnitely generated nilpotent group is ﬁnitely presented (P. Hall, see [53, 2.2.4]), and hence


                                          – 102 –
hg, hi embeds in the countable Cartesian power H N of H by Lemma 2.5.2. Let g and

h be the images of g and h in H N . Let g(i) and h(i) be the ith coordinates and let

Gi = hg(i), h(i)i. For some i and j, suppose that there is a homomorphism from Gi to
                                                                    ′
Gj such that g(i) 7→ g(j) and h(i) 7→ h(j). If g ′ and h are the elements obtained from

g and h by replacing the jth coordinates with identity elements then hg, hi is isomorphic
           ′
to hg ′ , h i.

     If g(i) and h(i) are linearly dependent modulo H ′ then, since H/H ′ is torsion-free, Gi

is cyclic modulo H ′ ∩ Gi . By Lemma 4.5.1, there are elements a ∈ Gi and b ∈ H ′ ∩ Gi

such that Gi = ha, bi. We have G′i = h[a, b]iGi ⩽ γ3 (H) and γc (Gi ) ⩽ γc+1 (H) = {1},
                                                   Q
so that Gi ∈ Nc−1 . If Gi is in Nc−1 for all i then C i∈N Gi is in Nc−1 and, since hg, hi
          QC
embeds in i∈N Gi , we have hg, hi ∈ Nc−1 , contradicting our assumptions. We ﬁx i ∈ N

such that the elements g(i) and h(i) are linearly independent modulo H ′ .

     The group Gi is free in Nc by Lemma 2.2.2 and hence Gi ∼
                                                            = H; moreover, Gi is freely
generated by g(i) and h(i). For each j, the group Gj ⩽ H is a 2-generator group in

Nc and there is a homomorphism Gi → Gj such that g(i) 7→ g(j) and h(i) 7→ h(j). It

follows that hg, hi is isomorphic to Gi ∼
                                        = H. Thus G contains an isomorphic copy of H
and hence G satisﬁes the existential theory of H. Since G is in ucl(H), it follows that G

is universally equivalent to H.

     Suppose now that G is universally equivalent to H and let g and h be free generators

of H. Then [g, h, . . . , h] 6= 1 and H satisﬁes the existential sentence θ deﬁned by
               | {z }
                   c−1

                                   ∃xy ([x, y, . . . , y ] 6= 1).
                                            | {z }
                                                 c−1

Thus G satisﬁes θ and G contains a 2-generator group which is not in Nc−1 .

     This result has important consequences in determining those groups universally equi-

valent to Cn wr H, where H = F2 (Nc ) with c ⩾ 2. Using Proposition 6.7.1, we can give

explicitly the collections of existential sentences VH used in the proof of Lemma 6.6.3. Let

G be a group in the universal closure of Cn wr H. Since a non-abelian nilpotent subgroup

of G satisﬁes the universal theory of H, a 2-generator nilpotent subgroup of G which is

not in Nc−1 is universally equivalent to H. We set

Now let c = 2 or 3, so that F2 (Nc ) generates Nc (see [27]); then Fk (Nc ) is universally

equivalent to F2 (Nc ) for all k ⩾ 2 by Theorem 2.5.1. For c = 2, if G is non-abelian then

G contains elements g and h such that [g, h] 6= 1; thus hg, hi is a non-abelian 2-generator

subgroup of G. Suppose now that c = 3. If G is a torsion-free group which is not in Nc−1

then G contains elements u, v and w such that [u, v, w] 6= 1 and hence [u, v, w]3 6= 1. It

follows that there exist elements g, h ∈ G such that [g, h, g] 6= 1 (Levi, see [44, 34.31]) and

G contains a 2-generator subgroup hg, hi which is not in Nc−1 . We have the following

corollary to Proposition 6.7.1:

Corollary 6.7.1. If G is in ucl(Fk (Nc )), with c = 2 or 3 and k ⩾ 2, then G is universally

equivalent to H if and only if G is not in Nc−1 .

   We have the following sets of sentences VH in Lemma 6.6.3:

   • VH = {∃ xy([x, y] 6= 1)} where H = Fk (N2 ), k ⩾ 2;

   • VH = {∃ xyz([x, y, z] 6= 1)} where H = Fk (N3 ), k ⩾ 2.

   Using Proposition 6.7.1, we are able to draw the lattice of universally closed classes

      If G is a non-nilpotent metabelian group in the universal closure of Z wr F2 (N2 ) then,

groups are either torsion-free or of exponent dividing n. Thus the sublattices of nilpotent

groups can be drawn explicitly. The only classes of groups in the lattice about which

our information is incomplete are those non-metabelian groups which are not universally

equivalent to Cn wr F2 (N2 ). These groups satisfy the condition that all of their nilpotent

subgroups are abelian.

                                             – 108 –
                                     Chapter 7


RESTRICTED WREATH PRODUCTS OF AN ABELIAN

GROUP OF SQUARE-FREE OR ZERO EXPONENT BY

              A TORSION-FREE SOLUBLE GROUP



We deﬁne a class of groups Bk as follows: a group G is in Bk if and only if every nilpotent

subgroup of G has class at most k. Let P be a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free group in

Pc ∩ Bk . If, for example, P is a free soluble group of derived length d ⩾ 3 then the

question of whether the universal theory of P is decidable is a very hard problem related

to Hilbert’s Tenth Problem over the rationals. See Chapter 1 for a discussion of this

diﬃcult open problem. In this chapter we consider the universal theory of groups U wr P ,

where U is abelian and either torsion-free or of ﬁnite square-free exponent, modulo the

potentially diﬃcult universal theory of P . We characterize those groups which satisfy the

universal theory of U wr P in two ways:

   • in terms of the module-theoretic properties of the Fitting subgroup and the universal

     theory of the quotient group by the Fitting subgroup;

   • in terms of the embeddability of ﬁnitely generated subgroups in certain restricted

     wreath products.

We also deﬁne a collection of universal sentences such that a group which is not in Pc

satisﬁes the universal theory of U wr P if and only if it satisﬁes these sentences. We

give some examples of ﬁnitely generated polynilpotent groups which are in the class Bk

for some positive integer k; these are groups for which the theorem holds. We also give

an example of a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free soluble group which is not in Bk for any


                                          – 109 –
positive integer k.

    Let G be a ﬁnitely generated group with an abelian normal subgroup A such that

G/A is a torsion-free polynilpotent group. If A is torsion-free as a Z[G/A]-module then G

embeds in Z(r) wr(G/A) for some positive integer r and hence ucl(G) ⊆ ucl(Z wr(G/A)).

If A is of ﬁnite square-free exponent n and A is torsion-free as an Fp [G/A]-module for
                                                            (r)
each prime divisor p of n then G embeds in Cn wr(G/A) for some positive integer r

and hence ucl(G) ⊆ ucl(Cn wr(G/A)). We consider some examples of groups where this

inclusion is strict.

    Throughout this chapter let n be a positive square-free integer or zero and let k, l and

c1 , . . . , cl be positive integers. Let c = (c1 , . . . , cl ) and let C = (c1 + 1) · · · (cl + 1).



7.1      Statement of theorems

We begin by deﬁning the notion of a ρn,P -group for a torsion-free group in Pc ∩ Bk .

This extends Deﬁnition 6.1.1 of ρn,H -groups where H is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free

nilpotent group. In this wider context we are unable to make a general statement about

the universal theory of a nilpotent subgroup of a ρn,P -group but we are able to place a

bound on the class of a nilpotent subgroup of a ρn,P -group.

Deﬁnition 7.1.1. (ρn,P -groups). Let P be a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free group in

Pc ∩ Bk . A group G is a ρn,P -group if the following conditions hold:

   1. G is in APc ;

   2. Fitt(G) is abelian and

        (a) if n = 0 then G is torsion-free;

        (b) if n 6= 0 then Fitt(G) is of exponent dividing n;

   3. G/ Fitt(G) satisﬁes the universal theory of P ;

   4. If G1 is a nilpotent subgroup of G then G1 has class at most k;

   5. (a) If n = 0 then Fitt(G) is torsion-free as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module;




                                                  – 110 –
      (b) If n 6= 0 then, for each prime divisor p of n, the submodule of Fitt(G) of

           elements of order p is torsion-free as an Fp [G/ Fitt(G)]-module.


In Section 7.2 below we shall deﬁne the collection Wn,P of sentences.

Theorem 7.1.1. Let P be a finitely generated torsion-free group in Pc ∩ Bk and let U

be a non-trivial abelian group of exponent n. If G is a group which is not in Pc then the

following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(U wr P );

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Wn,P ;

 (3) G is a ρn,P -group;

                                                                         (r)
 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in Cn wr Q for some r ∈ N

     and some Q such that Q |= Th∀ (P ).


Theorem 7.1.2. Let P be a finitely generated torsion-free group in Pc ∩ Bk and let U

be a non-trivial abelian group of exponent n. If G is a finitely generated group then the

following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(U wr P );

                              (r)
 (2) G can be embedded in Cn wr Q for some r ∈ N and some Q such that Q |= Th∀ (P );

 (3) Either G is a ρn,Q -group for some subgroup Q of P or G |= Th∀ (P ).


   We begin with some examples of polynilpotent groups which satisfy the conditions of

the above theorems. Consider the group


                   Pc = Hl wrNcl (Hl−1 wrNcl−1 (· · · (H2 wrNc2 H1 ) · · · )),


where each Hi is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free group in Nci .

Lemma 7.1.1. Let N be the base group of G = H wrNc K, where H is in Nc and K is a

torsion-free group. If a ∈ N \ {1} and g ∈ G then [g, a] = 1 implies g ∈ N .

   It follows from this, by the same argument as in Lemma 3.3.5, that every nilpotent

subgroup of G either is contained in N or embeds in K.

   We show, also by induction, that every nilpotent subgroup of Pc is nilpotent of class

at most c = max{c1 , . . . , cl }. If l = 1 then Pc is nilpotent of class at most c1 and the

result holds. Suppose that the result holds for Pcl−1 which is a torsion-free group. If K is

a nilpotent subgroup of Pc = Hl wrNcl Pcl−1 then either K is contained in the base group

of this verbal wreath product or K embeds in Pcl−1 . In the former case K is nilpotent of

class at most cl and in the latter case K is nilpotent of class at most max{c1 , . . . , cl−1 }

by induction; thus K is nilpotent of class at most c = max{c1 , . . . , cl }.

   If G is any ﬁnitely generated subgroup of Pc then there is a positive integer l such

that G is in Bl . It follows that, if U is a torsion-free abelian group of exponent n, then

the conclusions of Theorems 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 hold for U wr G.

   Now let F be the free group of rank r in Pc . By the Shmel′ kin embedding (see

Chapter 2), the group F can be embedded in Fr (Ncl ) wrNcl Fr (Pcl−1 ). Applying the


                                            – 112 –
Shmel’kin embedding repeatedly, we obtain the result that F can be embedded into the

left-iterated verbal wreath product
                                                                                      
           Pc = Fr (Ncl wrNcl Fr (Ncl−1 ) wrNcl−1 · · · Fr (Nc2 ) wrNc2 Fr (Nc1 ) · · · .

Thus, by the argument above, every subgroup of F is nilpotent of class at most c =

max{c1 , . . . , cl }. In fact there is a better bound on the class of nilpotent subgroups of

a free polynilpotent group P with class sequence c: every nilpotent subgroup of P is

either cyclic or contained in the verbal subgroup γcl−1 (γcl−2 (· · · γ1 (P )) (Baumslag, see

Lemma 2.4.4) and this verbal subgroup is nilpotent of class cl . Thus every nilpotent

subgroup of P is either nilpotent of class at most cl or abelian and cl gives the bound we

require.

Remark 7.1.1. The condition that there is a bound on the class of the nilpotent sub-

groups of P is a necessary one: without this bound we are unable to construct an exis-

tential formula deﬁning the Fitting subgroup. We give an example of a ﬁnitely generated

torsion-free soluble group P of derived length at most 4 such that, for every positive

integer c, the group P contains a nilpotent subgroup which is not nilpotent of class ⩽ c.

Lemma 7.2.1. If P is a finitely generated torsion-free group in Pc ∩ Bk then

                                      Cn wr P |= Wn,P .

Proof. Let D be the base group of the wreath product. It follows from Lemma 2.3.1 that

ﬁtt∃ (Cn wr P ) = Fitt(Cn wr P ) = D and it is clear that ﬁtt∀ (Cn wr P ) = D.

   Since P is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free soluble group, the group rings Z[P ] and

Fp [P ], where p is a prime, are integral domains by Theorem 3.1.1. If n = 0 then, since

D is a free Z[P ]-module, D is torsion-free as a Z[P ]-module. If n 6= 0 then D is a direct

product of groups Dp of exponent p, where p is a prime divisor of n, and each group Dp

is torsion-free as an Fp [P ]-module. It follows easily from these facts and the identities

(3.3.1)–(3.3.4) that Cn wr P |= Wn,c,k .

   It remains to show that Cn wr P |= U∗P ; the result follows immediately from the fact

that (Cn wr P )/D ∼
                  = P |= UP .

   As in previous chapters, each of the sentences in Wn,P contains only the universal

quantiﬁer ∀ when written in prenex normal form. As usual we have given the sentences

in a more transparently comprehensible form than the prenex normal form.

7.3      The universal closure of U wr P

Fix a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free group P in Pc ∩ Bk and suppose throughout this

section that G is a group in which the universal sentences Wn,P hold. Our aim is to

describe some of the properties of G that follow from this supposition.

    In Lemmas 7.3.1, 7.3.2 and 7.3.3 we establish the signiﬁcance of the universal formula

ﬁtt∀ (x) and the existential formula ﬁtt∃c,k (x). These formulae will allow us to describe,

using universal sentences, the subgroup Fitt(G) and the quotient group G/ Fitt(G). The

arguments used in the proofs of Lemmas 7.3.1 and 7.3.3 are almost identical to those of

their counterparts in Chapter 6.

Lemma 7.3.1. The Fitting subgroup of G is nilpotent of class at most c.

Proof. See Lemma 6.3.1.

Lemma 7.3.2. If G is not in Pc and g is an element of Fitt(G) then G |= ﬁtt∃c,k (g).

Proof. Let g be an element of Fitt(G). Since G 6∈ Pc , we may choose elements h1 , . . . , hC ∈

G such that h = sc (h1 , . . . , hC ) 6= 1. The element h is in the abelian normal subgroup

sc (G) of G and it follows that h ∈ Fitt(G). Thus hg, hi ⩽ Fitt(G) is nilpotent of class at

most k and [h, g, . . . , g ] = 1.
               | {z }
                      k

Lemma 7.3.3. If G is not in Pc then Fitt(G) is abelian and Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G).

Proof. See Lemma 6.3.3.

    In Lemma 7.3.4 we describe the universal theory of the quotient of G by its Fitting

subgroup provided that G 6∈ Pc . Again the proof is almost identical to the proof of the

corresponding lemma in Chapter 6.

Lemma 7.3.4. If G is not in Pc then G/ Fitt(G) satisfies the sentences UP .

Proof. See Lemma 6.3.5.

7.4     ρn,P -groups

Fix a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free group P in Pc ∩ Bk . In this section we establish the

relationship between the ρn,P -groups deﬁned in Section 7.1 and the sentences Wn,P . This

relationship plays a key role in our proof of Theorem 7.1.1.

Lemma 7.4.1. If G satisfies Wn,P and G is not in Pc then G is a ρn,P -group.

Proof. The validity in G of the sentences φc1 and φk2 implies that G ∈ APc ∩ Bk . By

Lemmas 7.3.3 and 7.3.2, the Fitting subgroup of G is abelian, ﬁtt∀ (G) = Fitt(G) and

Fitt(G) ⊆ ﬁtt∃c,k (G). If n = 0, the truth of the sentences φ03 (m) for all m ∈ N implies

that G is torsion-free and, if n 6= 0, the truth of the sentence φn,c,k
                                                                  3     implies that Fitt(G)

is of exponent dividing n. Lemma 7.3.4 implies that G/ Fitt(G) |= UH and hence G/A |=

Th∀ (P ).

   The same argument as in Lemma 6.4.1 completes the proof: if n = 0 then Fitt(G)

is torsion-free as a Z[G/ Fitt(G)]-module, and if n 6= 0 then, for each prime divisor p of

n, the submodule of Fitt(G) of elements of order p is torsion-free as an Fp [G/ Fitt(G)]-

module.

Lemma 7.4.2. If G is a ρn,P -group then G satisfies Wn,c,k .

Proof. Since G is in APc ∪ Bk , the sentences φc1 and φk2 hold in G. Also, since Fitt(G) is

abelian, Fitt(G) = ﬁtt∀ (G).

   In order to show that G satisﬁes the remaining sentences in Wn,c,k , it is enough to

check that ﬁtt∃c,k (G) ⊆ Fitt(G). Note that, since sc (G) is abelian, it is in Fitt(G). Let

g be an element of ﬁtt∃c,k (G), so that there is an element h = sc (h1 , . . . , hC ) 6= 1 with
                                            
h1 , . . . , hC ∈ G such that h, g, . . . , g = 1. Now h ∈ sc (G) ⩽ Fitt(G) and the result
                                 | {z }
                                   k
follows by the same argument as in the proof of Lemma 6.4.2.

Lemma 7.4.3. If G is a ρn,P -group then G satisfies U∗P .

Proof. The argument is almost identical to that of the proof of Lemma 6.4.4.

   Combining Lemmas 7.4.2 and 7.4.3 we have:

Lemma 7.4.4. If G is a ρn,P -group then G satisfies Wn,P .

7.5       Proof of theorems

In this section we prove the results stated in Section 7.1. For the reader’s convenience we

restate each theorem before proving it. Recall that n is a square-free positive integer or

zero.

Theorem 7.1.1 Let P be a finitely generated torsion-free group in Pc ∩ Bk and let U be

a non-trivial abelian group of exponent n. If G is a group which is not in Pc then the

following conditions are equivalent:

 (1) G ∈ ucl(U wr P );

 (2) G satisfies the universal sentences Wn,P ;

 (3) G is a ρn,P -group;

                                                                                  (r)
 (4) Every finitely generated subgroup of G can be embedded in Cn wr Q for some r ∈ N

        and some Q such that Q ∈ Th∀ (P ).

Proof. We prove the implications (1) =⇒ (2) ⇐⇒ (3) =⇒ (4) =⇒ (1).


(1) =⇒ (2). The group G is in ucl(U wr P ) and so G |= Th∀ (U wr H). By Lemma 3.4.1

        and Lemma 3.4.2, we have U wr P |= Th∀ (Cn wr P ); thus G |= Th∀ (Cn wr P ) and it

        follows, by Lemma 7.2.1, that G |= Wn,P .

(2) ⇐⇒ (3). The equivalence of (2) and (3) follows immediately from the results of

        Section 7.4.

(3) =⇒ (4). Suppose now that G is a ρn,P -group, so that G |= Wn,P by Lemma 7.4.4,

        and let G1 be a ﬁnitely generated subgroup of G. Since G is not in Pc , there exist ele-

        ments h1 , . . . , hC ∈ G such that sc (h1 , . . . , hC ) 6= 1 and we let G2 = hG1 , h1 , . . . , hC i.

        The subgroup sc (G2 ) is non-trivial and G2 is not in Pc . The sentences Wn,P are

        universal and so every subgroup of G satisﬁes Wn,P ; in particular G2 satisﬁes Wn,P ,

        and hence G2 is a ρn,P -group by Lemma 7.4.1. The quotient G2 = G2 / Fitt(G2 )

        satisﬁes the universal theory of P ; thus G2 is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free soluble

        group and hence the group rings Z[G2 ] and Fp [G2 ], where p is a prime, are integral



                                                   – 120 –
     domains by Theorem 3.1.1. It follows, by Lemma 3.1.2, that Z[G2 ] and Fp [G2 ] are

     Ore domains.

     If n = 0 then G2 is an extension of Fitt(G2 ) by G2 satisfying the conditions of

     Lemma 3.3.1, and G2 embeds in V wr G2 , where V is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free

     abelian group. It follows that G2 embeds in Z(r) wr G2 for some r ∈ N. If n 6= 0 then

     G2 is an extension of Fitt(G2 ) by G2 satisfying the conditions of Lemma 3.3.2. Thus

     G2 embeds in V wr G2 , where V is a ﬁnitely generated abelian group of exponent

     dividing n. We may write V = Cn1 × · · · × Cnr where Cnj is a cyclic group of

     exponent nj which divides n (see [53, 4.2.1]). Each cyclic group Cnj embeds in Cn

     and hence V embeds in the direct product of r copies of Cn . It follows that G2
                   (r)
     embeds in Cn wr(G2 ). In both cases we have G2 |= Th∀ (P ) and, since G1 ⩽ G2 ,
                                       (r)
     the subgroup G1 embeds in Cn wr G2 as required.

     of the form

                                    ∀x1 . . . xm ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ),

     where ϕ(x1 , . . . , xm ) is quantiﬁer-free. We let g1 . . . , gm be elements of G and let

     G1 = hg1 , . . . , gm i, so that G1 embeds in V wr Q, where V is a ﬁnitely generated

     abelian group of exponent n and Q |= UP . By Lemmas 3.4.1 and 3.4.2, the restric-

     ted wreath product V wr Q satisﬁes the universal theory of U wr P ; in particular

     V wr Q |= φ and hence ϕ(g1 , . . . , gm ) holds. This is true for all m-tuples in G and
                                                                              
     hence G |= φ. Thus G satisﬁes Th∀ U wr P and G is in ucl U wr P .

7.6      Non-split extensions

Let G be a ﬁnitely generated group with an abelian normal subgroup A such that G/A is a

torsion-free soluble group. If A is torsion-free as a Z[G/A]-module then, by Lemma 3.3.1,

the group G embeds in U wr(G/A), where U is a ﬁnitely generated torsion-free abelian

group, and hence G is in ucl(Z wr(G/A)). If A has exponent n and the submodule of A

of elements of order p is torsion-free as an Fp [G/A]-module for each prime divisor p of n

then, by Lemma 3.3.2, the group G embeds in U wr(G/A), where U is a ﬁnitely generated


                                          – 122 –
abelian group of exponent n, and hence G is in ucl(Cn wr(G/A)). We construct examples

of such groups using the Magnus and Shmel′ kin embeddings. See Chapter 2 for more

about these embeddings.

    Let H be an r-generator torsion-free polynilpotent group and let F be an absolutely

free group of rank r; then H is isomorphic to F/R for some R ⊳ F . By the Magnus

embedding, G = F/R′ can be embedded in (F/F ′ ) wr(F/R). The quotient F/F ′ is a non-

trivial torsion-free abelian group and hence, by [16, Lemma 1], is universally equivalent

to Z. Thus the group G is in ucl(Z wr H) and it follows that ucl(G) ⊆ ucl(Z wr H).

    Now let H be a free group of rank r in Pc , so that G is a free group of rank r in APc ;

the universal closure of G is contained in ucl(ZwrFr (Pc )). By a result of Baumslag (see

Lemma 2.4.4), every nilpotent subgroup of G is either cyclic or contained in the verbal

subgroup sc (G), which is abelian; thus every nilpotent subgroup of G is abelian. Let φ

denote the sentence

                                                                      
                      ∀xy ([x, y, x] = 1 ∧ [x, y, y] = 1) → [x, y] = 1 .


Then φ holds in G and it follows that every nilpotent group in ucl(G) is abelian. The verbal

subgroup scl−1 (H) is a nilpotent subgroup of H and hence of Z wr H. Since universal

closures are closed under taking subgroups, we have sc′ (H) ∈ ucl(Z wr H). If cl 6= 1 then

scl−1 (H) is not abelian and scl−1 (H) is not in ucl(G); thus the inclusion


                             ucl(Fr (APc )) ⊆ ucl(Z wr Fr (Pc ))


is strict.

    Let V be the set of words {[x, y], xp }. By the Shmel′ kin embedding, the group

Gp = F/V (R) can be embedded in (F/V (F )) wrV(F/R) = (F/V (F )) wr(F/R). Since

the quotient F/V (F ) is an abelian group of exponent p, Lemma 3.4.2 implies that

(F/V (F )) wr F/R is universally equivalent to Cp wr H and hence Gp ∈ ucl(Cp wr H):

for example, ucl(Fr (Ap Pc )) is contained in ucl(Cp wr Fr (Pc )). By the same argument as

above, this inclusion is strict when cl 6= 1.

    Part III

     THE
 THEORIES OF
   CERTAIN
SOLUBLE GROUPS
                                        Chapter 8


   COMMUTATOR LENGTHS AND THE THEORY OF

                        CERTAIN SOLUBLE GROUPS



We say that a group G is a Cn -group if there exists an integer t such that each element

of γn (G) can be written as a product of t commutators [h1 , g1 ] · · · [ht , gt ] with gi ∈ G and

hi ∈ γn−1 (G) for i = 1, . . . , t.

    In the ﬁrst part of the chapter we consider some examples of Cn -groups. It is known

that a group G is a C2 -group if it is in one of the following classes of soluble groups:

    • ﬁnitely generated nilpotent groups (Stroud, see [2]);

    • ﬁnitely generated abelian-by-nilpotent groups (Akhavan-Malayeri and Rhemtulla

      [2]);

    • ﬁnitely generated metanilpotent groups (Hartley [19]);

    • ﬁnitely generated abelian-by-metanilpotent groups (Rhemtulla [52]);

    • groups with an abelian normal subgroup such that the quotient satisﬁes the maximal

      condition for normal subgroups (Rhemtulla [52]);

    • groups of ﬁnite Prüfer rank (Akhavan-Malayeri [1]).

    For a number of these classes we can extend these results to all terms of the lower

central series. In the following pages we show that G is a Cn -group for all n ⩾ 2 if G is

in one of the following classes:

    • ﬁnitely generated ﬁnite-by-abelian-by-metanilpotent groups;



                                            – 125 –
   • ﬁnite-by-soluble groups satisfying the maximal condition on normal subgroups.

In the case of ﬁnitely generated abelian-by-metanilpotent groups we obtain an explicit

bound.

   We go on to give one-variable existential formulae deﬁning the terms of the lower

central series in a group which is a Cn -group for all n ⩾ 2. These formulae allow us to

say something about the elementary theory of such groups; in particular we show that

elementary equivalence is preserved under taking quotients by the terms of the lower

central series.

   The corresponding result for universal equivalence does not hold: Timoshenko [67,

Proposition 2] constructs a group universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free metabelian

group whose abelianization contains elements of ﬁnite order.



8.1      The lower central series

In this section we obtain some examples of Cn -groups. We note to begin with that a

ﬁnite-by-Cn group is a Cn -group. Let G be a group with a ﬁnite normal subgroup A

such that G/A is a Cn -group and let t be a positive integer such that every element

of γn (G/A) can be written as a product of t commutators. For a ∈ A ∩ γn (G), we

suppose that a = [h1 , g1 ] · · · [hta , gta ] with hi ∈ γn−1 (G) and gi ∈ G and we let t′ =

max{ta | a ∈ A ∩ γn (G)}; every element of γn (G) can be written as a product of t + t′

commutators.

   In his Ph.D. thesis Peter Stroud proved the following result (see [2]).

Lemma 8.1.1. Let G = hg1 , . . . , gn i be a nilpotent group. Every element of the commu-

tator subgroup G′ is a product of n commutators [g1 , h1 ] · · · [gn , hn ], for suitable elements

hi in G.

   Using the same argument, we extend the result to all terms of the lower central series.

Our result diﬀers from that of Oger [46, Lemma 1.1] for ﬁnite-by-nilpotent groups in that

we obtain an explicit bound on the number of commutators needed.

Lemma 8.1.2. Let G = hg1 , . . . , gr i be a nilpotent group. For n ⩾ 2, an element g


                                            – 126 –
of γn (G) can be written as a product of r commutators g = [h1 , g1 ] · · · [hr , gr ] with hi ∈

γn−1 (G) for i = 1, . . . , r.

Proof. Suppose that G is nilpotent of class c ⩾ 1 and proceed by induction on c. If c = 1

then G is abelian and γn (G) = {1} for all n ⩾ 2. Thus the result holds vacuously.

    Now let c ⩾ 2 and suppose that the result holds for c − 1. If n ⩾ c + 1 then γn (G) ⩽

γc+1 (G) = 1 and the result holds vacuously. Suppose therefore that n ⩽ c and let g be an

element of γn (G). The quotient G/γc (G) is nilpotent of class at most c − 1 and the image

of g in G/γc (G) is in γn (G/γc (G)). By induction, we may write g = [h1 , g1 ] · · · [hr , gr ]k

with hi ∈ γn−1 (G) and gi ∈ G for i = 1, . . . , r and k ∈ γc (G). Now γc (G) = [γc−1 (G), G]

and γc−1 (G) is contained in ζ2 (G). Thus, by [2, Lemma 3], we have k = [a1 , g1 ] · · · [ar , gr ]

with ai ∈ γc−1 (G) for i = 1, . . . , r. Since [ai , gi ] ∈ γc (G) ⩽ Z(G) for i = 1, . . . , r, we have

                                 g = [h1 , g1 ] · · · [hr , gr ]k

                                   = [h1 , g1 ] · · · [hr , gr ][a1 , g1 ] · · · [ar , gr ]

                                   = [h1 , g1 ][a1 , g1 ] · · · [hr , gr ][ar , gr ]

                                   = [a1 h1 , g1 ] · · · [ar hr , gr ]

with ai ∈ γc−1 (G) ⩽ γn−1 (G) and ai hi ∈ γn−1 (G) as required.

    We also extend the result of Akhavan-Malayeri and Rhemtulla [2, Theorem 2] about

commutator lengths in abelian-by-nilpotent groups.

Lemma 8.1.3. Let G be an abelian-by-nilpotent group generated by r elements. For

n ⩾ 2, an element g of γn (G) can be written as a product of r commutators g =

[u1 , v1 ] · · · [ur , vr ] with ui ∈ γn−1 (G) and vi ∈ G for i = 1, . . . , r.

abelian for some positive integer c. We let d = max{n − 2, c}, so that γd+1 (G) ⩽ γc+1 (G)

is abelian. By [2, Lemma 3], we have

                [γd+1 (G), G] = {[a1 , g1 ] · · · [ar , gr ] | ai ∈ γd+1 (G), i = 1, . . . , r}.

Let G = G/γd+2 (G), so that G is nilpotent and, by Lemma 8.1.2,

                    γn (G) = {[h1 , g 1 ] · · · [hr , g r ] | hi ∈ γn−1 (G), i = 1, . . . , r},

                                 g = [h1 , g1 ] · · · [hr , gr ][a1 , g1 ] · · · [ar , gr ],

with hi ∈ γn−1 (G) and ai ∈ γd+1 (G) ⩽ γn−1 (G) for i = 1, . . . , r. Thus we have

    The bound in Lemma 8.1.3 depends only on the number of generators of G. In

metanilpotent groups the bound we obtain depends on the number of generators, the

nilpotent class of the top group and the term of the lower central series that we are

considering. This next lemma extends Hartley’s result about the derived subgroup of a

metanilpotent group [19, Corollary 2].

Lemma 8.1.4. Let G be a metanilpotent group with class sequence (c1 , c2 ) generated by

r elements. For n ⩾ 2, an element g of γn (G) can be written as a product of at most t

commutators g = [u1 , v1 ] · · · [ut , vt ] with ui ∈ γn−1 (G) and vi ∈ G for i = 1, . . . , t where

the value of t depends only on n, r and c1 .

Proof. Let g1 , . . . , gr generate G and let d = max {n − 2, c1 }. We claim that the result

holds with t = 2r + r d+1 .

where s = r d+1 . By [19, Lemma 3], we have

Corollary 8.1.1. Let G be an abelian-by-metanilpotent group with class sequence (c1 , c2 , 1)

of at most s commutators g = [u1 , v1 ] · · · [us , vs ] with ui ∈ γn−1 (G) and vi ∈ G for

i = 1, . . . , s, where the value of s depends only on n, r and c1 .

Proof. Let d = max{n − c2 − 2, c1 } and let

                               γc2 +2 (γd+1 (G)) = [A, γd+1 (G)] ⩽ [A, G].

and by Lemma 8.1.4, each element of γn (G/[A, G]) can be written as a product of t =

with ui ∈ γn−1 (G), vi ∈ G for i = 1, . . . , t and k ∈ [A, G]. Since A is abelian, it follows

                                                        – 129 –
   Finally we show that a bound exists for soluble groups with the maximal condition on

normal subgroups (cf. [52, Corollary 1]). We recall that a group G satisﬁes the maximal

condition on normal subgroups (or max-n) if, for every series of normal subgroups of G

                               1 = G0 ⩽ G1 ⩽ · · · ⩽ Gn ⩽ · · · ,

there is some natural number N such that Gn = GN for all n ⩾ N . We require the

following intermediate result.

Lemma 8.1.5. Let G be a group satisfying max-n and let H be a normal subgroup of G.

For n ⩾ 2, the quotient G/γn (H) is a Cn -group if and only if G/γn (γn (H)) is a Cn -group.



Proof. The group G/γn (H) is a quotient of G/γn (γn (H)). Thus the result is clear in one

direction.

   Suppose now that G/γn (H) is a Cn -group. We may assume without loss of generality

that γn (γn (H)) is trivial, so that γn (H) is a nilpotent normal subgroup of G. Since G

satisﬁes max-n, γn (H) is ﬁnitely generated as a normal subgroup of G. By a result of

Hartley [19, Lemma 3], there is a positive integer s such that every element of [γn (H), G]

can be written as a product of commutators [h1 , g1 ] · · · [hs , gs ] with gi ∈ G and hi ∈

γn (H) ⩽ γn−1 (H). It is enough to show that G/[γn (H), G] is a Cn -group and we may

assume without loss of generality that [γn (H), G] is trivial, so that γn (H) ⩽ Z(G). Again

since G satisﬁes max-n, H is ﬁnitely generated as a normal subgroup of G. We suppose

                                      | {z }

Lemma 8.1.6. A soluble group satisfying max-n is a Cn -group for all n ⩾ 2.

Proof. Let G be a soluble group satisfying max-n so that G is ﬁnitely generated [53,

5.4.21]. Since G is soluble, it has ﬁnite m-nilpotent length for any m ⩾ 1. Fix n ⩾ 2 and

proceed by induction on the (n − 1)-nilpotent length of G.

    If G is nilpotent then G is a Cn -group by Lemma 8.1.2. Suppose now that every group

of (n−1)-nilpotent length k which satisﬁes the maximal condition for normal subgroups is

a Cn -group and that G has (n − 1)-nilpotent length k + 1. Let N = γn (γn (· · · γn (G) · · · )),
                                                                   |    {z        }
                                                                                          k−1
so that γn (γn (N )) = 1. The quotient G/γn (N ) has (n − 1)-nilpotent length k and hence,

by induction, G/γn (N ) is a Cn -group. Lemma 8.1.5 implies that G = G/γn (γn (N )) is a

Cn -group.

    Combining each of these results with our remark at the beginning of this section that

a ﬁnite-by-Cn group is a Cn -group, we have shown that G is a Cn -group for all n ⩾ 2 if

G is in one of the following classes:

   • ﬁnitely generated ﬁnite-by-abelian-by-metanilpotent groups;

   • ﬁnite-by-soluble groups satisfying the maximal condition on normal subgroups.



8.2     Elementary theory

In Section 8.1 we gave a number of examples of groups which are Cn -groups for all n ⩾ 2.

We now go on to consider the implications of being a Cn -group for the elementary theory


                                                   – 131 –
of a group.

Lemma 8.2.1. Fix a positive integer n and let H be a Cr -group for 2 ⩽ r ⩽ n. There is an

existential formula in one variable φn (x) such that, for any group G which is elementarily

equivalent to H, the formula φn (x) defines γn (G).

Proof. We proceed by induction on n. For n = 1, we have γ1 (G) = G and we deﬁne φ1 (x)

to be the formula x = x.

    Suppose now that the result holds for n − 1. For each k ⩾ 1, we deﬁne an existential

formula αk (x) by
                                             k
                                                                                             !
                                             ^
                  ∃y1 . . . yk z1 . . . zk         φn−1 (yi ) ∧ x = [y1 , z1 ] · · · [yk , zk ] .
                                             i=1

By assumption there exists a positive integer t such that every element h of γn (H) can be

written as a product h = [h1 , g1 ] · · · [ht , gt ] with gi ∈ H and hi ∈ γn−1 (H) for i = 1, . . . , t.

The sentence ∀x (αt+1 (x) → αt (x)) holds in H, and hence in G, since G is elementarily

equivalent to H. If φn (x) is the formula αt (x) then φn (x) deﬁnes γn (G).

    We come now to the main result of this section.

Theorem 8.2.1. Fix a positive integer n and let H be a Cr -group for 2 ⩽ r ⩽ n. If the

group G is elementarily equivalent to H then γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to γn (H)

and G/γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to H/γn (H).

Proof. Let φ(x) be the formula φn (x) as deﬁned in Lemma 8.2.1 and let ψ be a ﬁrst-order

sentence such that H/γn (H) |= ψ. We may assume without loss of generality that ψ is in

prenex normal form; thus ψ is of the form

We deﬁne ψ ∗ by

For any group Γ such that φ(x) deﬁnes γn (Γ), we have Γ |= ψ ∗ if and only if Γ/γn (Γ) |= ψ;

thus H |= ψ ∗ . Since G is elementarily equivalent to H, we have G |= ψ ∗ and hence

G/γn (G) |= ψ. Thus G/γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to G/γn (G).

   Now let θ be a ﬁrst-order sentence such that γn (H) |= θ and suppose without loss of

generality that θ is in prenex normal form. Thus θ is of the form


                               Q1 x1 . . . Qk xk σ(x1 , . . . , xk ),


where σ = σ(x1 , . . . , xk ) is quantiﬁer-free. We let σ0 = σ. Suppose that σi has been

and we take θ ∗ to be σk . For any group Γ such that φ(x) deﬁnes γn (Γ), we have Γ |= θ ∗

if and only if γn (Γ) |= θ; thus H |= θ ∗ . Since G is elementarily equivalent to H, we have

G |= θ ∗ and hence γn (G) |= θ. Thus γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to γn (H).

   The results of Section 8.1 give us examples of groups which are Cn -groups for all

integers n ⩾ 2. We can combine these results with Theorem 8.2.1 to obtain the following

statements:

   • If H is a ﬁnitely generated ﬁnite-by-abelian-by-metanilpotent group and G is ele-

     mentarily equivalent to H then, for all n ⩾ 2, the subgroup γn (G) is elementa-

     rily equivalent to γn (H) and the quotient G/γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to

     H/γn (H).

   • If H is a ﬁnite-by-soluble group satisfying the maximal condition on normal sub-

     groups and G is elementarily equivalent to H then, for all n ⩾ 2, the subgroup

     γn (G) is elementarily equivalent to γn (H) and the quotient G/γn (G) is elementarily

     equivalent to H/γn (H).




                                            – 133 –
                                      Chapter 9


   THE UNIVERSAL THEORY OF FREE GROUPS IN

                   CERTAIN SOLUBLE VARIETIES



Chapuis [12, Corollary 5.3] determines those 2-generator groups which are universally

equivalent to a non-cyclic free metabelian group: there are precisely two isomorphism

classes of such groups, namely the free metabelian group of rank 2, and the restricted

wreath product of two inﬁnite cyclic groups. In Chapter 4 we obtained a similar result

for the variety An A, where n is a square-free positive integer: there are precisely two non-

isomorphic 2-generator groups universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free group in An A,

namely the free group of rank 2 in An A, and the restricted wreath product of a cyclic

group of exponent n by an inﬁnite cyclic group. In [66], Timoshenko determines those

2-generator groups ﬁnitely presented in the variety of soluble groups of derived length d

which are universally equivalent to a non-cyclic free soluble group of derived length d:

again there are precisely two isomorphism classes of such groups, namely the free soluble

group of derived length d and rank 2, and the Sd−1 -verbal wreath product of two inﬁnite

cyclic groups. Since ﬁnitely generated metabelian groups satisfy the maximal condition

on normal subgroups, they are ﬁnitely presented in the variety of metabelian groups and

so Timoshenko’s result implies that of Chapuis.

   Timoshenko’s proof that F2 (Sd ) and Z wrSd−1 Z are universally equivalent appears to

contain a small error. We correct this error and extend the result to free groups in certain

other soluble varieties. We deal with product varieties VA where V satisﬁes the following

conditions: V contains the variety of abelian groups, the free groups of V are residually

ﬁnite p-groups for inﬁnitely many primes p and V is generated by its k-generator groups



                                          – 134 –
for some positive integer k. Under these conditions, we prove that the free group of

rank 2 in VA is universally equivalent to the V-verbal wreath product of two inﬁnite

cyclic groups.

   Consider now the variety VNc for c ⩾ 2, where V is a variety whose free groups are

residually ﬁnite p-groups for inﬁnitely many primes p. We show that a 2-generator group

ﬁnitely presented in this variety is universally equivalent to the free group of rank 2 in

VNc if and only if it is isomorphic to it. This contrasts with the earlier result for VA

where there are at least two non-isomorphic such groups. We also consider conditions for

a group in the universal closure of F2 (VNc ) to be universally equivalent to F2 (VNc ).



9.1    Universally equivalent 2-generator groups in VA

Corollary 4 of Timoshenko’s paper [66] (the proof that F2 (Sd ) and Z wrSd−1 Z are univer-

sally equivalent) appears to contain a small error in the deﬁnition of the normal subgroup

N . In Proposition 9.1.1 we correct this error. In Lemma 9.1.1 and Proposition 9.1.1 we

extend the results of Lemma 1 and Corollary 4 of [66] to a more general class of groups.

Lemma 9.1.1. Let V be a variety containing A such that the free groups of V are resi-

dually finite p-groups for infinitely many primes p. Let F = F2 (VA) and let g and h be

elements of F such that g ∈ F \ F ′ and h ∈ F ′ \ γ2 (F ′ ). The group hg, hi is isomorphic

to Z wrV Z.

Special cases:

   • V = Sd . The non-cyclic free soluble group of derived length d + 1 is universally

   • V = Pc . The non-cyclic free (polynilpotent with class sequence c)-by-abelian group

      is universally equivalent to the verbal wreath product Z wrPc Z.

                                          – 137 –
   As an immediate consequence of Lemma 9.2.1 we have the following proposition.

Proposition 9.2.1. Let V be a variety whose free groups are residually finite p-groups

for infinitely many primes p and let G be a 2-generator group which is finitely presented

in VNc . Then G is universally equivalent to F2 (VNc ) if and only if G is isomorphic to

F2 (VNc ).

   A ﬁnitely generated group in ANc is ﬁnitely presented in ANc . Taking V = A in

Proposition 9.2.1, we have the following result.

Corollary 9.2.1. If G is a 2-generator group universally equivalent to F2 (ANc ) then G

is isomorphic to F2 (ANc ).

   Thus there is precisely one isomorphism class of 2-generator groups universally equi-

valent to F2 (ANc ). This contrasts with the free soluble case, where there are at least two

isomorphism class of 2-generator groups universally equivalent to F2 (Sd ) and, in parti-

cular, with the metabelian case where there are precisely two such isomorphism classes.

   Taking V = E in Proposition 9.2.1, we have the following result.

Corollary 9.2.2. If G is a 2-generator group universally equivalent to F2 (Nc ) then G is

isomorphic to F2 (Nc ).

   Next we consider the implications of Lemma 9.2.1 for an arbitrary group in the uni-

versal closure of F2 (ANc ).

Proposition 9.2.2. A group G ∈ ucl(F2 (ANc )) is universally equivalent to F2 (ANc ) if

and only if G contains a 2-generator subgroup which is not in ANc−1 .

Proof. Let H be a 2-generator subgroup of G such that H 6∈ ANc−1 . Since G is in

ucl(F2 (ANc )) and universally closed classes are closed under taking subgroups, H is in

ucl(F2 (ANc )). By Lemma 9.2.1, the group H is isomorphic to F2 (ANc ). Thus G contains

an isomorphic copy of F2 (ANc ) and hence G satisﬁes the existential theory of F2 (ANc ).

Since G is in ucl(F2 (ANc )), it follows that G is universally equivalent to F2 (ANc ).

   For c = 2 or 3, the variety Nc is discriminated by its 2-generator free group and it

Lemma 9.2.2.

 (1) Let G ∈ ucl(F2 (AN2 )). Then G is metabelian if and only if every 2-generator

   Recall, from Section 7.6, that ucl(F2 (ANc )) is contained in ucl(Z wr F2 (Nc )). Thus,

by Theorem 6.1.1, either G is nilpotent of class at most c or the Fitting subgroup A of

G is abelian and torsion-free as a Z[G/A]-module. By Theorem 2.4.4, every non-cyclic

nilpotent subgroup of F2 (ANc ) is contained in γc+1 (F2 (ANc )), which is abelian. Hence

every nilpotent subgroup of F2 (ANc ) is abelian and F2 (ANc ) |= θ, where θ is deﬁned by


                       ∀xy ([x, y, x] = 1 ∧ [x, y, y] = 1 → [x, y] = 1).


Since G is in ucl(F2 (ANc )), we have G |= θ and every nilpotent subgroup of G is abelian;

thus if G is nilpotent, it is abelian and there is nothing to prove. Suppose therefore that

A = Fitt(G) is abelian and torsion-free as a Z[G/A]-module.



                                               – 139 –
    Let c = 2. For elements g, h ∈ G such that hg, hi is metabelian we have the following

identities:

                                                                  
                            [g, h, g](−[g,h]+1) = [g, h], [g, h, g] = 1,
                                                                  
                            [g, h, h](−[g,h]+1) = [g, h], [g, h, h] = 1.


Since G is abelian-by-(nilpotent of class 2), the elements [g, h, g] and [g, h, h] are in

A. Thus, since A is torsion-free as a Z[G/A]-module, either [g, h] ∈ A or [g, h, g] =

[g, h, h] = 1. In the latter case the group hg, hi is nilpotent, and hence abelian, and

[g, h] = 1 ∈ A.

    If every 2-generator subgroup of G is metabelian then, for all g, h ∈ G, we have

[g, h] ∈ A. It follows that G′ ⩽ A, which is abelian, and hence G is metabelian.

    Now let c = 3. For elements g, h ∈ G such that hg, hi is abelian-by-(nilpotent of class

2) we have the following identities:

                                                                        
                       [g, h, g, g](−[g,h,g]+1) = [g, h, g], [g, h, g, g] = 1,
                                                                        
                       [g, h, g, h](−[g,h,g]+1) = [g, h, g], [g, h, g, h] = 1,
                                                                        
                       [g, h, h, g](−[g,h,g]+1) = [g, h, g], [g, h, h, g] = 1,
                                                                        
                       [g, h, h, h](−[g,h,g]+1) = [g, h, g], [g, h, h, h] = 1.


Since G is abelian-by-(nilpotent of class 3), the elements [g, h, g, g], [g, h, g, h], [g, h, h, g]

and [g, h, h, h] are in A. Thus, since A is torsion-free as a Z[G/A]-module, either [g, h, g] ∈

A or [g, h, g, g] = [g, h, g, h] = [g, h, h, g] = [g, h, h, h] = 1. In the latter case hg, hi is

nilpotent, and hence abelian, and [g, h, g] = 1 ∈ A.

    If every 2-generator subgroup of G is abelian-by-(nilpotent of class 2) then, for all

g, h ∈ G, we have [g, h, g] ∈ A. It follows that G/A satisﬁes the law [x, y, x] and, since

G/A is torsion-free, G/A is nilpotent of class 2 (Levi, see [44, 34.31]). Thus γ3 (G) ⩽ A

which is abelian and hence G is abelian-by-(nilpotent of class 2).

    By combining Lemma 9.2.2 and Proposition 9.2.2, we obtain a necessary and suﬃcient

condition for a group in ucl(Fk (ANc )) with k ⩾ 2 to be universally equivalent to Fk (ANc )

when c = 2 or 3.

Proposition 9.2.3.

  1. Let G ∈ ucl(Fk (AN2 )) for k ⩾ 2. Then G is universally equivalent to Fk (AN2 ) if

        and only if G is not metabelian.

  2. Let G ∈ ucl(Fk (AN3 )) for k ⩾ 2. Then G is universally equivalent to Fk (AN3 ) if

        and only if G is not abelian-by-(nilpotent of class 2).

      We can now describe explicitly the lattice of universally closed classes of groups in

ucl(Fk (AN2 )) for k ⩾ 2 (see Figure 9.1). If G is a non-abelian metabelian group in

ucl(Fk (AN2 )) ⊆ ucl(Z wr F2 (N2 )) then G is a non-nilpotent ρ0,Z -group1 . Thus G is uni-

versally equivalent to Z wr Z (by [12, Lemma 4.9]) and hence to F2 (S2 ). This lattice occurs

as a sublattice in the lattice of universally closed classes of groups in ucl(Z wr F2 (N2 ))

(see Figure 6.2 on page 106).

      We do not have complete information about the lattice of universally closed classes of

groups in the universal closure of a non-cyclic free group in AN3 . The metabelian groups

in ucl(F2 (AN3 ) are once again those in ucl(F2 (S2 )) = ucl(Z wr Z). It would be interesting

to obtain examples of non-metabelian groups which are in ucl(F2 (AN3 )) ∩ AN2 but not

in ucl(F2 (AN2 )). It is not clear whether any such groups exist.

                                                 – 141 –
                                         Chapter 10


       THE THEORIES OF SOME RELATIVELY FREE

                                SOLUBLE GROUPS



Throughout this chapter, let V1 , . . . , Vk be non-trivial nilpotent varieties whose free

groups are torsion-free. Let Vi be any set of words which deﬁnes Vi and suppose that

Vi ⊆ Nci and Vi 6⊆ Nci −1 . Let G be a group. For i = 0, . . . , k − 1, we deﬁne Ui (G) to be

the verbal subgroup Vk−i (· · · (V1 (G)) · · · ) of G.

    As a consequence of the results discussed in Chapter 2, the free groups in Vi for

i = 1, . . . , k are residually ﬁnite p-groups for every prime p (by Lemma 2.2.1) and hence

the free groups in the product variety Vk · · · V1 are residually ﬁnite p-groups for every

prime p (by Lemma 2.4.1).

    We begin by obtaining one-variable formulae deﬁning a number of verbal subgroups

of a free group F in Vk · · · V1 . In particular we are able to ﬁnd universal and existential

formulae which deﬁne the verbal subgroups Ui (F ) for i = 0, . . . , k − 1. We use these

formulae to extend results of Romanovskiı̆ and Timoshenko in [57] and Chapuis in [13]

about the theories of free soluble groups.

    In [57, Theorem 3], Romanovskiı̆ and Timoshenko prove that if F is a free soluble

group of rank n and G is an n-generator group elementarily equivalent to F then G is

isomorphic to F . We use the deﬁnability of the derived subgroup to extend this result to

free groups in Vk · · · V1 .

    In Chapter 1 we discussed the questions posed by Tarski about the elementary theory

of absolutely free groups. Here we ask, and answer, the corresponding questions for the

free groups in the product variety Vk · · · V1 .



                                              – 142 –
   • Do free groups in Vk · · · V1 of distinct ranks have distinct elementary theories?

   • Is the elementary theory of a free group in Vk · · · V1 decidable?

To these we add the question of whether the universal theory of a free group in Vk · · · V1

is decidable.

   We show that two free groups in Vk · · · V1 of diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks have diﬀerent ∀∃-

theories by considering the abelianizations of the groups and using the results of Szmielew

[63] about free abelian groups.

   We go on to use the negative answer to Hilbert’s Tenth Problem over the integers to

show that a free group F in Vk · · · V1 of ﬁnite rank has undecidable ∀∃-theory. To each

polynomial P (X) in several variables with coeﬃcients in Z, we associate a ∀∃-sentence ψ

such that P (X) has a zero in Z if and only if F |= ψ. By Matiyasevich’s theorem [40],

no algorithm exists to determine whether a polynomial P (X) in several variables with

coeﬃcients in Z has a zero in Z. It follows that there does not exist an algorithm to

determine whether a ∀∃-sentence holds in F .

   The problem of determining whether a non-cyclic free soluble group of derived length

d ⩾ 3 has decidable universal theory is a very diﬃcult one. Chapuis [13, Theorem C1]

showed that an answer in the aﬃrmative would imply the existence of an algorithm to

determine whether a homogeneous polynomial in several variables with coeﬃcients in

Z has a non-trivial zero in Z. For ﬁxed d the proof associates to each homogeneous

polynomial P (X) an existential sentence ψ in the language of groups such that P (X)

has a non-trivial zero in Z if and only if ψ holds in a non-cyclic free soluble group of

derived length d. The existence of such an algorithm is equivalent to the decidability of

the universal theory of the ﬁeld of rationals [48, §9] which in turn is equivalent to Hilbert’s

Tenth Problem over the rationals (see Chapter 1). We extend Chapuis results to show

that the decidability of the universal theory of a free group of ﬁnite rank ⩾ 2 in certain

varieties Vk · · · V1 with k ⩾ 2 would imply a positive answer. We impose the following

conditions to expedite our proofs: either c1 ⩾ 2, or k ⩾ 3 and V2 = Nc2 .

   Throughout the remainder of this chapter let k be a positive integer such that k ⩾ 2.




                                           – 143 –
10.1       The definability of certain verbal subgroups

the product variety Vk · · · V1 are deﬁnable. In Lemmas 10.1.1 and 10.1.2 we obtain, for

each i, a universal formula θi∀ (x) and an existential formula θi∃ (x) which deﬁne the verbal

subgroup Ui (F ).

    Let x1 , x2 , . . . be free generators of F . Suppose that [h, x1 ] = 1 and that h lies in the

subgroup G = hx1 , . . . , xn i. (The generator x1 may or may not occur in h.) Consider the

free associative algebra A over Z generated by non-commuting indeterminates X1 , . . . , Xn

and let I be the ideal of A generated by all products Xi1 · · · Xic+1 . The subgroup of A/I

generated by the elements 1 + X1 , . . . , 1 + Xn is a free nilpotent group of class c and rank

n. Thus the map G → A/I : xi 7→ 1 + Xi for i = 1, . . . , n is an embedding; we associate G

with its image in A/I. The element h is in γc−1 (G) \ γc (G) and it expands as 1 + P + Q,

where P 6= 0 is homogeneous of weight c − 1 and Q is homogeneous of weight c. Then

[h, x1 ] expands as 1 + P X1 − X1 P and [h, x1 ] = 1 implies that P X1 − X1 P = 0. The

element P of A/I is homogeneous of weight c − 1 and hence we may write it as a sum of

monomials in the Xi of weight c − 1 where at least two variables occur in each monomial.

We have
                                               r
                                               X
                                         P =         δi mi ,
                                               i=1
where the δi are non-zero integers and the mi are monomials. We order the indeterminates

X1 > X2 > · · · > Xn and extend this to order the monomials lexicographically. We may

suppose, after suitable reordering, that m1 > m2 > · · · > mr . Then X1 m1 > · · · > X1 mr

and X1 m1 > m1 X1 > · · · > mr X1 . It follows that the leading term of P X1 − X1 P is

−δ1 X1 m1 which is non-zero and this contradicts our assumption that P X1 − X1 P = 0.

    It follows that there is no element g in CF (h) which is not in F ′ . A consideration of

commutator weights shows that F ′ ⩽ CF (h). Thus CF (h) = F ′ .

    Using the above result we obtain a description of the centre of a non-abelian free

nilpotent group which will allow us to deﬁne suitable universal formulae.

Lemma 10.1.4. Let F be a non-abelian free nilpotent group. If g is an element of F

then g ∈ Z(F ) if and only if there exist h1 , h2 ∈ F such that [h1 , h2 ] 6∈ γ3 (F ) and

[g, h1 ] = [g, h2 ] = 1.

Proof. The “only if” direction is clear. We suppose for the converse that g, h1 , h2 ∈ F

with [h1 , h2 ] 6∈ γ3 (F ) and [g, hi ] = 1 for i = 1, 2 and we proceed by induction on c.

    Suppose to begin with that F is nilpotent of class and rank 2; then F has presentation

hx, y, z|[x, y] = z, [x, z] = [y, z] = 1i. Every element of F can be written as a word of the


                                             – 148 –
form xr y s z t with r, s, t ∈ Z and the only trivial such word is the empty one. If g = xr y s z t

and hi = xri y si z ti for i = 1, 2 then


                          [h1 , h2 ] = [xr1 y s1 z t1 , xr2 y s2 z t2 ] = z r1 s2 −r2 s1


and

                              [g, hi ] = [xr y s z t , xri y si z ti ] = z rsi −ri s

for i = 1, 2. Thus [g, hi ] = 1 implies that rsi − ri s = 0 for i = 1, 2 and


                      (r1 s2 − r2 s1 )s = (rs2 − r2 s)s1 − (rs1 − r1 s)s2 = 0,

                      (r1 s2 − r2 s1 )r = (rs2 − r2 s)r1 − (rs1 − r1 s)r2 = 0.


Since [h1 , h2 ] 6= 1, we have r1 s2 − r2 s1 6= 0 and it follows that r = s = 0. Thus

g = z t ∈ Z(F ). The universal sentence θ deﬁned by
                                                                                   
             ∀x ∃y1 y2 [y1 , y2 ] 6= 1 ∧ [x, y1 ] = 1 ∧ [x, y2 ] = 1 → (∀z[x, z] = 1)


holds in F . Suppose now that F is a non-cyclic free nilpotent group of class 2 and any

rank. By Lemma 2.2.1, the group F is residually a ﬁnite p-group for every prime p.

Moreover, the group F generates the variety N2 . Thus, by Theorem 2.5.1, the group F

is universally equivalent to F and hence F |= θ. The result holds for all non-cyclic free

nilpotent groups of class 2.

    Suppose now that c ⩾ 3 and that the result holds for c − 1. Let F = F/γc (F ), so that

F is a free nilpotent group of class c − 1. Let g, h1 and h2 be the images of g, h1 and h2

in F . Since [h1 , h2 ] 6∈ γ3 (F ), the commutator [h1 , h2 ] is not in γ3 (F ). Moreover [g, hi ] = 1

in F for i = 1, 2. By induction, we have g ∈ Z(F ). In a free nilpotent group the terms

of the upper and lower central series coincide [68, Theorem 13]. Thus γc (F ) = Z(F ) and

hence g ∈ Z(F/Z(F )) = ζ2 (F )/Z(F ). The element g is in ζ2 (F ) = γc−1 (F ) and we may

apply Lemma 10.1.3. Since [h1 , h2 ] 6∈ γ3 (F ), the element h1 does not lie in F ′ and it

follows that g lies in Z(F ).

    We are now in a position to deﬁne the required formulae. Suppose that V2 = Nc2 and

let g be an element of F . Firstly we recursively deﬁne one variable universal formulae



                                                   – 149 –
σi∀ (x) for i = 0, . . . , c2 . Let σ0∀ (x) be the formula θk−2
                                                            ∀ (x). Now let i ⩾ 1 and suppose


that σi∀ (x) has been deﬁned. We deﬁne σi+1
                                        ∀ (x) to be the formula



                                          ∃
                                                                
                                      ∀y θk−1 (y) → σi∀ ([x, y]) .


Then, for g ∈ F , we have F |= σi∀ (g) if and only if the image of g in F = F/Uk−2 (F ) is in

ζi (Uk−1 (F )). Since Uk−1 (F ) is a free nilpotent group, ζi (Uk−1 (F )) = γc2 +1−i (Uk−1 (F )).

Hence F |= σi∀ (g) if and only if g ∈ γc2 +1−i (Uk−1 (F )).

    Next we recursively deﬁne one-variable existential formulae σi∃ (x) for i = 0, . . . , c2 . Let

10.2      Elementary equivalence and isomorphism

Romanovskiı̆ and Timoshenko [57, Theorem 3] showed that an n-generator group elemen-

tary equivalent to a free soluble group F of rank n is isomorphic to F . We prove the

analogous result for free groups in the product variety Vk · · · V1 .

Theorem 10.2.1. Let F be a free group of rank n in Vk · · · V1 . An n-generator group

G is elementarily equivalent to F if and only if G is isomorphic to F .

Proof. Since elementary equivalence is preserved by isomorphism, one of the implications

is trivial. Suppose that G is elementarily equivalent to F . If n = 1 then G is a torsion-free

abelian group of rank 1 and hence isomorphic to Z ∼
                                                  = F . Suppose therefore that n ⩾ 2.
    Let g1 , . . . , gn generate G and let x1 , . . . , xn be free generators of F . The group G

is non-trivial (since F is) and therefore at least one of the generators diﬀers from the

identity. Assume without loss of generality that g1 6= 1. Replacing any generator equal

to the identity with g1 we may assume that all the generators are non-trivial. Since G


                                                  – 150 –
is elementarily equivalent to F , it is in Vk · · · V1 and the map π : F → G : xi 7→ gi for

i = 1, . . . , n extends to a surjective homomorphism. Let R be the kernel of π, so that

G∼
 = F/R. Suppose that R is non-trivial: we show that this contradicts the elementary
equivalence of F and G. Let r = r(x1 , . . . , xn ) be a non-trivial element of R, so that

r(g1 , . . . , gn ) = 1.

    By the results of Section 10.1, there is a formula µn (x) deﬁning the derived subgroup

of F such that if g ∈ G′ then G |= µn (g). We deﬁne a sentence θ as follows:

                                   n
                                  ^                n
                                                    ^
  ∃y1 . . . yn ∀x∃u1 . . . un v         yi 6= 1 ∧         [yi , ui ] = 1
                                  i=1               i=1
                                                                                                                
                                                          ∧ r(y1 , . . . , yn ) = 1 ∧ µn (v) ∧ x = u1 · · · un v .


Every element g ∈ G can be written as a product g = h1 · · · hn k where hi is a power of gi

for i = 1, . . . , n and k is an element of G′ . Thus G satisﬁes θ and, since G is elementarily

equivalent to F , we have F |= θ.

    Let f1 , . . . , fn ∈ F play the role of the yi in the sentence. We may suppose that

f1 , . . . , fl 6∈ U1 (F ) and that fl+1 . . . , fn ∈ U1 (F ) for some l. Now let f be an element

of F and pick h1 , . . . , hn ∈ F and k ∈ F ′ such that [fi , hi ] = 1 for i = 1, . . . , n and

f = h1 · · · hn k. By Theorem 2.4.4, every non-cyclic nilpotent subgroup of F is contained

in U1 (F ). Thus the elements fi and hi are in the same cyclic subgroup for i = 1, . . . , l

and hl+1 , . . . , hn ∈ U1 (F ). The sentence θ implies that F/F ′ is generated by l elements;

however, F/F ′ is the free abelian group of rank n. Thus l = n and the elements f1 , . . . , fn

are linearly independent modulo F ′ . It follows, by Theorem 2.2.2, that f1 , . . . , fn are

free generators of the free group of rank n in Vk · · · V1 and the identity r(f1 , . . . , fn ) = 1

cannot hold.

    As a special case of Theorem 10.2.1 with Vi = Nci we have the following corollary.

Corollary 10.2.1. Let G be an n-generator group and let F be a free polynilpotent group

of rank n with class sequence c = (c1 , . . . , ck ). Then G is elementarily equivalent to F if

and only if G is isomorphic to F .




                                                      – 151 –
10.3       Relatively free groups of different finite ranks

We show that the rank of a free group in Vk · · · V1 has an eﬀect on the elementary theory.

Proposition 10.3.1. The free groups in Vk · · · V1 of different finite ranks have different

∀∃-theories.

Proof. Let F1 and F2 be two free groups in the product variety Vk . . . V1 of diﬀerent ﬁnite

ranks r1 and r2 respectively. If one of the groups is of rank 1 then it is abelian and therefore

not universally equivalent to the other which must be of rank strictly greater than 1 and

hence non-abelian. We may suppose without loss of generality that 2 ⩽ r1 < r2 .

    The quotients F1 /F1′ and F2 /F2′ are free abelian groups of rank r1 and r2 respectively.

It follows from results of Szmielew [63] that there exists a sentence ψ of the form
                                                            l
                                                            _
                                ∀x1 . . . xs ∃y1 . . . yt         wi (x, y) = 1,
                                                            i=1
where the wi (x, y) are words in the variables x1 , . . . , xs , y1 , . . . , yt , such that F1 /F1′ |= ψ

and F2 /F2′ |= ¬ψ. Consider, for example, the sentence ψ deﬁned by
                                                                  !
                                        _            _
                      ∀x1 . . . x2r1 ∃y   xi = y 2 ∨   xi xj = y 2 .
                                                i                   i6=j

Let φ(x) be the one-variable formula φr2 (x) as deﬁned in Section 10.1; the formula φ(x)

deﬁnes Fi′ for i = 1, 2. We deﬁne ψ ∗ to be the sentence
                                                                                      !
                                               _                    _
                          ∀x1 . . . x2r1 ∃y         φ(xi y 2 ) ∨           φ(xi xj y 2 ) .
                                                i                   i6=j

Since φ(x) is existential, ψ ∗ is a ∀∃-sentence. Moreover F1 |= ψ ∗ and F2 |= ¬ψ ∗ and hence

F1 and F2 have diﬀerent ∀∃-theories.

    As a special case with Vi = Nci we have the following corollary.

Corollary 10.3.1. Two free polynilpotent groups with class sequence c = (c1 , . . . , ck ) of

different finite ranks do not have the same ∀∃-theory.

    We note that Lawrence [26, Theorem 5] showed that, in a soluble variety, free groups

of diﬀerent ﬁnite ranks have distinct ∀∃∀-positive theories. In the case where k = 2, or

k = 3 and c3 = 1, we may use the results of Chapter 8 to obtain a positive existential

formula deﬁning the derived subgroups of F1 and F2 . In this case the same proof as that

of Lemma 10.3.1 shows that F1 and F2 do not have the same ∀∃-positive theory.

10.4      The undecidability of ∀∃-theory

We show that the elementary theory of a non-abelian ﬁnitely generated free group in

Vk · · · V1 is undecidable.

Theorem 10.4.1. A free group F of finite rank r ⩾ 2 in Vk · · · V1 has undecidable

∀∃-theory.

Proof. Let φr (x) and νr (x) be the one-variable formulae deﬁned in Section 10.1. We note

to begin with that there is a two-variable universal formula φ(x, y) such that, for g, h ∈ F ,

we have F |= φ(g, h) only if g and h are linearly independent modulo F ′ : we deﬁne φ(x, y)

to be the formula ¬νr ([x, y]). Let g and h be elements of F and let G = hg, hi; then g

and h are linearly dependent modulo F ′ if and only if G is cyclic modulo F ′ (since F/F ′

is torsion-free). By Lemma 4.5.1, this implies that G is generated by elements a ∈ F and

c ∈ F ′ and it follows that G′ ⩽ h[a, c]iG ⩽ γ3 (F ) and [g, h] ∈ γ3 (F ). Thus if F |= φ(g, h)

then g and h are linearly independent modulo F ′ .

    In order to prove our theorem it is suﬃcient to associate to each polynomial P (X)

in several variables with coeﬃcients in Z a ∀∃-sentence ψ in the language of groups such

that P (X) has a zero in Z if and only if F |= ψ. Let P (X1 , . . . , Xm ) be such a polynomial.

Following the proof of [13, Theorem C2] we set

                1(x, a) : (x = a),

the abelian subgroup generated by g and xi is cyclic for i = 1, 2, 3 and it follows that there
